lessons.title: What Is MIS? Data, Information and Systems
lessons.content:
Imagine you run a small grocery shop in Mohammadpur. Every day you sell rice, oil, eggs and biscuits. You write each sale in a khata: 2 kg rice, 1 litre oil, 12 eggs. At the end of the month you open the khata and it is just pages and pages of numbers. Then one evening you sit down and add things up. You notice that oil always runs out around the 20th of the month, and that you lose sales because of it. That one small discovery changes how you order stock next month. Without knowing it, you have just done Management Information Systems. You turned messy records into something useful, and then you used it to make a better decision.

What this course is about: Management Information Systems, or MIS, is the study of how organizations use information, people and technology together to run their daily work, make decisions and compete. It sits between computer science and business. A pure CSE course asks how a database or a network works inside. MIS asks a different question: when a bank, a garments factory or a shop uses that database or network, what problem does it solve, who uses it, what decisions does it support, and is it worth the money?

Why a CSE student should care: Most software in the world is not games or operating systems. It is business software: billing, payroll, inventory, banking, e-commerce, hospital records, school results. If you join a software company in Dhaka, there is a good chance you will build systems for banks, telecom companies, garments exporters or government offices. The best engineers are not the ones who only write clean code. They are the ones who understand why the client needs the system and what the client will do with the output. MIS gives you that view from the manager's chair.

Data: Let us start from zero. Data is raw facts, recorded but not yet organized or interpreted. A single sale like 2 kg rice, 140 taka, 10 March is data. A temperature reading of 31 degrees is data. A customer phone number is data. Data on its own does not tell you much. It is like bricks lying on the ground: useful material, but not yet a house.

Information: Information is data that has been processed, organized or put into context so that it means something to someone. If you take all the rice sales of March and add them up, you get: rice sales in March were 420 kg, up 15 percent from February. Now a manager can understand it and act on it. The key point is that information is data plus meaning for a purpose. The same data can become different information for different people. The cashier wants today's total; the owner wants the monthly trend.

Knowledge: Knowledge is the understanding, experience and rules of thumb that tell you how to use information. The shop owner knows that rice sales rise before Eid and during Ramadan, and that he should order extra stock two weeks earlier. That know-how did not come from one report. It came from years of seeing information and learning patterns. Some textbooks add a fourth level, wisdom, which is the judgment to know which actions are right and worth taking. You can remember the ladder as data, then information, then knowledge, then wisdom, with each step adding more meaning and more human judgment.

A tiny worked example: Suppose a pharmacy records these sales of paracetamol strips for one week: 30, 32, 29, 31, 85, 90, 88. Those seven numbers are data. Processing them, we see the average for the first four days was about 30 and the last three days was about 88. That comparison is information. The pharmacist remembers that a dengue and fever season usually pushes such demand up, so she orders more stock and talks to her supplier early. That use of experience is knowledge. Notice how each step needed something new: processing for information, and human understanding for knowledge.

What a system is: A system is a set of parts that work together to reach a goal. Every system has inputs, processing and outputs. A rice mill takes paddy as input, processes it by husking and polishing, and outputs rice. Most systems also have feedback: information about the output that goes back to adjust the input or processing. If the rice comes out broken, the miller adjusts the machine. Systems also have a boundary that separates them from their environment, the world outside that affects them, such as customers, suppliers and government rules.

What an information system is: An information system, or IS, is a set of interrelated components that collect (input), process, store and distribute information to support decision making, coordination and control in an organization. Input captures raw data, such as a barcode scan at a supershop counter. Processing turns it into meaningful form, such as adding up a bill and reducing stock. Output delivers the result to the people who need it, such as the printed receipt and the daily sales report. Feedback returns output to the right people to correct the input or the process, such as a report showing a stock count that does not match the shelves.

The four parts of an IS: It helps to think of every information system as four parts working together. People: the users, managers, data entry staff and IT team. Processes or procedures: the steps and rules people follow, such as how a refund is approved. Technology: the hardware, software and networks. Data: the facts the system stores and works on. If any one part is weak, the whole system fails. A brilliant app is useless if staff are not trained, and a well-trained team suffers if the data is full of errors.

IS is not the same as IT: Information technology, or IT, means the hardware and software an organization uses: computers, servers, phones, databases, networks and programs. An information system is bigger. It includes IT, but also the people, the organization and the business processes around it. A useful comparison: a hammer, nails and wood are like IT, while the house is like the information system. You can buy the most expensive tools and still build a bad house. Many organizations in Bangladesh and everywhere have spent money on computers and software and got little value because they ignored training, process change and data quality.

Information systems need not be computerized: A paper attendance register in a school is an information system too: it has input (teacher marks students), storage (the register), processing (counting absences) and output (a list of students who missed too many classes). Computers just make the processing much faster, cheaper and more accurate, and they let many people share the same data at the same time. In this course, when we say information system, we usually mean a computer-based one, but the ideas came from paper systems first.

The three dimensions view: Many MIS textbooks describe information systems as having three dimensions. The organization dimension covers people, structure, business processes and culture. The management dimension covers how managers set strategy, make decisions and solve problems. The technology dimension covers hardware, software, data management and networking. A good MIS professional looks at all three. A purely technical person sees only the third one, and that is exactly the gap this course tries to fill.

Why organizations invest in IS: Businesses usually spend on information systems for a few strategic reasons. First, operational excellence: doing the same work faster and cheaper, like a bank processing thousands of transfers per minute. Second, new products, services and business models: bKash built a whole service on mobile phones and agent networks. Third, customer and supplier intimacy: knowing customers well enough to serve them better. Fourth, improved decision making: managers who see accurate data in time make fewer guesses. Fifth, competitive advantage: doing something better than rivals. Sixth, survival: sometimes a business must use IT just because the law or the market demands it, such as banks connecting to national payment systems.

Real life example 1, a supershop: Think about a supershop chain in Dhaka. At the counter, a barcode scanner reads each item. That is input. The point-of-sale software looks up the price, adds the bill, applies discounts and reduces the stock count. That is processing and storage. The customer gets a receipt and the system records the sale. That is output. At night, the system prepares a report for each branch manager: best-selling items, items running low, cash collected. Head office sees a summary of all branches. When the report shows that a branch keeps running out of eggs on Friday morning, the manager changes the delivery schedule. That is feedback and a decision. People, process, technology and data all worked together.

Real life example 2, a garments factory: A garments exporter in Gazipur receives an order for 50,000 shirts from a foreign buyer. The merchandising team enters the order. The system works out how much fabric, thread and buttons are needed and checks what is in stock. Production supervisors enter how many pieces each line finishes per hour. Management sees a daily report: line 4 is behind target by 12 percent. They move workers or plan overtime so that the shipment is not late. Without the system, they might only discover the delay a week before shipping, when it is too late.

The MIS field and its roots: MIS grew because organizations had more data than people could handle by hand. Early business computers in the 1950s and 1960s did mostly accounting and payroll, which is transaction processing. Later, managers wanted summary reports, which gave rise to management reporting systems. Then came decision support, executive dashboards, enterprise systems that link the whole company, the internet and e-commerce, and today cloud, mobile and data analytics. This course follows roughly the same path: from basic types of systems to strategy, security and digital transformation.

Course map: In the next lessons we will look at how organizations are structured and how IS fits into them, what makes information valuable, and what business processes are. Then we will study the main types of information systems: transaction processing systems, management reporting systems, decision support systems, executive support systems and knowledge management systems. After that come decision making, IT infrastructure, cloud, data and business intelligence, networks, e-commerce, and enterprise systems like ERP, SCM and CRM. We finish with competitive strategy, ethics and privacy, security and controls, the value of IS projects and digital transformation. Database design and SQL were covered in the DBMS course, and the detailed steps of building a system belong to System Analysis and Design and Software Engineering, so here we only touch them from a manager's view.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up data and information. Remember: data is raw; information is processed and meaningful to someone; and the same fact can be data for one person and information for another. Another common mistake is to say an information system is just computers and software. That is IT, not IS. Exams often ask: define data, information and knowledge with examples; draw the input-processing-output-feedback model of an information system; explain the difference between IS and IT; and list the components of an information system. Use a small example from a shop, bank or factory in every answer. Examiners love concrete examples.

Recap: Data is raw facts; information is data processed into meaning for a purpose; knowledge is the experience to use information well. A system has input, processing, output and feedback inside a boundary. An information system collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support decisions and control, and it is made of people, processes, technology and data. IT is only the technology part. Organizations invest in IS for efficiency, new products, closer customers and suppliers, better decisions, competitive advantage and survival. Keep the shop owner and his khata in mind: MIS is simply that habit of turning records into decisions, done at the scale of a whole organization.
key_points: Data is raw facts; information is data processed and put in context so it means something to someone; knowledge is the experience to use information well.
A system has inputs, processing, outputs and feedback, inside a boundary and an environment.
An information system collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support decisions, coordination and control.
Every IS has four parts: people, processes, technology and data; a weakness in any one breaks the whole.
IT is only the hardware, software and networks; IS includes IT plus people, organization and processes.
Information systems have organization, management and technology dimensions.
Businesses invest in IS for operational excellence, new products and models, customer and supplier intimacy, better decisions, competitive advantage and survival.
MIS asks what problem a system solves, who uses it and whether it is worth it, not only how it works inside.
lessons.tip: For every new idea in this course, pick one real organization you know, like a local shop, your university office or bKash, and ask: what is the input, what is the output, and which decision does it help? It turns theory into something you can picture.
lessons.task: Choose one place you visit often, such as a pharmacy, a canteen or a mobile recharge shop. On paper, write three pieces of data it records, one piece of information it could make from that data, and one decision the owner could make with it. Then name its people, process, technology and data.

quiz.q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
options: A single receipt showing 2 kg rice sold
A phone number typed into a form
A report showing rice sales rose 15 percent this month
A barcode on a biscuit packet
quiz.explain: The monthly report has processed many sales into a meaningful comparison, so it is information. The others are raw facts.

quiz.q: What are the four parts of an information system used in this lesson?
quiz.explain: An IS is people following processes, using technology, working on data. Hardware and software alone are only the technology part.

quiz.q: What is the best way to describe the difference between IT and IS?
options: They are two names for the same thing
IT includes IS plus people and processes
IS is only paper-based, IT is only computer-based
IS includes IT plus the people, organization and processes around it
quiz.explain: IT is the technology; an information system is the whole working system of technology, people, processes and data.

quiz.q: In a system, what is feedback?
options: The raw material that enters the system
Output information sent back to adjust the input or processing
The boundary between the system and its environment
The final product delivered to customers
quiz.explain: Feedback returns information about the output so that people can correct the input or the process.

quiz.q: A shop owner knows from years of experience to order extra rice two weeks before Eid. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Knowing how to use information and patterns from experience to act is knowledge.

lessons.title: Information Systems in Organizations
lessons.content:
Think about a big wedding in a Bangladeshi family. One uncle handles the cooks and the biryani. An aunt handles the guest list and the gifts. A cousin handles the decorators and the lights. The eldest person in the family makes the big calls: which community centre, how many guests, how much money. Everyone has a job, everyone reports to someone, and they all keep calling each other on the phone to stay in sync. If the phone calls stop, the biryani arrives before the plates, and the lights go up after the guests leave. An organization works exactly like this, only every single day and with hundreds or thousands of people. Information systems are the phone calls, the lists and the notebooks that keep everyone in sync.

What an organization is: An organization is a stable, formal group of people and resources that takes inputs from its environment, processes them, and produces outputs, with a shared goal. A garments factory takes fabric, labour and electricity and produces shirts. A bank takes deposits and produces loans and payment services. A university takes students, teachers and money and produces graduates and research. That technical definition is the same input, processing and output idea we used for systems in lesson 1, which is no accident: an organization is itself a big system.

The behavioural view: An organization is also a collection of people with rights, duties, habits, friendships and politics. A purely technical view says the factory turns fabric into shirts. The behavioural view notices that the cutting section and the sewing section blame each other for delays, that an old supervisor resists any new software, and that people follow unwritten rules as much as written ones. Every real information system project meets both views. Ignoring the behavioural side is one of the most common reasons good software fails in real offices.

Structure and hierarchy: Most organizations are arranged as a hierarchy, a pyramid of authority. At the top sits a small group, such as the board and managing director. Below them are a larger number of managers, and at the bottom the largest group, the staff who do the daily work. Each person reports to a boss, and orders flow down while reports flow up. On paper this is drawn as an organization chart. Information systems often follow the same shape: data is captured at the bottom and summarized as it moves up.

Three levels of management: MIS books usually split an organization into levels, and each level needs different information. Operational level: supervisors and staff who run day-to-day activities, such as a line supervisor counting pieces or a bank teller handling deposits. They need detailed, current, accurate data. Middle management (tactical level): branch managers, department heads and factory managers who plan and control over weeks and months. They need summaries, comparisons and exception reports, such as which line is behind target this week. Senior management (strategic level): directors and the CEO who set long-term direction over years. They need very summarized information, trends and outside information about markets and competitors. Some books also add a knowledge worker level for engineers, designers and analysts who create new knowledge.

A quick check of levels: Ask who is making the decision and how far ahead it looks. Approving a customer's withdrawal of 5,000 taka today is operational. Deciding how many tellers a branch needs next quarter is tactical. Deciding whether to open 50 new branches or invest in a mobile app instead is strategic. Notice how the information gets less detailed and more future-focused as you go up.

Functional areas: Across the levels, organizations are divided into departments by function. Sales and marketing finds customers, sets prices, runs promotions and takes orders. Production or manufacturing (in a service company, operations) makes the product or delivers the service. Finance and accounting manages money: budgets, payments, salaries, loans and financial reports. Human resources (HR) hires, trains, pays and keeps the staff. Many organizations also have purchasing, logistics, research and development, and IT departments. Each function has its own information systems, such as a sales order system, a production scheduling system, a payroll system and a recruitment system.

The grid view: Put levels on one side and functions on the other, and you get a grid. For example, in finance: the operational level runs accounts payable and receivable, the middle level makes budgets and compares spending with budget, and the senior level plans long-term investment and profit. In HR: the operational level tracks attendance and payroll, the middle level analyses overtime and turnover by department, and the senior level plans how many people the company will need in five years. This grid is a handy way to answer exam questions about which system serves whom.

The problem of silos: When each department builds its own system, it usually keeps its own copy of the data. Sales has one customer list, accounts has another, and delivery has a third, each with slightly different addresses and phone numbers. These separate islands are called silos. They cause errors, duplicated typing and slow work, because one department has to phone another to check something. Much of the history of MIS, especially enterprise systems in lessons 16 to 18, is about breaking down silos with shared data and cross-functional processes.

How IS changes organizations, flatter structures: Middle managers once spent much of their time collecting reports from below and passing summaries up. When a system can show senior managers live numbers directly, fewer layers are needed. Organizations can become flatter, with fewer levels and each manager supervising more people. Decisions can also be pushed down: a branch manager with good data can decide on the spot instead of waiting for head office.

How IS changes organizations, speed and reach: Information systems reduce the cost of getting information and of coordinating people. A transaction that once needed a form, a signature and a courier now happens in seconds. Work can be spread across places: a buying house in Dhaka can coordinate with factories in Gazipur and Chattogram and with buyers in Europe the same day. Information systems also let organizations outsource work, because coordinating with an outside partner becomes cheap. Economists describe this as lowering transaction costs and agency costs, the costs of dealing with outsiders and of supervising employees.

How IS changes organizations, resistance: Change is not automatic. A new system changes who knows what, who decides what and whose job is still needed, so people may resist it quietly. An accounts clerk who was the only one who understood the old ledger may feel threatened by a system that everyone can query. That is why successful IS projects train people, explain the purpose and involve users early. We will return to change management in lesson 24.

The IS department: Most medium and large organizations have a department responsible for information systems. The CIO (Chief Information Officer) is a senior manager who leads IS strategy and makes sure technology serves business goals. Systems analysts act as translators between business people and the technical team: they study the business problem and turn it into requirements, a role covered in detail in System Analysis and Design. Programmers and software engineers build and maintain the software. Network and system administrators keep servers, networks and devices running. Database administrators look after the databases. Many organizations also have an information security officer and a help desk for user support. Small businesses may have one IT person, or none, and rely on outside vendors.

End users and shared responsibility: Information systems are not only the IS department's job. End users in sales, finance and HR use the systems daily, enter much of the data, and know the business rules best. Today many also build their own small tools with spreadsheets and cloud apps. Good organizations treat IS as a partnership: business managers decide what the system must achieve, and the IS team decides how to build and run it well.

Real life example 1, a commercial bank: At the operational level, tellers and the core banking system record deposits, withdrawals and transfers in real time at every branch. At the middle level, a branch manager sees a daily report of new accounts, loan collections and overdue loans, and calls the officers responsible for the worst cases. At the senior level, the board looks at monthly summaries of total deposits, profit and risk across all branches, plus outside information about interest rates and competitors, to decide whether to expand agent banking. The same transaction data feeds all three levels, but each sees it in a different shape.

Real life example 2, a garments exporter: Functionally, merchandising handles buyers and orders, production runs cutting, sewing and finishing, commercial handles letters of credit and export documents, accounts handles payments, and HR handles thousands of workers' attendance and wages. If HR's attendance system does not talk to production planning, the factory may plan a big order for a week when many workers are on leave. Connecting these systems helps managers see the whole picture instead of the view from one silo.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes mix up the levels of management with the functional areas. Levels are vertical (operational, middle, senior); functions are horizontal (sales, production, finance, HR). Another mistake is to think that information for senior managers must be more detailed because they are more important. The opposite is true: they need more summarized, future-oriented and external information. Exams often ask: describe the levels of management and the information each needs; explain how information systems make organizations flatter; list the functional areas with one system each; and describe the roles in an IS department such as the CIO and systems analyst.

Culture and standard procedures: Every organization also has a culture, the shared beliefs about how things are done, and standard operating procedures, the precise rules for routine work such as how a purchase is approved. A new system usually has to fit into these, or change them on purpose. If a factory culture says every purchase needs the owner's personal signature, an online approval system that skips him will be ignored, no matter how well it is coded. Smart designers learn the culture first and then decide which procedures the system will keep, change or remove.

A thinking question: Imagine a supershop chain gives every branch manager a phone app showing live sales and stock. What could happen to the regional manager layer between the branches and head office? Would branch managers need to wait for permission to reorder? Thinking through questions like these is exactly how MIS people predict the effect of a new system before it is built.

Recap: An organization is both a technical system that turns inputs into outputs and a social group with habits and politics. It is usually a hierarchy with operational, middle and senior levels, each needing different information, and it is split into functional areas like sales, production, finance and HR. Separate systems for each function create data silos. Information systems lower the cost of information and coordination, so organizations become flatter, faster and more able to work across places and partners, but people may resist the change. The IS department, led by a CIO, works with end users to build and run systems. Remember the wedding: everyone has a role, and information is what keeps the biryani and the plates arriving at the same time.
key_points: An organization is a technical system turning inputs into outputs and also a social group with habits, rules and politics.
Management has three main levels: operational (daily, detailed), middle or tactical (weeks to months, summaries and exceptions) and senior or strategic (years, trends and outside information).
Functional areas are sales and marketing, production or operations, finance and accounting, and human resources, each with its own systems.
Separate departmental systems create data silos with duplicated and conflicting data.
IS lowers the cost of information and coordination, making organizations flatter and faster and making outsourcing easier.
New systems change power and jobs, so people may resist; training and involvement matter.
The IS department includes the CIO, systems analysts, programmers, network and database administrators, security staff and the help desk.
Senior managers need more summarized, future-focused and external information, not more detail.
lessons.tip: Draw the level-by-function grid once on a single page and fill in one example system in each box. That one sheet answers a large share of short exam questions in this course.
lessons.task: Pick an organization you know well, such as your university, a bank branch or a relative's business. Draw a simple organization chart with three levels, then write one decision taken at each level and the information that decision needs.

quiz.q: Which decision is a strategic (senior management) decision in a bank?
options: Deciding how many tellers a branch needs next quarter
Fixing a wrong entry in today's ledger
Deciding whether to expand into agent banking across the country
quiz.explain: Strategic decisions set long-term direction for the whole organization. The other options are operational or tactical.

quiz.q: What kind of information do senior managers mostly need?
options: Highly summarized, trend and outside information
Every single transaction in full detail
Only the hardware list of the IT department
quiz.explain: Senior managers look years ahead, so they need summaries, trends and information about markets and competitors.

quiz.q: What is a data silo?
options: A secure backup room for servers
A separate departmental system with its own copy of data that does not connect to others
A large data warehouse used by senior managers
quiz.explain: Silos are isolated departmental systems whose data is duplicated and often conflicting.

quiz.q: Why can information systems make organizations flatter?
options: Because computers replace all senior managers
Because managers can see data directly, so fewer middle layers are needed to pass reports up
Because staff no longer need any supervision
quiz.explain: When systems deliver information directly, fewer middle layers are needed to collect and pass it on, and each manager can supervise more people.

quiz.q: Who acts as the translator between business users and the technical team?
quiz.explain: Systems analysts study business problems and turn them into requirements that the technical team can build.

lessons.title: What Makes Information Good and Valuable
lessons.content:
Imagine you are going to Sylhet by train, and you ask a friend what time it leaves. He says 7:30. You arrive at 7:25 and the train has already gone, because the schedule changed last month and your friend's information was old. Another day you ask the station and they give you a 40-page printed timetable for every train in the country. The answer is in there somewhere, but you miss the train while searching. In both cases you had information, but it was not good information. The first was not timely or accurate; the second was not concise or relevant. This lesson is about what makes information actually useful, and how to think about how much it is worth.

Why quality matters: In lesson 1 we said information is data processed into meaning for a purpose. But not all information helps. A manager who acts on wrong, late or confusing information can make a worse decision than one who simply guesses. Information systems cost money to build and run, so the organization must make sure the information they produce is good enough to be worth that cost. MIS textbooks describe this with a list of quality characteristics and a simple idea of the value of information.

Accurate: Accurate information is free from errors. If the stock report says 200 cartons of soybean oil are in the warehouse but there are really 20, the purchase manager will not reorder and the shop will run out. Accuracy depends first on the data entered. A single wrong digit typed at the counter, or a scanner that reads the wrong barcode, flows into every report built from it. Systems improve accuracy with validation rules, such as refusing a negative quantity or checking that a phone number has 11 digits.

Timely: Timely information arrives when it is needed, not after the decision is already made. A daily sales report delivered three days late is almost useless to a supershop deciding what to put on the shelves tomorrow. Timeliness has two parts: how fresh the information is (how recent the data) and how fast it reaches the user. Real-time systems such as mobile banking show balances instantly; a monthly report can be perfectly timely for a board meeting that happens once a month.

Complete: Complete information contains all the important facts. A loan officer who sees a customer's salary but not his existing loans may approve a loan he cannot repay. Completeness does not mean including everything; it means not leaving out what matters for the decision.

Relevant: Relevant information is related to the decision at hand. A production manager deciding overtime for next week needs line output and order deadlines. He does not need the marketing team's Facebook ad statistics. Irrelevant information is not harmless: it hides the relevant parts and wastes time.

Concise and well presented: Concise information gives what is needed without unnecessary detail. A one-page summary with a small chart can be more useful than a hundred pages of transactions. Presentation matters too: the same numbers can be clear in a sorted table or a simple graph and confusing in a long paragraph. Good systems let different users see different levels of detail, which is the idea behind drill-down reports in lesson 6.

Accessible, verifiable and secure: Accessible information is easy for authorized people to get, in the right format and place, such as on a phone for a field officer. Verifiable information can be checked, for example by tracing a total back to the transactions behind it or by comparing two sources. Secure information is protected from people who should not see or change it. These three pull in different directions: making information easier to access can make it harder to secure, so systems balance them with logins and permissions.

Other qualities in textbooks: Different books add a few more words: reliable (comes from trustworthy sources and methods), economical (worth what it costs to produce), flexible (usable for more than one purpose) and simple (not more complex than needed). You do not need to memorize one exact list. You need to understand the idea that information has several dimensions of quality, and that a weakness in any one can ruin a decision.

The three dimensions grouping: A neat way to organize these qualities is by dimension. Time dimension: timeliness, currency (up to date) and frequency (how often it is delivered). Content dimension: accuracy, relevance, completeness and conciseness. Form dimension: clarity, presentation, detail level and media (printed, screen, phone). If an exam asks you to classify quality attributes, this time, content and form grouping is a safe answer.

Garbage in, garbage out: GIGO is one of the oldest rules in computing. If the input data is wrong, the output will be wrong too, no matter how clever the program is. A beautiful dashboard built on badly entered sales data will confidently show the wrong numbers, and confident wrong numbers are dangerous because people trust anything that looks official. That is why many organizations spend real money on data quality: training data entry staff, validation checks, and regular cleaning of duplicate or outdated records. We look at data quality and governance in lesson 11.

Internal and external sources: Information comes from two kinds of sources. Internal information is produced inside the organization: sales, stock, salaries, production output and complaints. It is usually easier to check because the organization controls how it is collected. External information comes from outside: prices of competitors, exchange rates, government rules, weather, news about buyers' markets. It is often less complete and harder to verify, yet senior managers depend on it heavily. A garments owner deciding whether to take a large order must combine internal information (spare line capacity) with external information (cotton prices and the buyer's reputation). Good information systems bring both kinds together in one view.

Quality is judged by the user: The same report can be excellent for one person and poor for another. A detailed list of every overdue loan is perfect for the recovery officer who must call each customer, but it is far too detailed for the managing director, who only needs the total and the trend. So before designing any report, ask three questions: who will use it, which decision will it support, and how often is that decision made. The answers tell you the right level of detail, the right timing and the right format. This user-first thinking is the heart of MIS.

The value of information: Information has value only if it changes a decision for the better. A simple way to measure it is: value of information equals the value of the outcome with the information, minus the value of the outcome without it, minus the cost of getting the information. If the result is positive, the information was worth getting. If the information would not change what you do, its value is zero, however interesting it may be.

Worked example, a late stock report: A supershop branch sells about 100 packets of a popular biscuit each day and earns 5 taka profit per packet. The stock report reaches the manager every three days. One week, the stock runs out on Monday morning, but the report arrives on Wednesday evening, and new stock comes on Thursday. The shop loses about three days of sales: 3 x 100 x 5 = 1,500 taka of profit, on just one product. If a daily stock alert system costs 200 taka per day per branch and prevents such gaps across, say, 20 popular products, the benefit can easily exceed the cost. If the shop only had two slow-moving products, the same system might not be worth it. The numbers decide.

Worked example, a loan decision: Suppose a bank approves 1,000 small loans a year, and without a credit check about 5 percent go bad, losing 50,000 taka each on average. That is 50 bad loans and 25 lakh taka lost. A credit information check costs 300 taka per application, or 3 lakh taka per year. If the check helps the bank avoid even 10 of the bad loans, it saves 5 lakh taka, so the net value is about 2 lakh taka. These numbers are made up to show the method, but the logic is exactly how managers judge whether information is worth paying for.

Information overload: More information is not always better. When people receive more than they can process, they slow down, miss important points or ignore everything. A branch manager who gets 40 automatic emails a day stops reading them, including the one warning about a cash shortage. Good information systems filter, summarize and highlight exceptions so that people see what matters. This is why exception reporting and dashboards exist.

Trade-offs between qualities: You cannot maximize every quality at once. Making information more accurate may take more checking, which makes it less timely. Making it more complete may make it less concise. Real-time information is expensive; a nightly batch report is cheaper but older. Managers decide what level of each quality is good enough for each decision. A stock trader needs second-by-second prices; an HR planner is fine with monthly headcount.

Real life example 1, mobile banking balance: When you check your bKash or bank app balance, you expect it to be accurate to the last taka and instantly updated after a transaction. Here accuracy and timeliness are critical, because people make payments based on that number, and a wrong or stale balance could let someone spend money they do not have or block a valid payment. The system is designed so that every transaction updates the balance immediately and the history can be checked line by line, which also makes it verifiable.

Real life example 2, a garments buyer's order status: A foreign buyer asks a Bangladeshi garments exporter where her order stands. If the merchandiser checks three spreadsheets and sends a long email full of numbers about cutting, sewing and washing for all orders, the information is accurate but not concise or relevant to her. If the system instead shows one line, order 4521: 70 percent sewn, expected shipment on time, with a link to details, the same data becomes much more useful. Good information is shaped for the person who uses it.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse timely with fast. Timely means available when needed for the decision; a quarterly report can be timely. Another mistake is thinking more information is always more valuable; information that does not change a decision has no decision value, and too much creates overload. Exams commonly ask: list and explain the characteristics of good information with examples; explain GIGO; group qualities into time, content and form; and calculate or discuss the value of information with a simple example. Always link each quality to a decision that would go wrong without it.

Recap: Good information is accurate, timely, complete, relevant, concise, accessible, verifiable and secure, and these qualities can be grouped into time, content and form dimensions. Poor input data leads to poor output, which is the GIGO rule. Information is valuable only when it improves a decision by more than it costs to produce, and we can estimate that value with simple numbers. Too much information causes overload, and qualities trade off against each other, so managers decide what is good enough for each decision. Remember the Sylhet train: old information made you late, and too much information made you late too.
key_points: Good information is accurate, timely, complete, relevant, concise, accessible, verifiable and secure.
Qualities can be grouped into time (timeliness, currency, frequency), content (accuracy, relevance, completeness, conciseness) and form (clarity, presentation, detail, media).
Garbage in, garbage out: wrong input data produces wrong output however good the program is.
Value of information = value of the outcome with it minus value without it minus its cost.
Information that does not change a decision has no decision value.
Too much information causes overload; systems should filter, summarize and highlight exceptions.
Qualities trade off: more accuracy or completeness can cost timeliness, conciseness or money.
Timely means available when the decision needs it, not necessarily real time.
lessons.tip: When you learn each quality, attach a tiny story of a decision going wrong without it. In exams, a quality plus a one-line example scores far better than a bare list.
lessons.task: Open one report or notice you received recently, such as a result sheet, a bank SMS or a class schedule. Rate it out of 5 on accurate, timely, complete, relevant and concise, and write one change that would make it more useful.

quiz.q: A daily sales report reaches a shop manager three days late. Which quality is mainly missing?
quiz.explain: The report may be correct, but it arrives after the decisions it should support, so it is not timely.

quiz.q: What does GIGO mean?
options: Wrong input data produces wrong output
quiz.explain: Garbage in, garbage out: a system cannot produce correct output from incorrect input.

quiz.q: Information that will not change any decision has what decision value?
options: Very high, because it is interesting
quiz.explain: Value of information comes from improving a decision. If the decision stays the same, there is no decision value.

quiz.q: Which grouping of quality attributes is commonly used in MIS textbooks?
quiz.explain: Information qualities are often grouped into time, content and form dimensions.

quiz.q: A manager receives 40 automatic emails a day and stops reading them. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Too much information makes people miss important points; good systems filter and highlight exceptions.

lessons.title: Business Processes
lessons.content:
Think about ordering a kacchi biryani from a restaurant through a food delivery app. You choose the dish and pay. The restaurant gets the order on a tablet and starts cooking. A rider is assigned, picks up the packet, rides through traffic and hands it to you. You rate the food, and the restaurant gets its money a few days later. You saw one tap and one packet. Behind it, a chain of steps ran across at least three organizations and many people. That chain, a set of steps that together create something of value for a customer, is called a business process. Organizations are really bundles of processes, and information systems exist mostly to make those processes faster, cheaper and more reliable.

What a business process is: A business process is a set of logically related activities, done in a defined order, that turns inputs into an output of value to a customer or to the organization. It also includes the way work is coordinated: who does each step, what information they need and what rules they follow. Examples are taking a customer order, hiring a new employee, paying a supplier, approving a loan or launching a new product. Every process has a start (a trigger), a sequence of activities, and an end (a result someone cares about).

The parts of a process: Inputs are the materials, money and information that enter, such as a customer's order and the stock on hand. Activities are the steps that transform them, such as checking credit, packing, invoicing. Outputs are the results, such as a delivered parcel and a paid invoice. Resources are the people, machines and systems that do the work. Rules decide what happens at each decision point, such as orders above 1 lakh taka need a manager's approval. And there is always a customer of the process, internal or external, who judges whether the output is good.

Why processes matter: A company's products can be copied, but a really good process is harder to copy. A shop that can take an order at 10 am and deliver by 6 pm has an advantage that comes from its process, not its products. Processes also decide cost: every extra hand-off, signature or re-typing adds time and money. When managers say they want to improve efficiency, they usually mean improving processes.

Functional processes: Some processes stay mostly inside one department. In sales and marketing: identifying customers, making customers aware of the product, selling. In manufacturing: assembling the product, checking quality, producing bills of materials. In finance and accounting: paying creditors, creating financial statements, managing cash. In HR: hiring, evaluating job performance, enrolling employees in benefits. These are useful, but the most important processes usually cross departments.

Cross-functional processes: Most valuable processes run across several departments. Order fulfillment is the classic example. Sales receives the order. Accounting checks the customer's credit and later sends the invoice. The warehouse or production team makes or picks the goods. Shipping delivers them. Accounting records the payment. No single department owns the whole thing, so if each department only optimizes its own step, the customer can still wait a long time between steps. Information systems that share one set of data across departments are the main tool for coordinating cross-functional processes.

Order to cash, walked through: Order to cash covers everything from a customer order to money in the bank. Step 1, receive the order: a customer orders 500 cartons of noodles from a distributor. Step 2, check credit: the system sees the customer already owes 3 lakh taka with a limit of 5 lakh, and this order is worth 1.5 lakh, so it is allowed. Step 3, check stock and reserve goods: 500 cartons are reserved in the warehouse. Step 4, pick, pack and ship: the warehouse prints a picking list and the truck leaves with a delivery note. Step 5, invoice: an invoice for 1.5 lakh taka is generated. Step 6, receive payment: the customer pays by bank transfer within 30 days. Step 7, record and reconcile: accounting matches the payment to the invoice and the customer's balance updates. If any step is slow or wrong, cash arrives late or customers get angry.

Procure to pay, walked through: Procure to pay is the buying side, from needing something to paying the supplier. Step 1, a requisition: the store keeper of a garments factory sees that sewing thread is low and raises a purchase requisition. Step 2, approval: the purchase manager approves it. Step 3, purchase order: a PO is sent to the supplier for 2,000 cones at an agreed price. Step 4, goods receipt: when the thread arrives, the store counts it and records a goods received note. Step 5, invoice: the supplier sends a bill. Step 6, three-way match: accounts compares the purchase order, the goods received note and the invoice. If the PO says 2,000 cones at 80 taka, the receipt says 1,900 arrived and the invoice charges for 2,000, the mismatch is caught and only 1,900 are paid. Step 7, payment. This three-way match is a simple control that stops many errors and frauds.

How IS helps processes, automation: The first way information systems help is by automating steps that people did by hand. A system can check credit limits in milliseconds, calculate invoices without arithmetic mistakes and send payment reminders automatically. Automation makes existing steps faster and cheaper, but it keeps the same process design.

How IS helps processes, sharing and parallel work: The second way is by sharing information so that steps that used to be done one after another can happen at the same time, and hand-offs disappear. If sales, warehouse and accounts all see the same order in the same database, the warehouse can start picking while accounts prepares the invoice. Nobody has to retype the order or carry paper from desk to desk. Shared information also lets people check status: a customer can track an order without phoning anyone.

How IS helps processes, redesign: The third and most powerful way is enabling completely new process designs. Before mobile wallets, sending money to a village meant a bank visit, a slip, a queue and a trip by the receiver to a branch. With a mobile financial service the process becomes: type the number, type the amount, enter the PIN, done, and the receiver cashes out at a nearby agent. That is not the old process done faster; it is a different process that only exists because of information technology.

Business process reengineering (BPR): BPR means radically rethinking and redesigning a process from scratch to get dramatic improvements in cost, quality, speed and service. Instead of asking how to do the current steps faster, it asks why we do these steps at all. A famous textbook-style example: an accounts payable department that spent its time matching documents could be redesigned so that payment is triggered when goods are received and matched to the order in the database, removing the need to wait for and chase paper invoices. BPR can deliver big gains, but it is risky and disruptive: jobs change, people resist, and many reengineering projects failed because they ignored the people side.

Continuous improvement: The opposite style is continuous, incremental improvement: many small changes made steadily over time, often suggested by the people doing the work. Ideas such as Total Quality Management (TQM) and the Japanese term kaizen describe this approach. It is less dramatic than BPR, but also less risky. In practice, organizations mix both: a big redesign when a new system arrives, followed by steady small improvements.

Analysing and improving a process: A practical method has a few steps. First, identify the process to change, usually one that hurts customers or costs a lot. Second, map the current process (the as-is): list the steps, who does each, how long it takes and where it waits. Third, measure it: total time, cost, error rate. Fourth, design the new process (the to-be), removing unnecessary steps, approvals and re-typing. Fifth, implement it with the new system and train people. Sixth, keep measuring. Process maps are usually drawn as simple flowcharts or swimlane diagrams, with one lane per department, so you can see every hand-off. The formal modelling tools, such as data flow diagrams, belong to System Analysis and Design, so here we keep it to a manager's sketch.

A tiny measurement example: Suppose a bank's account opening process has 6 steps that take 10, 5, 30, 5, 120 and 10 minutes, and most of the 120 minutes is waiting for a manager's signature in another room. Total time: 180 minutes, of which only about 60 minutes is real work. If a tablet-based form sends the application to the manager's screen with a digital approval, the waiting step might drop to 10 minutes, bringing the total to about 70 minutes. Finding the waiting, not the working, is usually where the biggest gains hide.

Real life example 1, an e-commerce return: A customer on an online marketplace receives the wrong size of shoes. The return process includes: the customer requests a return in the app, the system checks the return policy, a pickup is scheduled, the courier collects the parcel, the warehouse inspects it, the refund is approved, and the money goes back to the customer's wallet or bank. If each step is tracked in the system, the customer can see where the return is, and the company can measure which step causes delay. Without that tracking, the customer keeps calling the help line, which costs the company money too.

Real life example 2, a university admission: Many Bangladeshi universities moved admission online. The old process: buy a printed form from a bank, fill it by hand, submit it in person, wait for a printed list on a notice board. The new process: apply online, pay through mobile banking, download an admit card, check the result on the website or by SMS. The new design removed queues and travel, and let the university process far more applicants with the same staff. It is a good example of redesign, not just automation.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse a process with a department. A department is a group of people; a process is a flow of work that often crosses many departments. Another mistake is to think that buying software automatically improves processes; automating a bad process just makes mistakes faster. Exams often ask: define business process with examples; explain order to cash or procure to pay; distinguish functional and cross-functional processes; explain how IS improves processes; and compare BPR with continuous improvement. Draw a small step diagram in your answer whenever you can.

Recap: A business process is an ordered set of activities that turns inputs into valuable outputs, with people, resources and rules. Some processes are functional, but the most important, such as order to cash and procure to pay, cross departments. Information systems improve processes by automating steps, sharing information so steps run in parallel without re-typing, and enabling entirely new designs. BPR redesigns radically and riskily; continuous improvement changes things in small steady steps. Map, measure, redesign and keep measuring. And remember the biryani: one tap for you, a whole well-run process behind it.
key_points: A business process is an ordered set of related activities that turns inputs into an output of value, with people, resources and rules.
Functional processes stay mostly inside one department; cross-functional processes like order fulfillment span several.
Order to cash: order, credit check, reserve stock, ship, invoice, receive payment, reconcile.
Procure to pay: requisition, approval, purchase order, goods receipt, invoice, three-way match, payment.
IS improves processes by automating steps, sharing data so steps run in parallel, and enabling new process designs.
BPR is radical redesign for dramatic gains and is risky; continuous improvement (TQM, kaizen) makes small steady changes.
Process improvement: identify, map as-is, measure, design to-be, implement, keep measuring.
Waiting time between steps is often the biggest source of delay; automating a bad process only makes mistakes faster.
lessons.tip: Learn order to cash and procure to pay as two short stories with numbers. Almost every later topic, from ERP to controls, reuses these two processes.
lessons.task: Pick a process you go through, such as getting a semester admit card, buying something online or paying a utility bill. Write every step, who does it and roughly how long it takes or waits. Circle the longest wait and suggest one change that removes it.

quiz.q: Which is a cross-functional business process?
options: Order fulfillment from customer order to payment
A single clerk typing a letter
quiz.explain: Order fulfillment involves sales, accounts, warehouse and shipping, so it crosses several functions.

quiz.q: In procure to pay, the three-way match compares:
options: Purchase order, goods received note and supplier invoice
Customer order, credit limit and price list
Bank statement, cash book and budget
quiz.explain: Matching the order, the receipt and the invoice catches errors such as being billed for goods that never arrived.

quiz.q: What best describes business process reengineering (BPR)?
options: Small daily improvements suggested by workers
Buying faster computers for the same process
Radical redesign of a process from scratch for dramatic gains
quiz.explain: BPR rethinks why steps exist and redesigns radically; small daily improvements are continuous improvement.

quiz.q: Why can automating an existing process sometimes fail to help?
options: Automation always costs more than paper
If the process itself is badly designed, automation just repeats its problems faster
quiz.explain: Automating a bad process keeps its unnecessary steps and errors; redesign may be needed.

quiz.q: In the bank account opening example, where was most of the delay?
quiz.explain: About 120 of 180 minutes was waiting for approval; removing waiting gives the biggest gain.

lessons.title: Transaction Processing Systems (TPS)
lessons.content:
Stand for five minutes beside the cash counter of a busy supershop on a Friday evening. Beep, beep, beep: the scanner reads one item after another. A receipt prints, the customer pays by card or cash, the drawer opens and closes, and the next customer steps up. Each beep is tiny and boring. But across every counter, every branch and every day, those beeps become the most important data the company owns. They tell it what was sold, how much money came in and what is left on the shelves. The system behind those beeps is a transaction processing system, and almost every other information system in an organization is built on top of the data it collects.

What a transaction is: A transaction is a single business event that the organization must record. A sale, a purchase, a cash deposit, a withdrawal, a salary payment, a bus ticket booking, a student paying semester fees, a parcel being handed over: each is a transaction. Transactions usually involve an exchange of money, goods or services, and they change the state of the business, such as reducing stock or increasing a customer's balance.

What a TPS is: A transaction processing system is a computerized system that performs and records the daily routine transactions needed to conduct business. It sits at the operational level of the organization. Its main jobs are to capture each transaction, process it correctly, store it, and produce the documents and updates that follow, such as receipts, invoices, pay slips and updated balances. In lesson 1 terms, it is the input and processing engine for the whole organization.

The TPS cycle: Textbooks describe a transaction processing cycle with a few steps. Data collection: capturing the data of each transaction, ideally at its source, such as scanning a barcode or reading a card. Data editing: checking the data for errors, such as a missing account number or an impossible date. Data correction: asking for re-entry or fixing errors that were found. Data manipulation: calculating, sorting and summarizing, such as adding the bill and computing VAT. Data storage: saving the transaction in the database. Document production: printing or sending receipts, invoices, pay slips and reports. Follow one supershop sale through these six steps and you will never forget them.

Characteristics of a TPS: Transaction processing systems handle a very high volume of similar, routine transactions. The tasks are structured: the rules are known in advance and the same every time, such as price times quantity minus discount. Accuracy matters enormously, because errors flow into accounts and customer balances. They need to be fast and reliable, often available around the clock. They must protect data with security and keep an audit trail, a record of who did what and when, so that every number can be traced. And they are the main source of data for other systems: management reports, decision support and executive dashboards all start from TPS data.

Batch processing: In batch processing, transactions are collected over a period of time and processed together as a group, or batch. A factory might collect all the daily attendance cards and run payroll once a month. A utility company might read meters for a whole area and produce bills in one run. Batch processing is efficient for large volumes that do not need instant results, and it was the main method when computers were expensive. Its weakness is that data in the system is only as fresh as the last batch: between runs, the records are out of date.

Online (real-time) processing: In online transaction processing, often called OLTP, each transaction is processed immediately as it happens, and the database is updated at once. An ATM withdrawal must update your balance immediately, or you could withdraw the same money twice from two machines. Mobile banking, airline and bus seat booking, and online shopping carts all use online processing. It gives up-to-date information, but it needs reliable networks and systems that can handle many users at the same moment.

A mixed approach: Many organizations combine both. A supershop processes each sale online at the counter, so the receipt and stock count update instantly, but it runs heavy jobs like the nightly sales summary, supplier payments or interest calculation in batches when the system is less busy. A bank updates balances in real time but might calculate monthly interest for all accounts in one batch run. Deciding which transactions need real time and which can wait is a classic MIS design choice.

Why online processing needs special care: When thousands of people use a system at the same time, two of them may try to change the same record. Imagine two family members with a shared account each withdrawing 8,000 taka from a balance of 10,000 at the same moment. The system must make sure only one succeeds. Databases solve this with transactions that are all-or-nothing and isolated from each other, the ACID properties you studied in the DBMS course. From a manager's view, the key point is simple: a TPS must never lose a transaction or count it twice.

Point of sale (POS) systems: A POS system is the TPS at a shop counter. It includes a terminal or computer, a barcode scanner, a receipt printer, a cash drawer and often a card or QR payment device. When an item is scanned, the POS looks up the product code in the database, finds the price, adds it to the bill, applies any discount, and when the sale is completed, reduces the stock count and records the payment. A small worked example: 2 packets of milk at 90 taka, 1 bread at 60 taka and 1 kg sugar at 140 taka gives a subtotal of 380 taka. If there is a 5 percent discount, 19 taka is taken off, and the customer pays 361 taka. The stock of milk drops by 2, bread by 1 and sugar by 1, all in the same moment.

ATM systems: An ATM is a TPS that lets a customer do banking without a teller. The card and PIN identify and authenticate the customer. The ATM sends the request over a secure network to the bank's system, which checks the balance and daily limit, approves or declines, updates the account and tells the ATM to dispense cash. If the cash fails to come out after the account was debited, the system must detect this and reverse the transaction. That reversal logic is part of good TPS design: not just the happy path, but what happens when something fails halfway.

Source data automation: The less typing, the fewer errors. Source data automation means capturing data automatically, at the point where the transaction happens, using machines rather than people re-entering it later. Examples include barcode and QR scanners, magnetic stripe and chip cards, RFID tags on cartons, biometric attendance machines that read fingerprints, and optical mark readers that grade multiple choice answer sheets. Each removes a manual step where typing errors used to creep in.

Editing checks in practice: The data editing step uses simple rules that catch most typing and scanning mistakes. A range check refuses a value outside sensible limits, such as an age of 250 or a quantity of minus 3. A format check makes sure a mobile number has 11 digits and starts with 01. A completeness check refuses a form with a required field left empty. A consistency check compares fields, such as a delivery date that is earlier than the order date. A check digit is an extra digit calculated from the other digits of a code, as in product barcodes, so that a single wrong digit or two swapped digits make the code invalid and the scanner or system rejects it. Each check is tiny, but together they stop many errors before they enter the database.

From transactions to management information: TPS data does not stay at the bottom. Every night or every hour, totals are taken from the transaction records and passed upwards. The thousands of individual sales of one day become one line per branch per product. Those lines become weekly and monthly summaries for middle managers and then trends for senior managers. If the transaction records are incomplete or wrong, every report above them is wrong too, which is the GIGO rule from lesson 3 in action. That is why good organizations treat the TPS as the foundation and protect it carefully.

TPS by function: Every functional area has its own transaction systems. Sales and marketing: order entry, POS, sales commission tracking. Manufacturing and production: purchasing, receiving, shipping, machine control, quality control records. Finance and accounting: accounts payable and receivable, general ledger, cash management. Human resources: attendance, payroll, employee records, recruitment. When these transaction systems share one database, as in ERP systems (lesson 16), the data flows smoothly between them.

TPS failure is business failure: Because a TPS runs the daily heartbeat of the business, its failure stops the business. If a bank's core system goes down, branches cannot serve customers. If a supershop's POS fails on a busy evening, queues grow and customers leave. That is why TPS are usually built with backup power, backup servers, regular data backups and procedures for working manually when the system is down. We will discuss business continuity in lesson 23.

Real life example 1, a mobile wallet transfer: When you send money from your mobile wallet to a friend, the system receives the request, checks your PIN, checks your balance and limits, debits your account and credits your friend's account, and sends both of you an SMS or notification with a transaction ID. Every one of those steps must succeed together, or none must. Millions of such transactions every day become the raw data from which the company learns about usage, fraud patterns and where to place more agents.

Real life example 2, payroll in a garments factory: Each worker's attendance is captured at the gate by a card punch or fingerprint machine. At month end, a batch payroll run combines attendance, overtime hours and wage rates to calculate each worker's pay, deductions and net wage. Pay slips are produced, and the payment is sent to workers' bank or mobile wallet accounts. The same transaction data later lets managers see overtime trends by line and month, which is information for the middle level.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think a TPS makes decisions. It mostly records and processes routine events under fixed rules; decisions are supported by other systems that use TPS data. Another confusion is between batch and online processing: remember that batch collects and processes later in groups, while online processes each transaction immediately. Exams often ask: define TPS and its characteristics; explain the TPS cycle; compare batch and online processing with examples; explain why TPS data is the foundation of MIS and DSS; and describe a POS or ATM as a TPS.

Recap: A transaction is a routine business event such as a sale or payment. A TPS captures, edits, corrects, manipulates, stores and documents these events at the operational level. It handles high volumes of structured, repetitive work and must be accurate, fast, reliable, secure and auditable. Batch processing groups transactions and runs them later; online processing updates records immediately; many systems use both. POS and ATM systems are everyday examples, and source data automation reduces errors. Above all, TPS data is the foundation that every other information system stands on. Every beep at the supershop counter is a brick in that foundation.
key_points: A transaction is a routine business event such as a sale, payment, deposit or booking.
A TPS records and processes daily transactions at the operational level and is the main data source for other systems.
TPS cycle: data collection, editing, correction, manipulation, storage and document production.
TPS characteristics: high volume, routine and structured, accurate, fast, reliable, secure, with an audit trail.
Batch processing groups transactions and processes them later; online (real-time) processing updates records immediately.
Many organizations mix both: online at the counter, batch for heavy periodic jobs like payroll or interest.
Source data automation (barcodes, cards, RFID, biometrics) captures data at the point of transaction and reduces errors.
When a TPS fails, the business stops, so backups and fallback procedures are essential.
lessons.tip: Memorize the TPS cycle by following one real receipt from your pocket through all six steps. If you can tell that story, you can answer any TPS question.
lessons.task: Take any receipt or SMS confirmation you have (shop, bus ticket, mobile wallet). List every piece of data on it, mark which ones were captured automatically and which typed by a person, and say whether the transaction was processed online or in a batch.

quiz.q: Which management level does a TPS mainly serve?
quiz.explain: TPS records daily routine transactions, which is operational-level work.

quiz.q: Which situation best fits batch processing?
options: Monthly payroll calculated for all workers at once
Booking the last seat on a bus online
quiz.explain: Payroll can be collected over the month and processed together; the others need an immediate update.

quiz.q: Why must an ATM use online rather than batch processing for withdrawals?
options: Batch processing is always more expensive
The balance must update immediately so the same money cannot be withdrawn twice
quiz.explain: Real-time updates prevent overdrawing the same balance from two places.

quiz.q: Which is an example of source data automation?
options: A clerk retyping handwritten forms at night
A barcode scanner reading products at the counter
A manager reading a monthly report
Emailing a spreadsheet to head office
quiz.explain: Source data automation captures data by machine at the point where the transaction happens.

quiz.q: In the TPS cycle, checking that an account number is not missing is called:
quiz.explain: Data editing checks input for errors before processing.

lessons.title: MIS Reports and Decision Support Systems
lessons.content:
Imagine two managers at a cold drinks distributor in Chattogram. The first one, every Monday morning, opens a report that shows last week's sales by area compared with the target. Most areas are fine, and two are marked in red. He calls those two area officers. The second manager has a harder question: summer is coming, the price of sugar has gone up, and she must decide whether to raise prices by 5 taka, keep prices and cut the promotion budget, or do both. No weekly report answers that. She needs a tool where she can try different numbers and see what might happen to profit. The first manager is using a management information system in the narrow sense: regular reports. The second needs a decision support system. This lesson explains both and the difference between them.

Two meanings of MIS: Be careful: the term MIS has two meanings. In the broad sense, as in the course title, it means the whole field of information systems in organizations. In the narrow sense, which we use in this lesson, a management information system is a specific type of system that serves middle managers by giving them reports summarizing the organization's basic operations, built mainly from TPS data. Exam questions usually make clear which meaning they want; when they list MIS next to TPS and DSS, they mean the narrow one.

What an MIS does: An MIS takes the detailed transactions captured by TPS, summarizes and compares them, and delivers reports that help middle managers plan, monitor and control. It answers routine questions that are known in advance: How much did each branch sell this month? Which products are below the reorder level? How does this quarter's spending compare with the budget? The questions are structured and repeated, so the reports can be designed once and produced again and again.

Characteristics of an MIS: MIS reports are mostly about internal data, from the organization's own transactions. They are usually produced on a fixed schedule or on simple request. They are mainly summaries and comparisons, not raw detail. They support structured and some semi-structured decisions. They are relatively inflexible: the report shows what it was designed to show, and they have little analytical power beyond totals, averages and comparisons. That is not a weakness; it is what makes them cheap, reliable and easy to read.

Scheduled reports: Scheduled or periodic reports are produced at regular intervals: daily, weekly, monthly. A daily cash collection report for each branch, a weekly sales report by area, a monthly payroll summary by department. Managers know when they arrive and what they contain. A key indicator report is a special scheduled report that summarizes the previous day's critical activities, often available at the start of each working day.

Exception reports: An exception report shows only the items that are unusual or need action, according to rules set in advance. Instead of listing all 2,000 products, it lists the 15 below the reorder level. Instead of all 300 loan accounts, it lists the 12 that are more than 90 days overdue. A simple worked example: a distributor sets a rule that any area whose weekly sales are more than 10 percent below target must be shown. Area A sold 95 of a target of 100, which is 5 percent below, so it is not shown. Area B sold 82 of 100, 18 percent below, so it is shown. Exception reports fight the information overload problem from lesson 3 by pointing attention where it is needed. The art is in setting the threshold: too low and the report is flooded; too high and real problems are missed.

Demand (on-demand) reports: A demand report is produced when a manager asks for it. A sales manager might request, right now, the list of all customers in Sylhet who bought more than 1 lakh taka last quarter. Modern systems let managers run such queries themselves through a menu or simple search, rather than waiting for the IT team.

Drill-down reports: A drill-down report starts with a high-level summary and lets the user click into more detail step by step. For example: total national sales this month, then sales by division, then by district within Dhaka division, then by individual outlet, then by product within that outlet. A manager notices that sales in one division fell, drills down and finds that the drop is in one district, then in two outlets, then in one product that was out of stock. Drill down is how one summary screen can serve both senior and middle managers.

What a DSS is: A decision support system is an interactive computer-based system that helps managers make semi-structured and unstructured decisions, the ones that cannot be fully solved by fixed rules. Where an MIS mostly reports what happened, a DSS helps answer what if and what should we do. It combines data with analytical models and a flexible user interface, and it supports the decision maker rather than replacing her judgment.

The three components of a DSS: First, the database (or data management component): the data the DSS works on, often taken from TPS and other internal systems plus external data such as market prices or exchange rates. Second, the model base: the mathematical and analytical models, such as a profit formula, a forecasting model, a statistical model or an optimization model. Third, the user interface (or dialogue component): screens, forms, sliders and charts that let the manager ask questions, change assumptions and see results easily. Some textbooks add a fourth component, the user, or a knowledge component. A good DSS is useful only if all three fit together: good data, sensible models and an interface the manager will actually use.

What-if analysis: What-if analysis means changing one or more input values and watching how the output changes. A small worked example for the cold drinks distributor: suppose it sells 10,000 bottles a month at 40 taka, with a variable cost of 25 taka per bottle and fixed costs of 1 lakh taka. Profit = 10,000 x (40 minus 25) minus 1,00,000 = 1,50,000 minus 1,00,000 = 50,000 taka. What if sugar costs push the variable cost to 28 taka? Profit becomes 10,000 x 12 minus 1,00,000 = 20,000 taka. What if she then raises the price to 45 and sales drop to 9,000 bottles? Profit becomes 9,000 x 17 minus 1,00,000 = 1,53,000 minus 1,00,000 = 53,000 taka. A spreadsheet with these formulas is already a simple DSS, and this kind of quick trial is exactly what managers use it for.

Sensitivity analysis: Sensitivity analysis is a special kind of what-if analysis that changes one input at a time, step by step, to see how sensitive the result is to that input. If a 1 taka change in variable cost changes profit by 10,000 taka, profit is very sensitive to cost, and the manager should watch costs closely and maybe lock in sugar prices with a supplier contract. Inputs that barely move the result need less attention.

Goal-seeking analysis: Goal seeking works backwards. Instead of asking what profit we get from given inputs, it asks what input we need to reach a target output. Using the numbers above with a variable cost of 28 taka and price of 40: how many bottles must we sell to make 50,000 taka profit? Profit = units x 12 minus 1,00,000 = 50,000, so units x 12 = 1,50,000, and units = 12,500 bottles. Spreadsheet tools such as Goal Seek do this automatically.
