Goal seeking is useful for questions like what sales level do we need to break even, or what interest rate makes this loan profitable.

Optimization and forecasting models: Some DSS use optimization models to find the best choice under constraints, for example the cheapest way to deliver goods from three warehouses to 50 shops with limited trucks, or the product mix that maximizes profit with limited machine hours. Linear programming is a common method. Others use forecasting models that use past data to predict future demand, such as monthly sales trends with a seasonal rise before Eid. The manager still decides, but with much better estimates.

Types of DSS: Some DSS are model-driven: they mainly use models, like the pricing spreadsheet above or a loan approval scoring model. Others are data-driven: they help managers explore large amounts of data to find patterns, which links to business intelligence and OLAP in lesson 12. There are also group decision support systems for teams meeting together, discussed in lesson 8, and geographic information systems (GIS), which help with location decisions using maps, such as where to open a new branch or where to place mobile wallet agents.

MIS versus DSS: The key differences are worth remembering as a table in your head. Purpose: MIS reports on and helps control routine operations; DSS helps analyse a specific, less structured decision. Decision type: MIS supports structured decisions; DSS supports semi-structured and unstructured ones. Flexibility: MIS reports are fixed and scheduled; DSS is interactive and flexible. Analysis: MIS gives summaries and comparisons; DSS uses models, what-if and goal seeking. Users: MIS mainly serves middle managers; DSS serves middle managers and analysts, and sometimes senior managers. Data: MIS mostly uses internal data; DSS uses internal plus external data.

Real life example 1, a bank branch: Every morning the branch manager receives an exception report listing loans that crossed 30, 60 and 90 days overdue, and a scheduled report of yesterday's deposits and withdrawals. That is MIS. When the bank is considering a new small business loan product, the credit team uses a DSS spreadsheet model with different interest rates, default rates and loan sizes to see expected profit and risk under each scenario. That is DSS. Both use the same transaction data underneath.

Real life example 2, a garments factory planning an order: The production manager's weekly MIS report shows each line's efficiency and output against target. When a buyer asks whether the factory can accept an extra 30,000 pieces with a delivery date six weeks away, the planning team uses a capacity model: available minutes per line, the standard minutes per garment, current orders and possible overtime. They try several what-if cases, such as with and without one extra shift, before replying to the buyer. The decision is still a human one, but it is based on numbers rather than a guess.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is mixing up the narrow and broad meanings of MIS. Another is saying that a DSS makes decisions; it supports the decision maker, who keeps responsibility. Students also confuse what-if with goal seeking: what-if changes inputs to see outputs, goal seeking fixes the output target and finds the input needed. Exams often ask: explain the types of MIS reports with examples; define DSS and its components; explain what-if, sensitivity and goal-seeking analysis with a small calculation; and compare MIS and DSS.

Recap: In the narrow sense, an MIS summarizes TPS data into reports for middle managers: scheduled, key indicator, exception, demand and drill-down reports. It supports structured, recurring decisions with internal data and is fixed but reliable. A DSS is an interactive system with a database, a model base and a user interface that supports semi-structured and unstructured decisions using what-if, sensitivity, goal-seeking, optimization and forecasting. MIS tells you what happened and where to look; DSS helps you think about what to do next. Remember the two managers in Chattogram: one reads the red lines in a weekly report, the other plays with numbers to choose the best path.

lessons.title: Executive, Knowledge and Collaboration Systems
lessons.content:
Think of the cockpit of a plane flying from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar. The pilot does not read a list of every bolt, wire and fuel drop. She looks at a few big dials: speed, height, fuel, direction, and warning lights that flash only when something is wrong. If a light flashes, she can look deeper. Now think of a senior aircraft engineer who has fixed one strange engine fault ten times over twenty years. When she retires, will that know-how leave with her? And think of the crew on the ground, a team in different rooms, sharing schedules and messages to get the plane ready on time. Those three pictures are this lesson: executive support systems are the cockpit, knowledge management systems keep the engineer's experience, and collaboration systems connect the crew. We finish by putting all the system types together into one pyramid.

What an ESS is: An executive support system, also called an executive information system, helps senior managers make strategic decisions. These are non-routine, often unstructured decisions about the long-term direction of the organization: entering a new market, buying a competitor, changing the product line, reacting to new government policy. An ESS gives top managers easy access to summarized internal information and important external information, presented simply, usually as dashboards with charts and indicators.

Characteristics of an ESS: An ESS is designed for people who have little time and are not technical, so it must be very easy to use. It shows highly summarized information, mostly in graphical form. It combines internal data from the organization's TPS, MIS and DSS with external data such as market trends, competitor news, exchange rates, commodity prices and economic indicators. It supports drill down, so a managing director who sees a falling number can click into the detail behind it. And it is flexible: executives' questions change constantly, so the system must answer new questions, not just print fixed reports.

Dashboards and KPIs: The heart of most ESS is a digital dashboard: a single screen showing the most important measures of performance, called key performance indicators or KPIs. For a supershop chain, KPIs might include total sales today, sales growth compared with last year, average bill size, stock-out rate and customer complaints. Each KPI is shown as a number, a small chart and a colour signal, such as green for on target, yellow for warning and red for problem. A good dashboard shows maybe five to ten KPIs, not fifty. If everything is on the screen, nothing stands out.

The balanced scorecard: A popular framework for choosing executive KPIs is the balanced scorecard. It argues that money is not the only thing to watch. It looks at four perspectives: financial (profit, revenue growth), customer (satisfaction, retention, market share), internal business process (speed, quality, cost of key processes) and learning and growth (employee skills, training, systems and innovation). A garments exporter might track profit margin, on-time shipment rate to buyers, defect rate per thousand pieces and worker training hours. The idea is that today's training and process quality drive tomorrow's customers and profit.

A tiny worked example of a KPI: Suppose on-time shipment rate is defined as shipments delivered on or before the agreed date divided by all shipments in the month. If a factory made 40 shipments and 34 were on time, the rate is 34 / 40 = 85 percent. If the target is 95 percent, the dashboard shows red. The managing director clicks and drills down: most late shipments came from one washing unit that had machine breakdowns. One number led straight to a concrete problem to fix.

What knowledge management is: In lesson 1 we said knowledge is the experience and understanding that tells us how to use information. Knowledge management (KM) is the set of business processes an organization uses to create, store, transfer and apply knowledge. Organizations care because much of their value lies in what their people know: how to fix a tricky machine, how to handle a difficult buyer, which supplier delivers on time. When experienced people leave, retire or move, that knowledge can disappear unless it is captured and shared.

Tacit and explicit knowledge: Explicit knowledge is knowledge that has been written down or recorded: manuals, procedures, reports, recipes, standard operating procedures, video tutorials. It is easy to store and share. Tacit knowledge lives in people's heads and hands: the experience, intuition and skill that are hard to put into words. A master tailor can tell from the feel of fabric how it will behave after washing; an experienced loan officer senses when a story does not add up. Tacit knowledge is often the most valuable and the hardest to manage. A big part of KM is turning tacit knowledge into explicit form where possible, and connecting people when it is not.

The knowledge management value chain: KM is often described as a chain of steps. Acquire: capture knowledge from documents, experts, customers and data. Store: put it in a repository such as a database, wiki or document library, organized so it can be found. Disseminate: share it through search, portals, training, messaging and communities. Apply: use it in real decisions and work, which is where the value is created. If any step is weak, for example knowledge is stored but nobody can find it, the effort is wasted.

Types of knowledge management systems: Enterprise-wide KM systems include document and content management systems that store files with versions and search, company wikis and intranets, FAQ and lessons-learned databases, and expert directories that tell you who knows what. Knowledge work systems are specialized tools for professionals who create knowledge, such as engineers using computer-aided design software or analysts using statistical tools. Some organizations also use intelligent techniques, such as expert systems that capture rules from human experts, and machine learning systems that find patterns in data, which we touch on in lesson 25.

Communities of practice: Not all knowledge sharing is technical. A community of practice is a group of people with a shared skill or interest who learn from each other, such as all the IT support staff of a bank, or all the quality inspectors across a group of factories. A simple group chat, a monthly meeting and a shared folder can do more than an expensive system if people actually use them. The technology should support the habit of sharing, not replace it.

Why KM often fails: People may not share because knowledge feels like job security. They may be too busy to write things down. The repository may fill with outdated documents nobody trusts. Good KM needs incentives and recognition for sharing, simple tools, someone responsible for keeping content fresh, and leaders who use it themselves.

Office automation systems: Office automation systems support general office work: word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, email, calendars, scanning and document management. They serve clerical staff and knowledge workers at every level. They seem ordinary, but a large share of real business information still lives in documents, spreadsheets and email.

Collaboration systems: Collaboration means working with others towards shared goals. Collaboration tools include email, instant messaging and group chat, video conferencing, shared calendars, shared documents that several people edit at once, project and task boards, and team workspaces. They let teams in different places, such as a buying house in Dhaka, a factory in Gazipur and a buyer's office abroad, work together almost as if in one room. Tools are usually classified by time and place: same time and same place (a meeting room with a shared screen), same time and different place (video calls), different time and same place (a shared team room or notice board), and different time and different place (email, shared documents, discussion threads).

The pyramid of information systems: Now we can put all the system types together. At the base, at the operational level, are transaction processing systems, capturing every event. Above them, at the middle level, management information systems summarize TPS data into reports, and decision support systems help analyse semi-structured decisions. At the top, executive support systems give senior managers summarized internal and external information for strategic decisions. Running across all levels are knowledge management, office automation and collaboration systems. Data flows upwards and becomes more summarized; decisions become less structured as you go up. Remember that real products often combine several types: a modern ERP includes TPS functions, MIS reports and sometimes DSS features and dashboards.

Comparing the four main types: TPS inputs are transactions and events, processing is sorting, listing, updating, outputs are detailed reports and documents, users are operations staff and supervisors. MIS inputs are summarized transaction data, processing is routine reports and simple models, outputs are summary and exception reports, users are middle managers. DSS inputs are optimized analytical data plus models, processing is interactive what-if analysis, outputs are special analyses, users are professionals and managers. ESS inputs are aggregated internal and external data, processing is graphics and simulations, outputs are projections and answers to queries, users are senior managers. This four-row comparison is a favourite exam table.

Real life example 1, a mobile financial service executive dashboard: The leadership of a mobile wallet company might watch a dashboard showing active users, daily transaction volume, number of active agents, average cash-in and cash-out per agent, fraud complaints and app crash rate, with trends over weeks and colour alerts. If complaints spike in one district, they drill down to see whether it is linked to one type of scam or one group of agents. External data such as new central bank rules or a competitor's offer is added to the same view to support strategic choices.

Real life example 2, knowledge sharing in a garments factory: An experienced maintenance technician knows how to fix a recurring fault on a certain sewing machine model. The factory asks him to record a short phone video and a one-page checklist, stores them in a shared folder linked to the machine model, and tags them in the maintenance system. Next time the fault appears at night when he is off duty, a junior technician finds the guide and fixes it in twenty minutes instead of stopping the line for hours. That is tacit knowledge partly turned into explicit knowledge, stored, shared and applied.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think an ESS is just a bigger DSS. The difference is the user and the decision: ESS serves senior managers with summarized internal and external information for strategic, unstructured decisions, with a very simple interface. Another mistake is confusing knowledge with information: a KMS is about capturing experience and know-how, not only storing data. Exams often ask: define ESS and its characteristics; explain dashboards and KPIs; distinguish tacit and explicit knowledge; describe the KM value chain; and draw the pyramid of information systems with users and decision types at each level.

Recap: An ESS gives senior managers a simple, graphical view of summarized internal and external information, with dashboards, KPIs and drill down, often guided by a balanced scorecard. Knowledge management helps organizations acquire, store, disseminate and apply knowledge, turning tacit know-how into explicit form where possible and connecting people when not. Office automation and collaboration systems support everyday work and teamwork across time and place. The pyramid ties it together: TPS at the base, MIS and DSS in the middle, ESS at the top, and knowledge and collaboration systems across all levels. The cockpit, the retiring engineer and the ground crew each need a different kind of system, and a healthy organization has all three.
key_points: An ESS supports senior managers' strategic, unstructured decisions with summarized internal and external information.
ESS features: very easy to use, graphical dashboards, KPIs, drill down, external data and flexibility.
A balanced scorecard tracks financial, customer, internal process and learning and growth perspectives.
Knowledge management is acquiring, storing, disseminating and applying knowledge.
Explicit knowledge is written or recorded; tacit knowledge is experience and skill in people's heads and hands.
KM systems include document management, wikis, lessons-learned databases, expert directories and knowledge work systems.
Collaboration tools are classified by same or different time and same or different place.
The IS pyramid: TPS at the operational base, MIS and DSS in the middle, ESS at the top, KMS and collaboration across all levels.

lessons.title: Decision Making in Organizations
lessons.content:
Think about two decisions a supershop branch manager in Uttara makes on the same Monday. At 9 am the system says there are only 40 bottles of soybean oil left, and the reorder level is 50. She clicks a button and a purchase order goes to the supplier. It takes ten seconds. At 4 pm head office asks her a very different question: should the chain open a new branch in Bashundhara next year? There is no button for that. She needs data about rents, traffic, competitors and income levels, and even then she will be guessing a little. Both are decisions, but they are completely different kinds of decisions. Information systems help with both, but in very different ways. This lesson is about understanding those differences.

What a decision is: A decision is a choice between two or more possible actions. Managers make decisions all day: what to order, whom to hire, which price to set, which supplier to trust, whether to launch a product. In the earlier lessons we met the different types of information systems: TPS, MIS reports, DSS, ESS and KMS. Each of them exists mainly to support certain kinds of decisions. If you understand decisions, you understand why those systems look the way they do.

Why decision making matters for IS: An information system that does not change any decision is mostly decoration. A beautiful dashboard that nobody acts on has zero value. The value of information, as we saw in lesson 3, comes from the better decisions it makes possible. So the first question an MIS professional asks is not which technology to use, but which decision we are trying to improve, who makes it, and how often.

Structured decisions: A structured decision is repetitive and routine, and there is a clear, known procedure for making it. You do not need to treat it as new every time. The stock reorder at 9 am is structured: if stock falls below the reorder level, order the standard quantity. Other examples: approving a leave request when the employee still has leave days left, calculating overtime pay, deciding whether a bank customer can withdraw money given the balance. Because the rule is clear, structured decisions can often be fully automated by a TPS or a simple program. In pseudo-code: if stock < reorder_level then create_order(item, standard_qty).

Unstructured decisions: An unstructured decision is new, important and non-routine. There is no agreed procedure, and the decision maker must use judgment, experience and insight to define the problem itself. Opening a branch in Bashundhara, entering a new export market, choosing a new CEO, or deciding how to respond to a new competitor are unstructured. Computers cannot simply calculate the answer. They can supply facts, trends and news, but the final call depends on human judgment.

Semi-structured decisions: Most interesting business decisions sit in the middle. In a semi-structured decision, part of the problem has a clear procedure and part needs judgment. For example, setting the Eid sales budget: past sales data and growth trends give a starting number, but the manager must also judge how inflation, a new competitor and the timing of Eid this year will change things. Deciding a loan for a small business is similar: a credit score gives a structured part, but the officer still judges the business plan. Decision support systems, which we met in lesson 6, are built mainly for semi-structured decisions.

Decisions and management levels: Decision types line up roughly with management levels. Operational managers and front-line staff mostly make structured decisions: how many units to produce today, which order to ship first. Middle managers make many semi-structured decisions: how to allocate the budget between branches, which supplier to choose this quarter. Senior managers face mostly unstructured decisions: long-term strategy, mergers, entering new markets. This is not a strict law. A senior manager also approves some routine things, and an operational supervisor sometimes faces a surprise. But it is a useful map, and exams often ask you to draw it as a table: level, type of decision, example, and the system that supports it (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS).

Simon's model of decision making: The economist and computer scientist Herbert Simon described decision making as a process with stages. The classic version has three: intelligence, design and choice. Many MIS textbooks add a fourth, implementation, and some add monitoring. The point is that a decision is not one moment. It is a process, and each stage needs different information.

Stage 1, intelligence: This is about discovering and understanding the problem. Something is wrong or an opportunity exists, and you notice it. A garments factory manager sees in the daily MIS report that rejected pieces on line 3 have doubled. That report raised the flag. Then she digs in: is it a machine, a new worker, a fabric batch? Exception reports, dashboards and data analysis tools help most at this stage, because they show what is unusual.

Stage 2, design: Now you create and evaluate possible solutions. For the rejection problem, options might be retraining workers, repairing a machine, changing the fabric supplier, or slowing the line. Each option has costs and effects. Here a decision support system can help by running what-if analysis: if we slow the line by 10 percent, how many pieces do we lose per day, and does the drop in rejects make up for it?

Stage 3, choice: You pick one option, or a mix. The manager may choose to repair the machine and retrain two operators. Tools at this stage include DSS models that rank options, cost-benefit tables, and sometimes group discussion. The choice depends on goals: lowest cost, fastest fix, least risk.

Stage 4, implementation and monitoring: A decision written on paper changes nothing. Someone must carry it out, and someone must check whether it worked. The machine is repaired, operators are retrained, and the MIS report keeps showing the rejection rate each day. If the rate falls, good. If it does not, we are back to intelligence: the problem was not what we thought. This loop is just the feedback idea from lesson 1 applied to decisions.

The rational model and its limits: Classic economics imagined a perfectly rational decision maker: someone who knows all options, knows all consequences, ranks them perfectly and chooses the best one. Real managers are not like that. They have limited time, limited information and limited brain power. Simon called this bounded rationality. Because of these limits, people usually satisfice, a word Simon made from satisfy and suffice. That means they choose the first option that is good enough, rather than searching forever for the perfect one. A buyer looking for a fabric supplier might accept the first one that meets quality, price and delivery requirements, instead of checking every supplier in the country.

Why bounded rationality matters for IS: If people cannot process everything, then a good information system should filter and summarize, not dump all data on them. That is why exception reports, KPIs and dashboards exist. They save attention for the things that matter. An information system that shows 300 numbers on one screen actually makes decisions worse, because the important number gets lost.

Biases in decisions: Human decisions are also affected by predictable mental shortcuts called biases. Confirmation bias means looking only for facts that support what you already believe. Anchoring means getting stuck on the first number you see; if last year's budget was 10 lakh taka, a manager tends to stay close to 10 lakh even when things have changed a lot. Overconfidence means believing your own estimates are more accurate than they are. Good use of data, asking for evidence, and looking at alternatives in the design stage can reduce these biases, though not remove them.

Group decisions: Many important decisions are made by committees and boards, not one person. Groups bring more knowledge, but they also have problems: one strong person dominates, quiet members do not speak, meetings take too long, and people agree just to avoid conflict, which is called groupthink. Group decision support systems, and today ordinary collaboration tools like shared documents, online polls and video meetings, try to help. Features such as anonymous idea entry and voting let everyone contribute without fear, and a shared record keeps the discussion organized.

Automated decisions: Some structured decisions are now made entirely by software in milliseconds. A bank's card system decides whether to approve a payment by checking balance, card status and fraud rules. An e-commerce site decides which products to show you. A mobile wallet may block a transaction that looks unusual. These automated decision rules must be designed carefully and checked by humans, because a wrong rule repeats the same mistake thousands of times very quickly.

Real life example 1, a bank loan: A bank in Dhaka receives a loan application from a small furniture business in Mirpur. The structured part: the system checks the applicant's credit history from the credit information records, the account turnover, and calculates ratios like monthly income versus the proposed monthly instalment. If basic rules fail, the application is rejected automatically. The semi-structured part: a credit officer visits the business, looks at the workshop and judges the owner's plan and experience. Intelligence (spot the request and gather facts), design (options: full loan, smaller loan, loan with guarantee), choice (approve 5 lakh instead of 8 lakh), implementation (disburse and monitor repayments). Every Simon stage appears.

Real life example 2, Eid stock at an online shop: An online fashion seller on Facebook and its own website must decide how many panjabis to stock before Eid. The intelligence stage uses last year's sales data by size and colour, plus page messages showing what customers are asking about. In the design stage the owner builds a small spreadsheet model: if demand grows 10, 20 or 30 percent, how much money is tied up in stock, and what is the risk of unsold items? In the choice stage she picks a middle option and orders more of the best-selling sizes. During Eid, daily sales reports show which designs are selling, so she reorders the fast movers and discounts the slow ones. That is monitoring and feedback.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think unstructured means unimportant or random. It actually means no fixed procedure exists; such decisions are usually the most important. Another mistake is thinking a DSS makes the decision. It supports the decision maker; the human still chooses. Also remember the classic three Simon stages are intelligence, design and choice; implementation is often added as a fourth. Typical exam questions: distinguish structured, semi-structured and unstructured decisions with examples; explain Simon's model; relate decision types to management levels and information systems; explain bounded rationality and satisficing.

Recap: A decision is a choice among alternatives. Structured decisions follow known rules and can be automated; unstructured decisions need judgment; semi-structured decisions mix both and are the main target of DSS. Operational, middle and senior managers face mostly structured, semi-structured and unstructured decisions respectively. Simon's model breaks decision making into intelligence, design and choice, often followed by implementation and monitoring. Real people have bounded rationality, satisfice and suffer biases, so good systems filter and summarize information and help groups think together. Keep the branch manager in mind: one click for the oil reorder, months of thinking for the new branch.
key_points: A decision is a choice between alternatives; IS creates value only when it improves decisions.
Structured decisions follow known rules and can be automated; unstructured decisions need judgment and insight.
Semi-structured decisions mix rules and judgment and are the main target of decision support systems.
Operational managers make mostly structured decisions, middle managers semi-structured, senior managers unstructured.
Simon's model: intelligence (find the problem), design (create options), choice (pick one), then implementation and monitoring.
Bounded rationality means people have limited time, information and attention, so they satisfice: choose a good-enough option.
Biases like anchoring, confirmation bias and groupthink distort decisions; good data and group support tools reduce them.
Automated decisions repeat mistakes fast, so their rules need careful design and human review.
lessons.tip: When you study any information system, name the exact decision it supports and its type: structured, semi-structured or unstructured. If you cannot name a decision, you have not understood the system yet.
lessons.task: Write down five decisions you or your family made this month, such as what to cook, which phone package to buy, or which university to apply to. Label each as structured, semi-structured or unstructured, and for one of them write the four Simon stages: intelligence, design, choice and implementation.

quiz.q: A system automatically creates a purchase order whenever stock falls below the reorder level. What type of decision is this?
quiz.explain: The rule is clear and repetitive, so it is a structured decision that can be automated.

quiz.q: Which stage of Simon's model is about noticing and understanding that a problem exists?
quiz.explain: Intelligence is the stage of searching for and understanding problems or opportunities.

quiz.q: What does satisficing mean?
options: Always finding the mathematically best option
Choosing the first option that is good enough
Letting a computer make every decision
Copying the decision of a competitor
quiz.explain: Because of bounded rationality, people usually accept a good-enough option instead of searching for the perfect one.

quiz.q: Which kind of decision are decision support systems mainly designed for?
options: Decisions with no data at all
quiz.explain: DSS combine data and models with human judgment, which fits semi-structured problems best.

quiz.q: A manager keeps next year's budget close to last year's 10 lakh taka even though costs have changed a lot. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Anchoring means sticking too close to the first or familiar number.

lessons.title: IT Infrastructure
lessons.content:
Think about a city like Dhaka. Every house, shop and office depends on things nobody notices until they fail: roads, electricity lines, water pipes, gas connections, drains. A restaurant owner does not build her own power plant. She plugs into the shared electricity grid and focuses on cooking. When there is a load-shedding hour, suddenly everyone remembers how much they depend on it. Organizations have the same kind of hidden foundation for their information systems. It is called IT infrastructure. The billing app, the ERP and the mobile banking service all sit on top of it, and when it breaks, everything above it stops.

What IT infrastructure is: IT infrastructure is the shared technology resources that give an organization the platform for its specific information systems. It includes hardware, software, networks, data management systems and the people and services needed to run them. The key word is shared. A single sales report is an application. The servers, the database engine, the office network, the email system and the help desk that every application uses are infrastructure. Managers think of it as a set of services the whole firm depends on, a bit like a city's utilities.

Why managers must understand it: Infrastructure is often the biggest part of an IT budget, and decisions about it last for years. If a bank chooses the wrong core system or a factory buys servers it cannot maintain, it lives with that mistake for a long time. A CSE graduate who can explain infrastructure choices in money and business terms, not only in technical terms, becomes very valuable. Here we look at infrastructure from a manager's chair; the deep technical side of operating systems, networks and databases belongs to their own courses.

Component 1, hardware platforms: These are the physical computers. Client devices are what users touch: desktops, laptops, tablets, smartphones and point-of-sale terminals. Servers are powerful computers that serve many users at once, such as a database server or a web server. Many organizations keep servers in a data centre, a room or building with cooling, backup power and security. Large firms may still use mainframes, very powerful and reliable machines often used by big banks and airlines for huge transaction volumes. Storage systems hold the data, from hard disks and SSDs to large shared storage arrays.

Component 2, operating system platforms: Every computer needs an operating system. On servers, common choices are Linux and Windows Server. On desktops, Windows and macOS are common, and on phones Android and iOS. The OS choice matters to managers because it affects which software can run, licence costs and which skills the IT staff need. Your Operating Systems course covers how they work inside; here the question is which one fits the business.

Component 3, enterprise software applications: These are large packages that run core business processes across the whole firm, such as ERP, supply chain management and customer relationship management systems. We will study them in lessons 16 to 18. From the infrastructure view, they are major investments that need servers, databases, networks and trained people, and they often shape the rest of the infrastructure around them.

Component 4, data management and storage: Organizations need database management systems to store and organize data, such as Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL and PostgreSQL. They also need storage capacity, backup systems and, for analysis, data warehouses. Data grows every year, so storage planning is a continuing cost, not a one-time purchase. Lesson 11 covers data management in more detail.

Component 5, networking and telecommunications: Computers are useless for most business purposes unless they are connected. This includes the local area network inside an office, links between branches, internet connections, Wi-Fi, mobile networks and the equipment that ties them together like routers and switches. A bank with 200 branches depends on network links to reach its central database. Lesson 13 covers networks from a business view.

Component 6, internet platforms: Websites, web servers, app servers and the hosting services that run a company's online presence and online services. An e-commerce company's website and mobile app backend are part of this.

Component 7, consulting and system integration services: Most organizations cannot build and connect everything themselves. They hire consultants and system integrators to plan infrastructure, install enterprise software, connect old systems with new ones and train staff. In Bangladesh, many local software firms earn much of their income from this kind of work for banks, telecoms and government. People are part of infrastructure too: network engineers, database administrators and help desk staff.

Evolution, the mainframe era: Business computing infrastructure has gone through several stages. From the late 1950s, big organizations used mainframes: one large central computer in a special room, used by many people through simple terminals. All processing and data were in the centre, controlled by professional IT staff. It was powerful and reliable but expensive and slow to change.

Evolution, personal computers: From the early 1980s, personal computers put computing on individual desks. Staff could use word processors and spreadsheets without waiting for the central IT department. This gave freedom but also scattered data across many machines that did not talk to each other.

Evolution, client/server: In client/server computing, desktop clients send requests over a network to servers that store data and run shared services. A simple version has two tiers: client and database server. A common version has three tiers: the client, an application server that holds the business logic, and a database server. This let firms share data across departments without one giant mainframe, using cheaper machines.

Evolution, enterprise internet: From the mid 1990s, organizations adopted internet standards, web browsers and web-based applications. A user could reach a system from any computer with a browser, and companies could link with customers and suppliers. Then came the cloud and mobile era: computing power, storage and software delivered over the internet as services, accessed from phones and laptops anywhere. Many firms today use a mix of all these stages at once: an old core system, client/server tools, web portals and cloud apps.

Why hardware keeps getting cheaper: Moore's law is the observation, first made by Gordon Moore in 1965 and later revised, that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled about every two years. In practice this meant computing power rose and cost per unit of computing fell very fast for decades, although the pace has slowed in recent years. Storage cost per gigabyte and network cost per bit have also fallen dramatically. For managers, the lesson is that hardware bought today will look slow and cheap in a few years, so planning should expect replacement cycles. Another useful idea is the network effect, sometimes called Metcalfe's law: a network becomes more valuable as more users join, which is why connecting branches and customers can pay off much more than the cost of the cables.

Total cost of ownership: The purchase price is only the beginning. Total cost of ownership, or TCO, adds up all the costs of owning a technology over its life: hardware, software licences, installation, training, support, maintenance, power and cooling, downtime, and finally disposal. Worked example: a small company buys 10 laptops at 70,000 taka each, which is 7 lakh taka. Over 4 years it also pays for software licences of about 10,000 taka per laptop per year, which is 4 lakh; training of 50,000 taka; repairs and support of 1 lakh per year, which is 4 lakh; and electricity and accessories of about 50,000 taka per year, which is 2 lakh. TCO is 7 + 4 + 0.5 + 4 + 2 = 17.5 lakh taka. The purchase price was only 40 percent of the real cost. Many projects go over budget because they look only at the price tag.

Build, buy or rent: For each piece of infrastructure, managers usually face a choice. Build means develop it in-house, giving full control but needing skilled staff and time. Buy means purchase packaged software or hardware, which is faster but may not fit every need. Rent means use cloud services or outsourcing, paying monthly instead of a big upfront cost. There is no single right answer. A large bank may build or heavily customize its core systems; a small shop should almost always rent ready-made software. Lesson 10 looks at cloud computing in detail.

Standards and compatibility: Infrastructure works better when parts follow common standards. Internet protocols like TCP/IP, web standards like HTML and HTTP, and file formats like PDF let products from different companies work together. Standards reduce cost, prevent lock-in to one vendor and make it easier to connect with partners. Managers should be careful when a supplier offers a closed system that only works with its own products.

Real life example 1, a bank branch: When you deposit money at a bank branch in Rajshahi, the teller uses a client PC. It connects over the bank's network to application servers and the core banking database, often in a central data centre in Dhaka, with a backup site elsewhere. The ATM outside, the mobile app on your phone and the internet banking website all reach the same core system. Every one of these channels depends on shared infrastructure: servers, databases, network links, security devices and the operations team watching them day and night.

Real life example 2, a growing online shop: A new online shop in Chattogram starts with a free social media page and a spreadsheet for orders. As it grows, it moves to a hosted e-commerce website on a cloud platform, uses a payment gateway service and a courier's online booking system, and buys three laptops and a barcode printer for the warehouse. It never builds a data centre. Its infrastructure is mostly rented services plus a few devices, which keeps upfront cost low while it tests whether the business will last.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse infrastructure with applications. A payroll program is an application; the servers, network and database engine it uses are infrastructure. Another mistake is treating the purchase price as the total cost; always mention TCO. Typical exam questions: define IT infrastructure and list its components; describe the eras of IT infrastructure evolution; explain client/server and three-tier architecture; explain Moore's law and its business impact; calculate or explain TCO.

Recap: IT infrastructure is the shared technology platform beneath all of an organization's applications. Its components are hardware platforms, operating systems, enterprise software, data management and storage, networking, internet platforms, and consulting and integration services, plus the people who run them. Infrastructure evolved from mainframes to personal computers, client/server, enterprise internet and now cloud and mobile. Moore's law and falling storage and network costs drive constant change. Total cost of ownership counts every cost over the life of a technology, not just the price tag, and managers must decide whether to build, buy or rent each part. Like roads and power lines in a city, good infrastructure is invisible when it works.
key_points: IT infrastructure is the shared technology resources and services that every application in a firm depends on.
Components: hardware, operating systems, enterprise software, data management and storage, networking, internet platforms, and consulting and integration services.
Infrastructure evolved from mainframes to PCs, client/server, enterprise internet, and cloud and mobile; many firms mix several eras.
Three-tier client/server splits the client, the application server with business logic, and the database server.
Moore's law: transistor counts roughly doubled about every two years, making computing cheaper; the pace has slowed recently.
Total cost of ownership adds purchase, licences, training, support, power, downtime and disposal over the whole life.
Managers choose to build, buy or rent each piece; there is no one right answer for every firm.
Common standards reduce cost and vendor lock-in and make connecting systems easier.
lessons.tip: When a question mentions any system, draw two layers: the application on top and the shared infrastructure underneath. Labelling the bottom layer with the seven components is a quick way to score marks.
lessons.task: Pick your university, a bank or a shop you know. List at least one example for each infrastructure component: hardware, operating system, enterprise software, database, network, internet platform and services or people. Then estimate a simple 3-year TCO for one laptop, including purchase, software, repairs and electricity.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of IT infrastructure rather than a specific application?
options: A report of this month's top customers
The shared database server used by all departments
A sales target for one branch
quiz.explain: The shared database server is a resource many applications depend on, so it is infrastructure.

quiz.q: In three-tier client/server architecture, where does the business logic usually run?
quiz.explain: The middle tier, the application server, holds the business logic between client and database.

quiz.q: What does total cost of ownership include?
options: Only the salary of the IT manager
All costs over the life of the technology, including support, training and downtime
quiz.explain: TCO counts every cost of owning the technology across its life, not just the price tag.

quiz.q: Moore's law is best described as:
options: A law that requires companies to upgrade every year
The rule that network value equals the number of users
The observation that transistor counts on chips roughly doubled about every two years
A legal limit on computer prices
quiz.explain: Moore's law is an observation about transistor density growth, which made computing cheaper over time.

quiz.q: A small new online shop should most likely:
options: Build its own data centre first
Rent cloud and online services and buy a few devices
quiz.explain: Renting services keeps upfront cost low and lets a small business grow without big infrastructure investment.

lessons.title: Cloud Computing for Business
lessons.content:
Imagine you need to travel from Dhanmondi to Gulshan every day. You have three choices. You can buy a car: you pay a lot upfront, pay for fuel, servicing, parking and a driver, and the car sits idle most of the day. You can rent a car with a driver by the month: no big upfront cost, but you still decide the route. Or you can call a ride-sharing app each time: you pay only for the trips you take, and someone else worries about the car entirely. Cloud computing gives businesses the same kinds of choices for computers and software. Instead of buying and running their own servers, they can rent computing power, storage and software over the internet and pay for what they use.

What cloud computing is: Cloud computing is a model in which computing resources, such as processing power, storage, networks, platforms and software, are provided as services over a network, usually the internet, and can be increased or decreased quickly with little effort. The customer does not need to know which physical machine in which building is doing the work. The provider owns and runs large data centres, and many customers share them.

How it works underneath: The trick that makes cloud possible is virtualization. Special software called a hypervisor lets one powerful physical server pretend to be many separate virtual machines, each with its own operating system, memory and disk. If one customer's virtual machine is idle, the physical server's power can be used by another customer's. Providers connect thousands of such servers in huge data centres and add software that automatically creates, moves and deletes virtual machines when customers ask. Containers are a lighter version of the same idea, packaging an application with what it needs so it can start in seconds. The customer sees a simple web page or command that says create a server, and a few moments later it exists. Your Operating Systems course explains virtual memory and processes; virtualization extends that idea to whole computers.

The five essential characteristics: The widely used definition from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology lists five characteristics. On-demand self-service: a customer can get more resources, like another server, from a web console without calling anyone. Broad network access: services are reached over the network from phones, laptops and other devices. Resource pooling: the provider's hardware serves many customers at the same time, and resources are assigned as needed. Rapid elasticity: capacity can grow or shrink quickly, so an online shop can handle a sale-day rush and then scale down. Measured service: usage is metered, like electricity, so customers pay for what they use.

Why it matters to managers: Cloud changes IT from a big capital expense, buying servers once every few years, into an operating expense, a monthly bill that rises and falls with use. It lets a small start-up get the same kind of computing power that once only large firms could afford. It also changes skills: fewer people racking servers, more people managing services, costs and security settings. Many of the systems you will build after graduation will run in the cloud.

Service model 1, IaaS: Infrastructure as a Service gives the customer basic building blocks: virtual servers, storage and networks. The customer installs and manages the operating system, databases and applications. It is like renting an empty flat: the building and utilities are provided, but you bring your own furniture and do your own cleaning. Examples are virtual machines from providers such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.

Service model 2, PaaS: Platform as a Service gives developers a ready platform to build and run their applications without managing servers or operating systems. The provider handles the OS, runtime, scaling and patching; the developer uploads the code and data. It is like renting a furnished flat: you just move in with your clothes. Managed database services and app hosting platforms are typical PaaS offerings.

Service model 3, SaaS: Software as a Service delivers complete applications over the internet, usually through a browser or app, on a subscription. The customer only uses the software; the provider handles everything underneath. It is like staying in a hotel: you just use the room. Gmail, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, online accounting tools and cloud CRM systems are common SaaS examples. For most small businesses, SaaS is the easiest entry to the cloud.

Who manages what: A simple way to compare the three is to ask who looks after each layer. With on-premises IT, the company manages everything: building, hardware, network, OS, database, application and data. With IaaS, the provider manages the building, hardware and virtualization; the customer manages the OS and above. With PaaS, the provider also manages the OS and runtime; the customer manages the application and data. With SaaS, the provider manages almost everything; the customer manages its own data, users and settings. In every model, the customer remains responsible for who has access and for using the service safely. This idea is called the shared responsibility model.

Deployment model 1, public cloud: In a public cloud, the provider's infrastructure is shared by many organizations and the general public can sign up. It offers the lowest entry cost and the most elasticity. Most start-ups and many large firms use public cloud services.

Deployment model 2, private cloud: A private cloud is cloud-style infrastructure used by one organization only. It may be in the company's own data centre or hosted by a provider but dedicated to that company. It gives more control and can help with strict rules on data, but it costs more and does not offer the same flexibility. Some banks and government bodies prefer this for sensitive systems.

Deployment models 3 and 4, hybrid and community: A hybrid cloud combines private and public clouds, with some work kept in-house and some sent to the public cloud. For example, a bank may keep its core banking database in its own data centre while using a public cloud SaaS tool for email and staff training. A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common needs, such as a group of universities. Many companies today also use multiple public cloud providers, which is called multi-cloud.

Pay-as-you-go economics, a worked example: Suppose an online shop's website normally needs 2 servers, but during the Eid sale week it needs 10. If it buys its own servers, it must buy 10 to survive the peak, and 8 of them sit idle about 51 weeks a year. Say each owned server costs 1.5 lakh taka a year including purchase spread over its life, power and maintenance: 10 servers cost 15 lakh a year. In the cloud, suppose a similar server costs 15,000 taka per month or about 3,500 taka per week. Normal weeks: 2 servers x 51 weeks x 3,500 = 3,57,000 taka. Eid week: 10 x 3,500 = 35,000 taka. Total about 3.9 lakh taka. The numbers are only illustrative, but they show the principle: when demand is uneven, paying for use can be much cheaper than owning for the peak.

When cloud is not cheaper: If a workload runs at full power all day, every day, for many years, owning the hardware can sometimes cost less than renting it. Data transfer fees, premium support and forgotten resources that keep running can also make bills larger than expected. Good cloud management means watching usage, switching off unused servers and choosing the right size. Some companies have moved certain workloads back from the cloud for these reasons.

Benefits of cloud: Lower upfront cost, fast setup in minutes instead of months, elasticity for peaks, access from anywhere, automatic software updates in SaaS, and access to advanced tools like analytics and machine learning services without building them. Big providers also spread data across multiple data centres, which can give better reliability than a small company's single server room.

Risks and concerns: Vendor lock-in: once data and applications are built around one provider's special services, moving away can be slow and expensive. Outages: if the provider or your internet connection fails, you cannot work; even big providers have had outages. Data location and law: data may be stored in another country, and some sectors, such as banking, may face rules about where certain data can be kept, so managers must check current regulations. Security and privacy: the provider secures the infrastructure, but misconfigured settings by the customer, like a storage folder left open to the public, are a common cause of data leaks. Cost control: easy self-service can lead to surprise bills.

Real life example 1, a small Bangladeshi business choosing SaaS: Consider a 30-person garments buying house in Banani. It needs email, shared documents, accounting and a way to track buyer orders. Running its own email server and accounting server would need an IT person, a server room, backup power and regular maintenance. Using SaaS email and office tools, an online accounting service and a simple cloud order tracker costs a monthly fee per user, works on laptops and phones, and keeps data backed up by the provider. The main things to check: reliable internet with a backup connection, strong passwords with two-step verification, who owns and can export the data, and the monthly cost as staff grows. For a business like this, SaaS is usually the sensible default.

Real life example 2, a university in exam season: A private university's result website gets very little traffic most of the year, then thousands of students check results within the same hour. If the site runs on a single small server, it crashes. If the university buys a big server for that one hour, the server idles the rest of the year. Hosting on an elastic cloud platform lets the site scale up automatically during result publication and scale down afterwards. Meanwhile, students and teachers may already be using SaaS tools such as online classrooms and shared drives.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think the cloud means data is not stored anywhere physical. It is stored in real data centres; you just do not manage them. Another mistake is mixing up service models and deployment models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe what is provided; public, private, hybrid and community describe who shares it. Also, cloud does not remove the customer's responsibility for security. Typical exam questions: define cloud computing and its characteristics; compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with examples; compare public, private and hybrid clouds; discuss benefits and risks for a business; explain why pay-as-you-go helps with uneven demand.

Recap: Cloud computing delivers computing resources as metered, elastic services over a network. Its five characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. IaaS rents infrastructure, PaaS rents a platform for developers, and SaaS rents finished applications; the higher you go, the less the customer manages. Clouds can be public, private, hybrid or community. Cloud turns capital spending into operating spending and suits uneven demand, but brings risks of lock-in, outages, data location rules, misconfiguration and surprise bills. Like choosing between owning a car, renting one or calling a ride, the right choice depends on how you travel.
key_points: Cloud computing provides computing resources as services over a network that can scale up and down quickly.
Five characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.
IaaS rents servers, storage and networks; PaaS rents a ready platform for developers; SaaS rents complete applications.
Higher service models mean the provider manages more layers, but the customer always stays responsible for access and data use.
Deployment models: public, private, hybrid and community; using several public providers is called multi-cloud.
Cloud turns big capital spending into pay-as-you-go operating spending, which suits uneven demand.
Risks include vendor lock-in, outages, data location rules, misconfiguration leaks and surprise bills.
For most small businesses, SaaS tools are the easiest and most sensible start.
lessons.tip: Remember the service models with the housing analogy: IaaS is an empty flat, PaaS is a furnished flat, SaaS is a hotel room. Then just ask who cleans what.
lessons.task: Open your phone and list five apps or services you use that are SaaS, for example email, cloud storage or online classes. For one of them, write what you manage yourself (account, data, settings) and what the provider manages. Then write one risk for you if that service stopped working for a day.

quiz.q: A company rents virtual servers and installs its own operating system and database on them. Which service model is this?
quiz.explain: In IaaS the provider gives raw infrastructure and the customer manages the OS and everything above it.

quiz.q: Which cloud characteristic lets an online shop add servers for a sale day and remove them afterwards?
quiz.explain: Rapid elasticity means capacity can grow and shrink quickly with demand.

quiz.q: A bank keeps its core database in its own data centre but uses a public cloud email service. This is a:
quiz.explain: Combining private and public cloud resources is a hybrid cloud.

quiz.q: Which of these is a SaaS example?
options: An online email and office suite used through a browser
A server bought for the company's own room
A network cable between two branches
quiz.explain: SaaS delivers complete software over the internet; the customer just uses it.

quiz.q: Which is a real risk of cloud computing for a business?
options: It always needs a big upfront hardware purchase
Data is never stored in any physical place
Vendor lock-in and outages that stop work
The customer has no responsibility for security
quiz.explain: Lock-in and outages are real risks; cloud data is in real data centres and the customer still shares security responsibility.

lessons.title: Data Resource Management
lessons.content:
Imagine a family where everyone keeps their own list of relatives' phone numbers. Your father has Mama's old number, your mother has the new one, your sister spelled the name differently, and nobody has the number of the cousin who moved to Sylhet. When there is a wedding invitation to send, half the calls go to wrong numbers. Now imagine one shared, carefully updated family contact list that everyone uses. Same people, same phones, but far fewer mistakes. Organizations face exactly this problem at a much bigger scale. Their customers, products, suppliers and employees are recorded in many places, often differently. Data resource management is the discipline of treating data as a shared, valuable resource and looking after it properly.

What data resource management is: Data resource management means planning, organizing, controlling and protecting an organization's data so that it is accurate, available to the right people and used well. It covers how data is stored, who is responsible for it, which rules it must follow, how its quality is checked, and how it is kept secure. In the earlier lessons we said that information drives decisions. If the data underneath is wrong, the decisions will be wrong too.

Data as an asset: We usually think of assets as buildings, machines and money. But for many modern businesses, data is one of the most valuable assets. A bank's records of accounts and transactions, a telecom company's subscriber records, an e-commerce company's order history and customer reviews: these are hard to rebuild and give the firm knowledge its competitors do not have. Like any asset, data has value, has costs to maintain, can be stolen and can lose value if neglected. Thinking of data as an asset helps managers justify spending on its quality and security.

The old file approach, briefly: Before databases, each department kept its own files for its own programs. Sales had a customer file, accounts had another, delivery had a third. Your DBMS course explained the problems in detail: data redundancy (the same data stored many times), data inconsistency (the copies disagree), program-data dependence (changing a file format breaks programs), poor sharing and weak security. From a manager's view, the result is simple: different departments give different answers to the same question, like how many active customers we have.

The database approach, from a manager's chair: A database collects related data in one logically shared place, managed by a DBMS, so many applications and users can use the same data. The manager does not need to know about B+ trees or query optimizers. What matters is the business effect: one version of the customer, consistent reports across departments, easier new applications, controlled access and proper backup. When a bank customer changes their phone number once, the ATM alerts, the mobile app and the call centre all see the new number.

The logical view: Managers and users see data in terms of business entities and their relationships: a customer places orders, an order contains products, a product comes from a supplier. Database designers turn this into tables with keys, which you learned in the DBMS course with ER diagrams and normalization. In an MIS role, your job is often to make sure the database actually reflects the business: does the system allow one customer to have two delivery addresses? Can an order be split into two shipments? Wrong business assumptions in the design cause endless trouble later.

Data quality: Data quality means how well data fits its purpose. The common dimensions are accuracy (is it correct?), completeness (is anything missing?), consistency (do different systems agree?), timeliness (is it up to date?), validity (does it follow the format and rules, such as a phone number having the right number of digits?) and uniqueness (is the same customer recorded only once?). Poor data quality has real costs: parcels sent to wrong addresses, bills sent to customers who left, double counting of sales, and managers who stop trusting reports.

Where bad data comes from: Most bad data comes from simple causes. Typing mistakes at data entry, free-text fields where people write the same thing differently (Dhaka, Dhaka City, DHK), missing validation in forms, copying data between systems by hand, merging two companies' records, and data that simply goes out of date because people move or change numbers. A useful worked example: a courier company finds that 4 percent of 10,000 daily parcels have incomplete addresses. That is 400 parcels a day that may be delayed or returned. If each failed delivery costs 60 taka in extra handling, that is 24,000 taka a day, or roughly 87 lakh taka a year, from one data quality problem.

Fixing data quality: There are two sides. Prevention means stopping bad data from entering: drop-down lists instead of free text, format checks, mandatory fields, verifying phone numbers with an OTP, and checking for duplicates before creating a new customer. Cleansing means finding and correcting bad data already stored: standardizing formats, merging duplicates, filling gaps from reliable sources. Prevention is almost always cheaper. A data quality audit, checking a sample of records against reality, tells managers how big the problem is.

Measuring quality with simple numbers: What gets measured gets managed, so good teams turn data quality into a few simple percentages. Suppose an audit checks 500 customer records. 30 have no email, 15 have a phone number in the wrong format, and 25 turn out to be duplicates of other records. Completeness for email is (500 - 30) / 500 = 94 percent; validity of phone numbers is (500 - 15) / 500 = 97 percent; and the duplicate rate is 25 / 500 = 5 percent. The manager can set targets, such as fewer than 1 percent duplicates, and check the same numbers every month on a small dashboard. This turns a vague complaint, our data is bad, into a problem that can be tracked and fixed.

Master data: Master data is the core shared data about the key business entities: customers, products, suppliers, employees, locations. It changes slowly and is used by many processes. Transaction data, in contrast, records events: a sale, a payment, a delivery. Master data management, or MDM, is the set of processes and tools that keep one trusted, consistent version of master data across all systems. For example, a supershop chain decides that the product code, name, unit and VAT rate for every item are created only by one central team, and every branch's point-of-sale system receives them from that master list.

Data governance: Data governance is the set of policies, roles and processes that decide who owns which data, who can create or change it, what quality standards apply, how long it is kept, and how privacy and legal rules are followed. Typical roles include a data owner, usually a business manager responsible for a set of data such as customer data, and data stewards who look after its quality day to day. Governance answers questions like: can the marketing team use transaction history to send offers, and does the customer need to agree first?

Data administration versus database administration: These two sound similar but are different. Data administration is a business and management function. It sets policies, defines data standards and the meaning of key terms, plans data needs and works with governance. Database administration is a technical function. The database administrator (DBA) designs and tunes the physical database, manages access rights, backups, recovery and performance. In short, the data administrator decides what the data should mean and who should use it; the DBA makes the database work correctly and efficiently.

A data dictionary: To make data shareable, an organization needs agreed meanings. A data dictionary, or metadata repository, describes each data element: its name, meaning, type, format, allowed values, owner and which systems use it. For example, the term active customer might be defined as a customer with at least one transaction in the last 90 days. Without such a definition, sales may count 50,000 active customers and finance may count 35,000, and both are right according to their own private meaning.

Data lifecycle and retention: Data has a life: it is created, stored, used, shared, archived and finally deleted. Some data must be kept for a certain time because of laws or regulations, such as financial records for tax or audit. Other data, especially personal data, should not be kept longer than needed. Old data that nobody uses still costs money to store and protect, and it can become a liability if leaked. Managers should know the retention rules that apply to their sector rather than guessing.

Access and security, briefly: Data resource management includes deciding who can see and change which data. A teller may see a customer's balance but not change the interest rate; a branch manager may approve but not delete transactions. These access rights, along with backup and encryption, protect the data asset. Lessons 22 and 23 cover security and controls in depth.

Real life example 1, a mobile financial service: A mobile financial service like bKash keeps records of millions of customers and their transactions. Each customer must be uniquely identified, usually linked to a verified phone number and national ID information collected during registration. If the same person accidentally got two accounts, or an account was linked to the wrong ID, fraud checks and regulatory reporting would fail. Strong validation at registration, consistent customer master data and strict control over who can view or change records are central to running such a service safely.

Real life example 2, a hospital: A private hospital in Chattogram has a lab system, a pharmacy system and a billing system bought from different vendors. A patient is registered as Md. Rahim Uddin in one, Rahim Uddin in another and M. Rahim in the third, with different phone formats. Doctors cannot see all test results together, and billing misses some charges. The hospital creates a single patient registration process that issues one patient ID, used by all three systems, and appoints a records officer as the data steward. Within months, duplicate records fall, and doctors trust the combined patient history.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often treat data management as only a technical database topic. In MIS it is mainly about ownership, quality, policy and business value. Another mistake is mixing up data administration and database administration. Also remember that master data is shared reference data, while transaction data records events. Typical exam questions: explain why data is an organizational asset; list problems of the traditional file environment and how the database approach solves them; describe data quality dimensions with examples; explain data governance and master data management; distinguish data administrator and DBA roles.

Recap: Data resource management treats data as a valuable shared asset and plans, organizes, controls and protects it. The database approach gives one shared, consistent version of data instead of scattered department files. Data quality has dimensions like accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness, and prevention is cheaper than cleansing. Master data management keeps key entities consistent across systems, and data governance sets ownership, standards and rules. Data administration is the policy side; database administration is the technical side. Like that shared family contact list, good data management means fewer wrong numbers and better decisions for everyone.
key_points: Data resource management plans, organizes, controls and protects data so it is accurate, available and used well.
Data is an organizational asset: valuable, costly to maintain, hard to rebuild and worth protecting.
Scattered department files cause redundancy, inconsistency and different answers to the same question; a shared database fixes this.
Data quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness.
Preventing bad data at entry is cheaper than cleansing it later.
Master data is core shared data about customers, products, suppliers and employees; MDM keeps one trusted version.
Data governance sets owners, stewards, standards, access rules and retention.
Data administration is the policy and business side; database administration is the technical side run by the DBA.
lessons.tip: In exam answers about data, always link the technical idea to a business cost: a duplicate customer means two bills, a missing address means a returned parcel. Examiners in MIS reward that link.
lessons.task: Open the contacts list on your phone and check 20 contacts. Count duplicates, missing names, inconsistent formats (with or without +88) and out-of-date numbers. Write the percentage of records with at least one quality problem, and write two rules that would have prevented them.

quiz.q: The same customer is recorded three times with different spellings. Which data quality dimension is mainly violated?
quiz.explain: Uniqueness means each real entity is recorded once; duplicates break it.

quiz.q: Which of these is master data rather than transaction data?
options: A product's code, name and VAT rate
quiz.explain: Master data describes key entities like products; transactions record events like payments.

quiz.q: Who mainly handles physical database tuning, backups and recovery?
quiz.explain: Database administration is the technical function performed by the DBA.

quiz.q: What is data governance?
options: Policies, roles and processes that decide ownership, standards, access and retention of data
A program that deletes old files automatically
The speed of a database query
quiz.explain: Governance sets the rules and responsibilities for how data is managed and used.

quiz.q: Why is preventing bad data usually better than cleansing it later?
options: Prevention is usually cheaper and stops wrong decisions before they happen
Databases cannot be changed after data is stored
Prevention removes the need for any backups
quiz.explain: Stopping errors at entry costs less and avoids the damage bad data causes before it is found.

lessons.title: Business Intelligence and Analytics
lessons.content:
Think of a cricket team's analyst. During the match, the scorer records every ball: who bowled, who batted, how many runs, where the ball went. That is the day-to-day record. After the series, the analyst takes thousands of these ball-by-ball records and asks bigger questions. Which bowler does our opener struggle against? On which grounds do we lose wickets early? What happens to our run rate in the last five overs? The scorer's sheet keeps the game going; the analyst's work changes the strategy for the next tour. Businesses work the same way. Their transaction systems record every sale and payment, and business intelligence turns that mountain of records into answers that change strategy.

What business intelligence is: Business intelligence, or BI, is the set of technologies, processes and practices for gathering, storing, analysing and presenting data so that managers can make better decisions. It includes data warehouses, reporting tools, OLAP, dashboards and data mining. Business analytics usually refers to the analysis side: using statistics, models and other techniques to understand the past and predict the future. In everyday use the two terms overlap a lot, and many people say BI and analytics together.

Why managers need it: The transaction processing systems we met in lesson 5 hold huge amounts of data, but they are built to record events quickly, not to answer big questions. A branch manager cannot easily ask the point-of-sale database, how did sales of each product category change in every region over the last three years? BI provides the data structures and tools for exactly these questions, and it lets managers explore data themselves instead of waiting weeks for the IT team to write a report.

OLTP versus OLAP, a quick recap: Your DBMS course introduced the two kinds of workload. Online transaction processing, OLTP, handles many short operations on current data: insert one sale, update one balance. It must be fast and correct for each transaction. Online analytical processing, OLAP, handles fewer but much bigger queries over lots of historical data: total sales by month, region and product for five years. Running heavy analytical queries on the live transaction database can slow it down for customers at the counter. That is one big reason organizations copy data into a separate store built for analysis.

The data warehouse: A data warehouse is a database that stores current and historical data from many sources across the organization, organized for reporting and analysis. A classic definition describes it as subject-oriented (organized around subjects like customer, product, sales rather than applications), integrated (data from different systems made consistent), time-variant (keeps history over time) and non-volatile (data is loaded and read, not constantly updated). Managers can query the warehouse freely without disturbing the operational systems.

The data mart: A data mart is a smaller, focused subset of the warehouse for one department or subject, such as a sales data mart or a finance data mart. It is easier and cheaper to build, and gives a department exactly the data it needs. Some organizations start with one data mart to prove value before building a full warehouse, though separate marts built without a common plan can recreate the islands of data that warehouses were meant to fix.

ETL, getting data in: Data reaches the warehouse through a process called ETL. Extract: copy data from source systems such as POS, ERP, the website and spreadsheets. Transform: clean and convert it so it fits together. For example, one system writes the date as 05/03/2025 and another as 2025-03-05; one says Dhaka and another DHK; one stores amounts in taka and another in dollars. Transform also removes duplicates and calculates fields like profit. Load: write the cleaned data into the warehouse, usually on a schedule such as every night. The transform step is where much of the real work is, and it connects directly to the data quality ideas from lesson 11.

The data cube idea: Analysts like to think of warehouse data as a cube. Each side of the cube is a dimension: for example time, product and region. Each cell holds a measure, such as sales amount. One cell might say: in March 2025, rice, in Khulna region, sales were 18 lakh taka. Real cubes often have more than three dimensions, like customer type and sales channel, but the cube picture helps. In database terms, this is often stored as a star schema: a central fact table of sales surrounded by dimension tables for time, product, store and customer. Your DBMS course showed the schema; here we focus on how managers use it.

OLAP operations: Managers explore the cube with a few standard operations. Slice: fix one dimension to one value and look at the rest, such as only the year 2024.
