Dice: choose a sub-cube by picking ranges on several dimensions, such as only Dhaka and Chattogram, only food and cosmetics, only the last two quarters. Drill down: go from summary to detail, such as from yearly sales to monthly, then to daily. Roll up: go the other way, from detail to summary, such as from districts up to divisions. Pivot: rotate the view, putting products in rows and regions in columns instead of the reverse. Worked example: a supershop CEO sees that total 2024 sales fell 5 percent. She drills down by region and sees Sylhet fell 20 percent while others were flat. She drills down in Sylhet by month and finds the drop began in June. She slices by store and sees one large store's sales dropped sharply after a new competitor opened nearby. In five clicks, a vague worry became a specific problem.

Dashboards and KPIs: A key performance indicator, or KPI, is a measure that shows how well the organization is achieving an important goal. Examples: daily sales per store, on-time delivery rate, customer complaints per 1,000 orders, average loan default rate, production efficiency per line. A dashboard shows a few KPIs together on one screen, often with charts and traffic-light colours: green for on target, amber for warning, red for trouble. A good dashboard has few, carefully chosen KPIs, each with a target, and links to drill down. Remember bounded rationality from lesson 8: a dashboard with 50 numbers helps nobody.

Three levels of analytics: Analytics is often grouped by the question it answers. Descriptive analytics asks what happened: last month's sales, top products, the number of complaints. Most reports and dashboards are descriptive. Predictive analytics asks what is likely to happen: next month's demand, which customers may leave, which loans may default. It uses statistics and machine learning on historical data. Prescriptive analytics asks what we should do: the best order quantity, the best delivery routes, which price to set. It uses optimization and simulation, often on top of predictions. Some books also mention diagnostic analytics, why did it happen, which is what the drill-down example above was doing.

Data mining: Data mining means discovering useful patterns in large data sets. Common pattern types: associations (customers who buy bread often buy eggs too), sequences (customers who buy a phone often buy a cover within a week), classification (sorting loan applicants into likely-to-repay and risky groups), clustering (finding natural groups of customers with similar habits) and forecasting (estimating future values from trends). A supershop that finds tea and biscuits are often bought together might place them close to each other or offer a combo deal. Patterns are clues, not proof of cause, so managers should test them before acting.

Big data: Big data refers to data sets so large or fast or varied that traditional tools struggle to handle them. It is usually described with three Vs. Volume: huge amounts, such as every click and every call record. Velocity: data arriving very fast, such as real-time payment streams or sensor readings. Variety: many forms, including text, images, video, location data and social media posts, not just neat tables. Some writers add veracity, meaning how trustworthy the data is, and value. Handling big data needs distributed storage and processing across many machines, and it is often done on cloud platforms.

Self-service BI: In the past, every new report meant a request to the IT department and a long wait. Modern BI tools let business users connect to prepared data, drag fields onto a chart and build their own views. This is called self-service BI. It speeds things up, but it needs two things to work: a well-governed data source, so that everyone's numbers agree, and data literacy, meaning managers who can read a chart, understand an average versus a median, and spot a misleading scale.

Limits of BI: BI shows patterns, not causes. Ice cream and soft drink sales both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other. BI also looks backward unless predictive models are added, and predictions can be wrong when conditions change suddenly, as happened to many demand forecasts during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Finally, insight has value only if someone acts on it. A dashboard nobody opens is just an expensive picture.

Real life example 1, a mobile operator: A mobile operator in Bangladesh has millions of subscribers making calls, using data and recharging. Its BI team loads daily usage and recharge data into a warehouse. Descriptive dashboards show revenue by region and package. A predictive model flags subscribers whose usage has fallen sharply and who stopped recharging, a sign they might switch to another operator. The marketing team sends those customers a targeted offer. This is the link between BI and the CRM ideas we will see in lesson 18.

Real life example 2, a garments factory: A knitwear factory in Narayanganj collects production data from each line every hour: pieces made, defects, machine downtime. A BI dashboard on the production manager's screen shows efficiency per line with colour codes. When line 7 turns red, she drills down and sees most defects come from one operation, attaching collars, during the night shift. She arranges extra training and a machine check. Over months, the factory uses historical data to predict how long new styles will take, which helps merchandisers give buyers realistic delivery dates.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes think a data warehouse is just a bigger backup of the operational database. It is a separate, integrated, historical store designed for analysis. Another mistake is mixing up drill down and roll up, or slice and dice: slice fixes one dimension, dice picks a sub-cube on several. Also, BI tools do not make decisions by themselves; poor data in means poor insight out. Typical exam questions: define BI and analytics; compare OLTP and OLAP; describe the characteristics of a data warehouse and the ETL process; explain OLAP operations with an example; distinguish descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics; explain the Vs of big data.

Recap: Business intelligence gathers, stores, analyses and presents data so managers decide better. Transaction systems are built for OLTP; analysis needs OLAP on a separate data warehouse that is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile, fed by ETL. Data marts serve single departments. Managers explore data cubes with slice, dice, drill down, roll up and pivot, and watch KPIs on dashboards. Analytics can be descriptive, predictive or prescriptive, data mining finds patterns, and big data is marked by volume, velocity and variety. Like the cricket analyst, BI turns ball-by-ball records into a smarter plan for the next match.
key_points: Business intelligence is the technologies and processes that turn stored data into insight for decisions; analytics is the analysis side.
OLTP handles many short operations on current data; OLAP handles big analytical queries on historical data.
A data warehouse is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile; a data mart is a focused subset for one department.
ETL extracts data from sources, transforms and cleans it, and loads it into the warehouse.
OLAP operations: slice, dice, drill down, roll up and pivot on a data cube of dimensions and measures.
Dashboards show a few KPIs with targets and colours; too many numbers defeat the purpose.
Descriptive analytics says what happened, predictive what will likely happen, prescriptive what to do.
Big data is described by volume, velocity and variety; data mining finds associations, clusters, classifications and forecasts.
lessons.tip: For OLAP questions, always draw a small three-dimensional cube with labelled axes (time, product, region) and show one slice and one drill down with arrows. A clear diagram explains it faster than a paragraph.
lessons.task: Make a small table in a notebook or spreadsheet of your own spending for two weeks: date, category (food, transport, mobile, study) and amount. Then roll up by week, drill down into the biggest category by day, and write one KPI with a target you would track next month.

quiz.q: Which property means a data warehouse keeps data over time rather than only the current value?
quiz.explain: Time-variant means the warehouse keeps historical data so trends can be analysed.

quiz.q: A manager moves from yearly sales to monthly sales to daily sales. Which OLAP operation is this?
quiz.explain: Drill down goes from summary to more detailed levels.

quiz.q: In ETL, which step converts formats, removes duplicates and makes data from different systems consistent?
quiz.explain: The transform step cleans and converts data so it fits together before loading.

quiz.q: Predicting which customers are likely to leave next month is an example of:
quiz.explain: Predictive analytics estimates what is likely to happen using historical data.

quiz.q: Which set lists the three classic Vs of big data?
quiz.explain: Big data is classically described by volume, velocity and variety; veracity and value are sometimes added.

lessons.title: Telecommunications and the Internet for Business
lessons.content:
Not long ago, a garments worker in Gazipur who wanted to send money to her mother in a village in Rangpur had few good options. She could send it with a trusted person going home, use the post office, or wait until she could go home herself. Each option was slow, risky or both. Today she presses a few keys on a basic phone, and the money reaches her mother's mobile wallet in seconds. Her mother walks to a nearby shop agent and takes out cash. Nothing about the money itself changed. What changed was the network that connects people, phones, agents and a central system. This lesson is about telecommunications networks and the internet seen from a business point of view: what they are, how organizations use them, and why they have changed whole industries.

What telecommunications means for a business: Telecommunications is the transmission of information over distance using electronic means: cables, radio waves, satellites and the equipment that connects them. For an organization, a network is what connects its people, branches, customers, suppliers and systems so that information can move between them. A bank's branches, ATMs and mobile app all depend on networks to reach the central database. Without the network, each branch would be an island.

What this lesson covers and what it does not: Your Data Communication and Computer Networks courses explain how signals, protocols, routing and the TCP/IP stack actually work. Here we look at networks the way a manager does: what types of networks a business uses, what services they provide, what they cost, how they create new business models, and what risks they bring. If a technical term appears, it is only to name the idea, not to teach its internals.

The basic parts of a business network: Even a small office network has a few standard parts. Client devices such as PCs, laptops and phones. Servers that provide shared services such as files, email or applications. Network interface hardware built into every device. A connection medium, either wired cables or wireless radio. Switches that connect devices inside a local network, and routers that connect one network to another, such as the office network to the internet. Network operating system features and security devices such as firewalls. For a manager, the important thing is that each part has a cost, needs maintenance, and can be a point of failure.

Bandwidth and cost, a manager's sum: Network capacity is measured as bandwidth, in bits per second. A manager does not need to know modulation, but should be able to estimate needs. Suppose a branch has 20 staff, and each needs about 2 Mbps on average for the core banking app, email and video calls. That is 40 Mbps. Adding a safety margin of about 50 percent for busy hours gives roughly 60 Mbps. If the main link fails, a backup link of even 20 Mbps keeps the most important work running. This kind of rough sum helps compare offers from internet providers and avoid paying for far too much, or far too little.

Types of networks by area: A local area network, or LAN, connects devices in one building or campus, such as a factory office. A metropolitan area network covers a city. A wide area network, or WAN, connects locations over long distances, such as a bank's head office in Motijheel with branches in Bogura, Barishal and Cox's Bazar. Many organizations rent WAN links from telecom operators or use secure connections over the internet instead of building their own lines.

Why the internet changed business: The internet is a global network of networks that all use the same set of open standards, mainly TCP/IP. Because the standards are open and shared, any organization can connect to everyone else at relatively low cost. Before the internet, connecting with a supplier's computer often meant an expensive private link set up just for that partner. With the internet, a garments factory can exchange emails, files and order data with buyers in Europe, suppliers in China and banks in Dhaka using the same connection. This universal connectivity is the foundation of e-commerce, cloud computing and mobile services.

Key internet services for business: The internet is the road; services are the vehicles. Email and instant messaging for communication. The World Wide Web for websites, online stores and web applications. Voice over IP, or VoIP, which sends phone calls as data over the internet, often at lower cost than traditional calls. Video conferencing for meetings with partners and remote staff. File transfer and cloud storage for sharing documents. Each of these replaced slower or more expensive older methods, such as fax, courier and long-distance phone calls.

Intranet: An intranet is a private network inside an organization that uses internet technologies such as web browsers and web servers, but is accessible only to employees. A company might put its HR policies, leave forms, phone directory, training materials and internal news on its intranet. Because staff already know how to use a browser, little training is needed. The benefit is that everyone sees the same, current version of documents, instead of old printed copies in different offices.

Extranet: An extranet is a private network that uses internet technologies and allows controlled access to selected outsiders, such as suppliers, distributors or key customers. A garments exporter might give a foreign buyer extranet access to see the status of each order: fabric received, cutting started, sewing at 60 percent, shipment booked. A pharmaceutical company might let distributors place orders and check stock through an extranet. The key word is controlled: outsiders see only what they are allowed to see.

VPN: A virtual private network, or VPN, creates an encrypted, secure connection across the public internet, so that it behaves like a private line. A sales manager working from home or travelling can connect to the company network through a VPN and use internal systems safely. Companies also use VPNs to connect branch offices over the internet instead of renting expensive dedicated lines. The trade-off is that performance depends on the quality of the internet connection underneath.

Mobile and wireless: Wireless networks let users connect without cables. Wi-Fi gives wireless access within a building or area. Cellular networks, from 2G to 4G and 5G, give mobile voice and data across the country. For businesses this means staff can work from the field: a sales representative takes orders on a tablet in a shop in Jessore, a delivery rider updates parcel status on a phone, a field officer of a microfinance institution records loan collections in a village. Even simple technologies matter: SMS for alerts and OTPs, and USSD codes that work on basic feature phones without internet.

Mobile financial services in Bangladesh: Mobile financial services, or MFS, let people store, send and receive money using a mobile phone account. Bangladesh is well known for MFS. Services such as bKash, Nagad and Rocket allow users to send money, pay bills, buy airtime, pay merchants and receive salaries or government allowances. The sector is regulated by Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. A key idea is the agent network: shops in towns and villages act as agents where customers can cash in (give cash, get e-money) and cash out (give e-money, get cash). This combines a digital network with a physical one.

Real life example 1, how an MFS transaction flows: When a user sends 1,000 taka, her phone sends a request over the mobile network, through an app or a USSD menu, to the provider's central system. The system checks her PIN, her balance and any limits, then in one transaction subtracts 1,000 from her account and adds it to the receiver's account, records the transaction, and sends confirmation messages to both parties. This is the TPS idea from lesson 5 running over a telecom network. Because the whole service depends on the network and the central system, uptime, speed and security are critical. A short outage on a salary day can affect huge numbers of people.

Why MFS mattered: Before MFS, many people in Bangladesh, especially in rural areas, had no bank account. Opening one meant travelling to a branch, filling in forms and keeping a minimum balance. A mobile wallet only needs a phone and a valid ID, and agents are close by. This brought many people into the formal financial system, a process called financial inclusion. It also changed businesses: garments factories began paying wages digitally, small shops started accepting digital payments, and e-commerce sites gained another payment option besides cash on delivery.

Internet of Things in business, briefly: The Internet of Things, or IoT, means everyday objects with sensors that send data over a network. Examples in business include GPS trackers on delivery trucks, temperature sensors in cold storage for medicines or fish, smart electricity meters, and machine sensors on factory lines that report downtime automatically. IoT gives managers real-time data without manual entry, but it also creates more devices to secure and more data to manage.

Benefits and risks of networks for business: Benefits include faster communication, lower costs, the ability to work from anywhere, real-time data, closer links with customers and suppliers, and entirely new business models like MFS and ride sharing. Risks include dependence on connectivity (an internet outage stops the business), security threats from outside attackers, costs that grow with bandwidth needs, and unequal access, since rural areas may have weaker coverage. Managers should plan backup connections, such as a second internet provider or mobile data as backup, for critical operations.

Real life example 2, a pharmaceutical distributor: A medicine distributor in Bogura serves hundreds of pharmacies. Its sales representatives carry phones with an ordering app. When a pharmacy orders, the order travels over the mobile network to the company's system, which checks stock in the regional depot and schedules a van. Pharmacies can also check their account balance through an extranet portal. Head office managers, connected by a VPN when travelling, see daily orders by area. The distributor did not build any of the networks itself; it uses the mobile operators and the internet, and focuses on the business.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up intranet and extranet. Intranet is for insiders only; extranet gives controlled access to selected outsiders. Another common confusion is between the internet and the web: the internet is the network; the web is one service that runs on it. Also, a VPN is not a separate physical cable; it is an encrypted tunnel across a public network. Typical exam questions: explain the components of a business network; compare LAN and WAN; define intranet, extranet and VPN with business examples; discuss how mobile technology and MFS have changed business in Bangladesh; list the benefits and risks of networks for organizations.

Recap: Telecommunications networks connect people, branches, partners and systems so information can flow. Businesses use LANs inside buildings and WANs between locations, and the internet's open standards made universal, low-cost connection possible. Key services include email, the web, VoIP and video conferencing. Intranets serve employees, extranets give controlled access to partners, and VPNs create secure tunnels over the public internet. Mobile and wireless networks, from SMS and USSD to 4G, enabled field work and mobile financial services like bKash, Nagad and Rocket, which brought many people into the financial system. Like the money that travels from Gazipur to Rangpur in seconds, a good network makes distance almost disappear for a business.
key_points: A business network connects people, branches, partners and systems so information can flow between them.
Basic parts: clients, servers, connection media, switches inside a network, routers between networks, and security devices.
LANs cover a building or campus; WANs connect distant locations such as a bank's branches.
The internet's open TCP/IP standards made low-cost universal connection possible, enabling e-commerce and cloud.
An intranet is for employees only; an extranet gives controlled access to selected outsiders; a VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the public internet.
Mobile and wireless networks, including SMS and USSD, let staff work in the field and reach customers on basic phones.
Mobile financial services such as bKash, Nagad and Rocket, regulated by Bangladesh Bank, use agent networks for cash in and cash out and widened financial inclusion.
Networks bring speed and new business models but also dependence on connectivity and security risks.
lessons.tip: For network questions in MIS, always answer with a business example: who is connected, what information flows, and what decision or service it makes possible. Pure protocol detail belongs to the networks course.
lessons.task: Draw a simple diagram of how money moves when you send 500 taka by a mobile wallet: your phone, the mobile network, the provider's central system, the receiver's phone and an agent for cash out. Label where the PIN check, the balance update and the confirmation message happen.

quiz.q: A garments exporter lets a foreign buyer log in and see the status of its orders. This is best described as:
quiz.explain: An extranet gives controlled access to selected outsiders such as buyers and suppliers.

quiz.q: What does a VPN do?
options: Creates an encrypted secure connection across the public internet
Replaces the need for any internet connection
Physically lays a private cable between offices
Stores files on the user's phone
quiz.explain: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel that makes a connection over the public internet behave like a private one.

quiz.q: Which network type connects a bank's head office in Dhaka with its branches in different districts?
quiz.explain: A wide area network connects locations over long distances.

quiz.q: In mobile financial services, what does cash out mean?
options: Giving cash to an agent to add e-money
Giving e-money to an agent and receiving cash
quiz.explain: Cash out converts e-money in the wallet into physical cash through an agent.

quiz.q: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
options: They are exactly the same thing
The web is the network, the internet is a website
The internet is the global network; the web is one service running on it
The internet works only on phones
quiz.explain: The internet is the network of networks; the web is a service of linked pages and applications that uses it.

lessons.title: E-commerce I: Concepts and Types
lessons.content:
Think about how your family bought a new pressure cooker twenty years ago. Someone took a rickshaw to New Market, walked from shop to shop, asked prices, bargained, carried the box home and hoped it worked. Today your cousin opens an app on her phone at 11 at night, compares ten pressure cookers with photos and reviews, taps Order, and a delivery rider brings it to the door two days later. She pays cash when it arrives. Nothing about cooking changed. What changed is how buying and selling happen. That change has a name: electronic commerce, or e-commerce.

What e-commerce is: E-commerce means using the internet and digital technology to carry out business transactions between organizations and individuals. A transaction here means an exchange of value: money for goods or services. If you only look at a product on a website and then buy it in a shop, that is online marketing, not quite e-commerce. When the order, and usually the agreement to pay, happens through a digital channel, that is e-commerce. A related but wider term is e-business, which means using digital technology for all of a firm's internal and external processes, such as inventory, HR and supplier coordination, not only selling.

Why it matters for this course: E-commerce is where information systems touch customers most directly. Behind every online order sit the systems we have studied: a transaction processing system records the order, a database stores product and customer data, networks carry the messages, and reports tell managers what sells. In this lesson we look at what makes e-commerce different and the main types. In the next lesson we look at how e-commerce businesses earn money, how payment works and why logistics and trust are so hard.

A short history: Businesses exchanged orders electronically long before the web, using a method called electronic data interchange (EDI), where companies sent standard formatted documents like purchase orders and invoices directly between their computers. The web arrived for the public in the early 1990s, and by the late 1990s online stores were selling books, music and travel. The big boom of online shops, the crash of many weak dot-com companies around 2000, and then the slow, steady growth that followed taught one lesson: a website alone is not a business. Smartphones after about 2007 moved e-commerce from the desk to the pocket, and that is the form most people in Bangladesh know.

What makes e-commerce different: Textbooks usually list several unique features of e-commerce technology compared with a normal shop. We will go through them one by one, because exam questions love this list.

Ubiquity: E-commerce is available everywhere, at any time. A traditional market is a physical place; you must go there during opening hours. An online shop is open at 3 a.m. and you can reach it from a bus, a village or a hospital bed. This creates what is called a marketspace, a market that is not tied to a place. It also lowers the customer's cost of searching: you do not spend time and rickshaw fare to compare prices.

Global reach: The technology crosses national borders easily. A small handicraft seller in Rajshahi can, in principle, show her nakshi kantha to a buyer in another country. In practice, shipping, customs and payment limits still make cross-border selling harder than local selling, but the reach of the storefront itself is global.

Universal standards: The internet runs on shared technical standards, such as TCP/IP, HTTP and HTML, that are the same everywhere. A seller does not need a special network for each customer. This makes it cheap for a business to go online and cheap for customers to reach many sellers. Compare this with old EDI, where two companies often needed a costly private setup to talk.

Richness: Richness means how complex and detailed a message can be. A shopkeeper talking face to face can show the product, answer questions and read your expression, which is very rich, but reaches few people. A newspaper ad reaches many but carries little. E-commerce can combine both: photos, videos, specifications, reviews and live chat reaching millions at once.

Interactivity: The technology allows two-way communication. A customer can ask a question, get an answer, filter products and see the price change as she chooses size and colour. A TV advert cannot do that.

Information density: E-commerce greatly increases the amount and quality of information available to everyone. Customers can compare prices easily, which pushes prices toward transparency. Sellers, in turn, learn a great deal about customers: what they search, what they leave in the cart, when they buy.

Personalization and customization: Because sellers know so much, they can personalize: show different products to different people based on past behaviour, such as recommending cricket bats to someone who bought a ball. Customization means changing the product itself to the customer's wishes, such as printing a name on a T-shirt.

Social technology: Modern e-commerce lets users create and share content: reviews, ratings, photos, videos, live streams and shares with friends. The users themselves become part of the marketing. A product with 500 honest reviews sells differently from one with none.

Types by who trades with whom: The most common way to classify e-commerce is by the nature of the buyer and seller. Business-to-consumer (B2C) is a business selling to individual customers, like an online shop selling phones to you. Business-to-business (B2B) is a business selling to other businesses, like a fabric mill selling cloth to a garments factory through an online procurement system; B2B is usually larger in total value than B2C, because businesses buy in bulk and often. Consumer-to-consumer (C2C) is individuals selling to other individuals, usually through a platform that brings them together, like a classifieds site where you sell your old bicycle. Government-to-citizen (G2C) is the government providing services online, such as applying for a passport, paying utility bills or checking exam results. Some books also mention G2B and B2G for government and business dealings, like online tendering.

Types by technology and channel: Mobile commerce, or m-commerce, means buying and selling using phones and tablets, through apps or mobile websites. In a country where many people's first and only internet device is a phone, m-commerce is not a side channel; it is the main road. Social commerce means selling through social networks. In Bangladesh many small businesses, often called f-commerce, run entirely from a Facebook page: they post photos, take orders through messages and comments, and deliver through courier services. Local commerce means e-commerce focused on nearby customers, such as ordering food from restaurants in your area.

Following one order through the systems: Let us trace what happens when you tap Order. Step 1: the app sends your cart, address and payment choice over the internet to the seller's servers. Step 2: the order system checks that each item is in stock and reserves it, so two people cannot buy the last unit. Step 3: if you pay online, a payment system contacts your bank or mobile wallet and waits for approval; if you chose cash on delivery, the order is simply marked unpaid. Step 4: the warehouse system creates a picking list, a worker packs the box and a shipping label is printed. Step 5: the delivery system assigns the parcel to a rider and route, and you get tracking updates by SMS or notification. Step 6: when you receive it, the payment is confirmed, the sale is recorded for accounting, and the data flows into reports about what sells where. Every step is an information system task, and a failure in any one, such as wrong stock data, means an angry customer.

A small worked comparison: Suppose a home baker in Chattogram makes cakes. Option one: a small shop with rent of 20,000 taka a month, open 10 hours a day, reaching people who walk past. Option two: a Facebook page costing nothing to set up, plus some money on boosting posts, open for orders all day, reaching anyone in the city who sees the page. Option two lowers fixed costs and widens reach, but adds new work: answering messages fast, arranging delivery and building trust with buyers who cannot touch the cake before paying. That trade-off, lower entry cost but new kinds of work, is the heart of e-commerce.

Real life example 1, an online marketplace: Daraz is a well-known online marketplace in Bangladesh. The customer side is B2C: you open the app, search, compare sellers and order. But many of the products come from separate sellers who list their goods on the platform, so it brings many sellers and buyers together in one place. Notice the unique features in action: ubiquity (order any time), richness (photos, specs, reviews), interactivity (filters, chat with seller), personalization (recommendations based on what you browse) and social technology (ratings and reviews). The information system behind it must handle product catalogues, orders, payments, delivery tracking and returns for many sellers at once.

Real life example 2, online grocery: Chaldal is an online grocery service in Dhaka. Unlike a pure marketplace, it is known for keeping its own stock in warehouses and delivering groceries to homes. For a customer the value is time: no traffic, no queue, no carrying heavy bags. For the business the hard parts are perishable goods, accurate stock information and fast delivery in heavy traffic. This shows that e-commerce is never only a website. It is a website plus inventory systems, warehouses, delivery routes and customer service working together.

Limits and costs of e-commerce: It is not all good. Customers cannot touch or try products, so returns are more common, especially in clothing. Fraud and fake products damage trust. Delivery in crowded cities and remote villages is costly. Many people still prefer cash and want to see the product before paying, which is why cash on delivery is popular here. Internet access and digital skills are not equal across the country, so some customers are left out. And sellers face tough price competition because buyers can compare in seconds.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse e-commerce with e-business; remember that e-commerce is about transactions, while e-business is the wider digital running of the firm. Another mistake is to call any Facebook post e-commerce; it becomes e-commerce when an order and payment agreement happen through the digital channel. Exams often ask: list and explain the unique features of e-commerce technology; classify e-commerce by type with examples (B2C, B2B, C2C, G2C); explain m-commerce and social commerce; and discuss the benefits and limitations for a developing country. Use Bangladeshi examples you actually know, and avoid inventing statistics.

Recap: E-commerce is buying and selling through digital channels, mainly the internet and phones. Its unique features are ubiquity, global reach, universal standards, richness, interactivity, information density, personalization and customization, and social technology. By participants, it divides into B2C, B2B, C2C and G2C; by channel, there is m-commerce, social commerce and local commerce. It lowers the cost of reaching customers, but adds work in trust, delivery and returns. Next lesson we follow the money: business models, revenue models and payments.
key_points: E-commerce is using the internet and digital technology to carry out business transactions; e-business is the wider digital running of all a firm's processes.
Unique features: ubiquity, global reach, universal standards, richness, interactivity, information density, personalization and customization, social technology.
Ubiquity creates a marketspace and lowers customers' search cost.
B2C, B2B, C2C and G2C classify e-commerce by who buys and who sells; B2B is usually larger in total value than B2C.
M-commerce uses phones and tablets; social commerce (f-commerce in Bangladesh) sells through social networks like Facebook pages.
E-commerce lowers entry costs but adds work in trust, delivery, returns and fast customer service.
Behind every online shop sit TPS, databases, networks and reports working together.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with the eight unique features as rows and one app you use as the column, and write one concrete thing from that app for each feature. It is the fastest way to remember the list for exams.
lessons.task: Pick three online sellers you or your family have used (an app, a website and a Facebook page). For each, write which type it is (B2C, C2C, B2B or G2C), which channel it uses, and two unique features of e-commerce you noticed while using it.

quiz.q: Which feature of e-commerce means it is available everywhere at any time?
quiz.explain: Ubiquity means the market is reachable anywhere, any time, creating a marketspace not tied to a place.

quiz.q: A fabric mill sells cloth to a garments factory through an online procurement system. What type of e-commerce is this?
quiz.explain: Both buyer and seller are businesses, so it is business-to-business.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between e-commerce and e-business?
options: E-commerce is about digital transactions; e-business covers all of a firm's digitally enabled processes
They mean exactly the same thing
E-business is only about selling on Facebook
quiz.explain: E-business is wider: inventory, HR, supplier work and more, while e-commerce focuses on buying and selling.

quiz.q: A small business takes orders through comments and messages on its Facebook page. This is best called:
quiz.explain: Selling through social networks is social commerce, often called f-commerce in Bangladesh.

quiz.q: Which is a real limitation of e-commerce, especially in a developing country?
options: Shops can only open during the day
Customers cannot touch products before buying, so trust and returns are harder
quiz.explain: Not being able to inspect products, plus fraud and delivery costs, makes trust and returns a big challenge.

lessons.title: E-commerce II: Business Models, Payments and Logistics
lessons.content:
Two friends in Dhaka both start online businesses selling phone covers. Rafi buys 1,000 covers from a wholesaler in Chawkbazar, keeps them in his room and sells them through his own Facebook page. Nadia buys nothing. She builds a small website where many cover sellers can list their products, and she takes 10 taka from every sale. Both are e-commerce. Both sell the same kind of product. But they make money in completely different ways, carry completely different risks and need completely different information systems. That difference is what we call the business model. In the last lesson we learned what e-commerce is; in this lesson we follow the money.

Business model: A business model is a description of how a firm creates value for customers and how it captures part of that value as money. It answers questions like: who are our customers, what do we offer them, how do we deliver it, what does it cost us and how do we get paid? A revenue model is a smaller part of the business model: it describes only how the firm earns revenue. Students often mix these up. Think of the business model as the whole recipe and the revenue model as the line in the recipe that says how you charge for the dish.

Why managers care: Two online shops can look the same on screen but have very different health underneath. One may earn a small fee on every order and hold no stock; another may own a warehouse full of goods that might not sell. When a company asks you, as a software engineer, to build a platform, the business model decides what the system must track: seller accounts and commissions, or warehouse stock and purchase orders, or subscriptions and renewal dates. So the business model is not only a management topic; it is a requirements topic.

Revenue model 1, sales: The firm earns money by selling goods, information or services directly to customers. An online shop that buys shoes at 1,200 taka and sells them at 1,600 taka earns 400 taka of gross margin per pair before delivery, marketing and other costs. This is the simplest model and the one most people imagine when they hear online shop.

Revenue model 2, advertising: The firm provides content or a service, often free, and earns money by showing ads to its audience. News portals, video sites and many free apps work like this. The more visitors and the more time they spend, the more ad space can be sold. The catch is that the business depends on attention and data about users, which raises privacy questions we meet in a later lesson.

Revenue model 3, subscription: Customers pay a regular fee, monthly or yearly, for access to content or services. Video and music streaming services, online newspapers behind a paywall and many business software tools use this. The big advantage is predictable income. The challenge is churn: customers who stop paying. If 1,000 customers pay 200 taka a month and 5 percent leave every month, you must win 50 new customers every month just to stay level.

Revenue model 4, transaction fee: The firm earns a fee or commission for enabling or executing a transaction. Marketplaces take a percentage of each sale; ride-sharing apps take a share of each fare; payment services charge a small fee for some transfers. Nadia in our opening story uses this model. Her income grows with the number and value of transactions, not with stock she owns.

Revenue model 5, affiliate: The firm sends customers to another business and earns a referral fee or a percentage of the resulting sales. A tech review blog that links to an online store and earns a small commission when a reader buys is an affiliate.

Revenue model 6, freemium: The basic service is free and a premium version costs money. Many apps let you use core features free and charge for extra storage, no ads or advanced tools. The idea is that a large free user base brings in a smaller group of paying users. The danger is that too few people ever upgrade. Many real firms mix several revenue models, for example sales plus advertising plus a paid membership.

Common e-commerce business models: Textbooks list several B2C business models. An e-tailer is an online retail store that sells goods, either online-only or as the online branch of a physical shop. A marketplace or market creator builds a digital space where buyers and sellers meet, like an online auction or a multi-seller shopping platform. A transaction broker processes transactions for customers, such as online travel booking or stock trading. A content provider sells or gives away digital content like news, music or videos. A portal is a gateway to many services and content, like a big web home page. A service provider offers services online, such as online tutoring or cloud storage. A community provider creates an online space where people with similar interests interact, like social networks. In B2B, there are e-distributors that sell to many businesses, e-procurement firms that help businesses buy, and private industrial networks that link a firm with its own suppliers.

Marketplace vs inventory model, a worked comparison: Let us compare Rafi and Nadia. Rafi uses the inventory model: he buys 1,000 covers at 80 taka each, spending 80,000 taka upfront. He sells at 150 taka. If he sells all of them, revenue is 150,000 taka and gross profit is 70,000 taka. But if only 600 sell and the rest go out of fashion, revenue is 90,000 taka and gross profit drops to 10,000 taka, and 400 unsold covers sit in his room. Nadia uses the marketplace model: she takes 10 taka per sale and holds no stock. If her site handles 3,000 sales a month she earns 30,000 taka with no stock risk. But she needs many sellers and buyers before the site is useful, and she has less control over product quality and delivery. Inventory model: higher margin per item, more control, more risk. Marketplace model: low risk per item, needs scale, harder quality control. Many large platforms run a hybrid: some products from their own stock and many from outside sellers.

Payments: An online sale is not finished until the money moves. In Bangladesh the main options are cash on delivery, debit and credit cards, mobile financial services like bKash and Nagad, and internet banking. Cash on delivery, or COD, means the customer pays the delivery person in cash on receipt. It is popular because it removes the fear of paying for something that never arrives, and because many people do not use cards. But COD has real costs for the business: cash must be collected, counted, carried back and deposited; riders handle risky amounts of cash; and customers can refuse the parcel at the door, so the seller pays delivery both ways and earns nothing.

How a payment gateway works: A payment gateway is a service that connects an online shop to banks, card networks and mobile wallets so the shop can accept digital payments safely. Step by step: you click Pay; the shop sends the amount and an order ID to the gateway; the gateway shows you a secure payment page; you choose card or wallet and enter details, often with an OTP sent to your phone; the gateway passes the request to your bank or wallet provider, which checks your balance and approves or declines; the gateway tells the shop the result; the shop marks the order paid; and later the money, minus the gateway's fee, is settled into the shop's bank account. The shop never needs to store your card number, which is a big security benefit. Local gateways such as SSLCommerz, and the payment services offered by banks and wallets, play this role for many Bangladeshi sites.

Logistics, the hidden giant: In physical shops the customer does the delivery: she carries the bag home. In e-commerce the business must do it. The final step from a local hub to the customer's door is called last-mile delivery, and it is usually the most expensive and hardest part, especially with traffic, unclear addresses and customers who are not home. Many sellers use third-party courier companies, while larger platforms build their own delivery networks. The information system must assign parcels to riders, plan routes, track status and collect COD cash records.

Returns and reverse logistics: When a customer sends a product back, the flow runs in reverse: pickup, inspection, restocking or disposal, and refund. This is called reverse logistics. It costs money and time, and it is common in clothing and shoes because size and colour may not match expectations. Good product photos, accurate size charts and honest descriptions reduce returns. A clear return policy increases trust, which can increase sales even if it costs something.

Trust, the real currency: Because customers cannot touch the product or see the seller, trust is the biggest barrier in e-commerce. Businesses build trust through ratings and reviews, clear contact information, secure payment, quick replies, return and refund policies, delivery tracking and holding payments until delivery is confirmed. Fake products, fake reviews and sellers who vanish damage trust for the whole market, not only for themselves. That is why platforms invest in seller verification and complaint handling, and why governments create consumer protection rules.

Real life example 1, a marketplace platform: On a multi-seller platform like Daraz, a seller registers, lists products and receives orders through a seller dashboard. The platform handles the customer app, search, promotions, payment collection and often delivery. When the order is delivered and confirmed, the platform pays the seller the sale amount minus commission and fees. So the platform's revenue model is mainly transaction fees, and its information systems must track thousands of sellers, their stock levels as they report them, their ratings, and the money owed to each.

Real life example 2, a ride and delivery app: Pathao began with ride-sharing and also offers food and parcel delivery. Its revenue comes mainly from a share of each trip or delivery fee, a transaction fee model. The information system must match customers with nearby riders in real time, calculate fares, take payment in cash or digitally, and split the money between rider and company. The business only works if there are enough riders for customers and enough customers for riders, an example of a two-sided platform we discuss again under network effects.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Do not confuse business model with revenue model; the revenue model is only the money part. Do not assume online means low cost; delivery, returns, marketing and payment fees can eat the margin. In exams you may be asked to list and explain the main revenue models with examples, describe several B2C business models, compare marketplace and inventory models, explain how cash on delivery affects an e-commerce firm, and describe the steps of an online payment. Draw the payment flow as boxes and arrows: customer, shop, gateway, bank or wallet, and back.

Recap: A business model explains how a firm creates and captures value; a revenue model explains only how it earns money. Main revenue models are sales, advertising, subscription, transaction fee, affiliate and freemium, often mixed. The inventory model gives more control and margin but more risk; the marketplace model has less risk per item but needs scale. Payments in Bangladesh mix cash on delivery, cards, mobile wallets and banking, joined by payment gateways. Logistics, returns and trust are where many e-commerce businesses succeed or fail.
key_points: A business model describes how a firm creates and captures value; the revenue model is only how it earns money.
Six main revenue models: sales, advertising, subscription, transaction fee, affiliate and freemium; real firms often mix them.
B2C business models include e-tailer, market creator, transaction broker, content provider, portal, service provider and community provider.
Inventory model: more margin and control but stock risk; marketplace model: commission income, low stock risk, needs many buyers and sellers.
Cash on delivery builds customer trust but adds cash handling, risk and refused-parcel costs.
A payment gateway links the shop to banks and wallets, approves the payment and settles money later, so the shop need not store card details.
Last-mile delivery and reverse logistics (returns) are among the costliest parts of e-commerce.
Trust, built through reviews, secure payment, clear policies and verification, is the biggest barrier and asset in e-commerce.
lessons.tip: When you look at any app, ask two quick questions: who pays, and for what? Answering those two lines tells you its revenue model and helps you guess what its database must track.
lessons.task: Pick five apps or websites on your phone. For each, write its main revenue model (sales, advertising, subscription, transaction fee, affiliate or freemium) and one reason you think so. Then draw, on paper, the boxes and arrows of an online payment from your click to the shop getting its money.

quiz.q: A platform that earns a commission on each sale made by outside sellers mainly uses which revenue model?
quiz.explain: Earning a fee or commission for enabling each transaction is the transaction fee model.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of the inventory model compared with the marketplace model?
options: Unsold stock ties up money and may lose value
quiz.explain: The firm buys stock upfront, so unsold items mean lost money and storage costs.

quiz.q: Why is cash on delivery costly for an e-commerce business?
options: It prevents customers from ordering at night
It removes the need for delivery riders
Cash must be collected and handled, and refused parcels cost delivery both ways
quiz.explain: COD adds cash handling, security risk and losses when customers refuse parcels at the door.

quiz.q: What does a payment gateway do?
options: Connects the shop to banks and wallets to approve and settle payments securely
Stores all customers' card numbers in the shop's database
quiz.explain: The gateway handles the secure payment step and settles money, so the shop need not keep card details.

quiz.q: A music app gives basic listening for free and charges for no ads and offline downloads. This is:
quiz.explain: Free basic service plus a paid premium tier is the freemium model.

lessons.title: Enterprise Systems I: ERP
lessons.content:
Picture a garments factory in Ashulia where every department keeps its own records. Merchandising has the buyer's order in an Excel sheet. The store room has fabric stock in a register. Production writes daily output on a whiteboard and then in another sheet. Accounts keeps its own software for invoices and salaries. One morning the buyer calls: can you ship 5,000 more pieces of the same style in three weeks? The general manager asks a simple question: do we have the fabric, do we have line capacity, and what will it cost? Nobody can answer quickly. Merchandising calls the store, the store checks the register, production says they will look at their sheet, and accounts says the latest fabric prices are not entered yet. Two days later the numbers arrive, and they do not even agree with each other. This is the problem that enterprise resource planning, or ERP, was built to solve.

Islands of information: When each department has its own separate system and its own copy of data, we call them islands of information. Each island may work fine alone. The trouble starts when a business process crosses departments, and almost every important process does. The same customer, product or supplier is typed again and again in different places, with small differences. Data does not flow automatically; people re-enter it, phone each other and send spreadsheets by email. Reports from different departments disagree. Managers cannot see the whole picture, so decisions are slow and often wrong.

What ERP is: An enterprise resource planning system is an integrated software package that supports the core business processes of a whole organization using a single, shared, central database. Enterprise means the whole organization, not one department. Resource planning reflects its roots in planning materials and production. The key idea is integration: when one department records something, every other department that needs it sees it at once, because they all read and write the same database. Enterprise systems is the wider family name that also includes SCM and CRM, which we cover in the next two lessons.

A short history: ERP grew out of manufacturing. In the 1970s, material requirements planning (MRP) systems calculated what raw materials were needed and when, based on the production plan. In the 1980s, MRP II added more of the factory: capacity, shop floor and some finance. In the 1990s, vendors extended this to the whole firm, covering finance, HR, sales and procurement, and the name ERP took hold. Well-known ERP vendors today include SAP, Oracle and Microsoft Dynamics, and there are open-source options like Odoo and ERPNext that smaller firms often use, as well as local software firms building ERP for Bangladeshi industries.

How integration works, step by step: Let us follow one sales order in an ERP. Step 1: a salesperson enters an order for 10,000 shirts for a buyer. Step 2: the ERP checks finished goods stock and, finding not enough, creates a production requirement. Step 3: using the bill of materials, which lists the fabric, thread, buttons and labels per shirt, it calculates the total materials needed and compares them with stock. Step 4: for missing items, it raises purchase requisitions for the procurement team. Step 5: when materials arrive, the store records a goods receipt, and stock and accounts payable update automatically. Step 6: production records output; finished stock rises. Step 7: shipping records delivery and the system creates the invoice; accounts receivable updates. Step 8: when the buyer pays, cash is recorded and the order is closed. Each department did only its own step, but every step updated the one shared database, so the general manager can see the order's status, cost and profit at any time.

The main ERP modules: An ERP is usually sold as a set of modules that can be added as needed. Finance and accounting covers the general ledger, accounts payable and receivable, cash, fixed assets and financial reports. Sales and distribution covers quotations, orders, pricing, delivery and billing. Materials management or procurement covers purchase requisitions, purchase orders, vendors, goods receipt and inventory. Production planning covers bills of materials, work orders, capacity and scheduling. Human resources covers employee records, attendance, payroll and leave. Many ERPs also offer quality management, plant maintenance, project management and reporting modules. The modules are separate screens and functions, but they share one database.

The single database, why it matters: Because all modules use the same tables, a product, customer or supplier is stored once, as master data. If the price of a fabric changes, it changes in one place for everyone. Reports from sales, production and finance are built from the same numbers, so they agree. This also means data entered badly in one module hurts every other module, which is why ERP projects pay a lot of attention to data cleaning and data ownership before going live.

Best practices built in: ERP vendors design their software around standard ways of doing business processes, often called best practices, taken from many companies. When a firm adopts an ERP, it usually has to change some of its processes to fit the software. For example, the ERP may require that every purchase has an approved purchase order before goods can be received. A factory used to buying fabric on a phone call will have to change. This is often good, because the standard process may be more controlled. But it can also remove something special about how the firm works.

Customization, the big trade-off: A firm that dislikes the standard process has two choices: change the business to fit the software, or change the software to fit the business, which is called customization. Customization feels comfortable, but it is expensive, slows the project, can introduce bugs and makes later upgrades painful, because every vendor update must be checked against the custom code. A common piece of advice is to customize only where the process gives real competitive advantage, and accept the standard elsewhere. Configuration, meaning choosing settings the software already offers, is much safer than customization, meaning writing new code.

Benefits of ERP: First, integrated, consistent data across the firm. Second, faster processes because data flows automatically, such as quicker order fulfilment and month-end closing. Third, better control: approvals, audit trails and fewer chances for fraud. Fourth, better decisions because managers see real-time, company-wide information. Fifth, standard processes that make it easier to grow, open new branches or train new staff. Sixth, it can support compliance requirements, such as audit and reporting rules.

Costs and risks of ERP: ERP projects are famous for being difficult. Costs include software licences or subscriptions, hardware or cloud fees, consultants, customization, data migration, training and ongoing support. The hidden costs, such as staff time and the drop in productivity during the change, are often larger than the software cost. Risks include going far over budget and time, poor data migration, users resisting the new way of working, and a shaky go-live where orders cannot be shipped for days. Many ERP failures are not technical at all; they come from weak leadership, unclear processes and poor training.

Implementation approaches: There are two broad ways to switch on an ERP. Big bang means all modules go live at once across the company on one date. It is faster but very risky. Phased means going live module by module or site by site, such as finance first, then procurement, then production. It is slower but safer. Usually a project includes process mapping, deciding on configuration, data migration, testing, training, go-live and support after go-live. The detailed analysis and design steps belong to System Analysis and Design; here the key message is that ERP is as much an organizational change project as a software project.

A worked cost view: Suppose a medium factory estimates its ERP like this: software subscription 30 lakh taka over three years, consultants and configuration 25 lakh, customization 10 lakh, training and data migration 10 lakh. That is 75 lakh taka of visible cost. Now suppose it expects to save 15 lakh a year from lower stock, 8 lakh a year from fewer manual clerks moving to other work and 5 lakh a year from fewer late shipment penalties, which is 28 lakh a year. On paper, payback comes within about three years. But if customization doubles and the go-live delays production for two weeks, the picture changes quickly. This is why managers track the full cost, not just the licence price. We will learn proper project value methods in lesson 24.

Real life example 1, ERP in a garments factory: In the Bangladeshi RMG sector, an ERP typically follows the order from the buyer through costing, fabric and trims planning, purchasing, cutting, sewing, finishing, inspection and shipment. Merchandisers can see whether fabric has arrived, production planners can assign orders to lines, and finance can see the cost per order and compare it with the buyer's price. When the buyer asks for 5,000 more pieces, the manager can check fabric stock, open line capacity and estimated cost in minutes instead of days. The factory also gets better records for compliance and buyer audits.

Real life example 2, ERP in a supershop or distribution company: A company that distributes consumer goods across Bangladesh needs stock in many warehouses, sales orders from many dealers, credit limits for each dealer, and daily collections. With an ERP, a sales officer's order checks the dealer's credit limit and warehouse stock immediately; finance sees the receivable; and management sees sales by region every morning. Without integration, the same company would wait for each region to send spreadsheets, and stock-outs and overdue payments would be found too late.

Cloud ERP and small firms: Earlier, ERP needed expensive servers and large IT teams, so only big firms could afford it. Today many ERPs are offered as cloud services, paid per user per month, which lowers the starting cost and lets smaller firms use them. The trade-offs we saw in the cloud lesson still apply: dependence on the internet and the vendor, and questions about where data is stored.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often describe ERP as just accounting software; it is the integration of many functions around one database. Another mistake is thinking ERP success depends mainly on the software brand; it depends more on process change, data quality, training and leadership. Exams often ask: what are islands of information and how does ERP solve them; list ERP modules; explain the role of the central database; discuss best practices versus customization; list the benefits and challenges of ERP implementation; compare big bang and phased go-live. A step-by-step order flow through modules makes an excellent exam answer.

Recap: Separate departmental systems create islands of information with duplicate, inconsistent data. ERP integrates core processes across finance, sales, procurement, production and HR on one shared database, so one entry updates everyone. It came from MRP and MRP II. ERP brings built-in best-practice processes; firms must balance changing their process against costly customization. Benefits are consistent data, speed, control and better decisions; costs and risks are high and mostly organizational. Next we look outward from the firm to its suppliers with supply chain management.
key_points: Islands of information are separate departmental systems with duplicated, inconsistent data and no automatic flow between them.
ERP is an integrated suite of modules that runs core processes of the whole organization on one shared central database.
ERP grew from MRP (materials planning) and MRP II (wider manufacturing planning).
Common modules: finance and accounting, sales and distribution, procurement and materials, production planning, human resources.
ERP embeds best-practice processes; firms trade off changing processes against expensive, upgrade-breaking customization.
Configuration (choosing built-in settings) is far safer than customization (writing new code).
Benefits: consistent data, faster processes, better control and real-time decisions; risks: high cost, overruns, poor data migration and user resistance.
Go-live can be big bang (all at once, risky) or phased (step by step, safer).
lessons.tip: To understand any ERP, follow one order from start to finish and write down which module touches it at each step. If you can tell that story, you understand integration.
lessons.task: Think of your university or a business you know. List four departments it has and one piece of data each keeps separately (for example a student's fees, results, library fines and hostel records). Write two problems caused by these islands, and how one shared database would fix them.

quiz.q: What is the core idea that makes a system an ERP?
options: It is only used by the accounts department
Many business functions share one integrated central database
It runs only on mainframe computers
Each department keeps its own copy of data
quiz.explain: Integration through one shared database across functions is the heart of ERP.

quiz.q: ERP originally grew out of which earlier systems?
options: MRP and MRP II in manufacturing
quiz.explain: Material requirements planning and its extension MRP II were the roots of ERP.

quiz.q: Why is heavy customization of an ERP risky?
options: It removes the need for training
It raises cost, delays the project and makes vendor upgrades hard
quiz.explain: Custom code must be built, tested and rechecked at every upgrade, raising cost and risk.

quiz.q: A firm switches on all ERP modules in all sites on the same day. This is called:
quiz.explain: Going live with everything at once is the big bang approach: faster but riskier.

quiz.q: Which statement about ERP failures is most accurate?
options: They are always caused by bad hardware
They happen only in small firms
Many come from organizational issues like weak leadership, poor data and poor training
quiz.explain: ERP is an organizational change project; people, processes and data cause many failures.

lessons.title: Enterprise Systems II: Supply Chain Management
lessons.content:
Think about the T-shirt you are wearing. Cotton was grown on a farm, perhaps in another country. It was shipped to a spinning mill and turned into yarn. The yarn went to a knitting mill and became fabric, then to a dyeing unit, then to a garments factory in Gazipur where it was cut and sewn. Buttons, labels and cartons came from other suppliers. The finished shirts went by truck to Chattogram port, by ship to a foreign warehouse, then to a shop, and finally to someone who bought it. Dozens of companies, thousands of kilometres, many weeks. If any one link is late, the whole chain waits. Managing this whole flow is called supply chain management.

What a supply chain is: A supply chain is the network of organizations and business processes that procure raw materials, transform them into intermediate and finished products, and deliver the finished products to customers. It includes suppliers, manufacturers, warehouses, distributors, retailers and customers, plus the transport between them. Three things flow through it: materials or products moving mostly from supplier toward customer, information such as orders, forecasts and shipment status moving in both directions, and money moving mostly from customer back toward suppliers.

Upstream and downstream: It helps to stand at one company and look both ways. The upstream part of the supply chain is everything toward the suppliers: the company's suppliers, their suppliers, and the processes for managing them. For a garments factory, upstream means fabric mills, yarn spinners, trims suppliers and the cotton farms behind them. The downstream part is everything toward the customer: distribution, warehouses, retailers and the final buyer. For the same factory, downstream means the shipping agents, the foreign buyer's warehouses and stores. Inside the company there is also internal supply chain work: moving materials from store to cutting to sewing to finishing.

Supply chain management: Supply chain management, or SCM, is the coordination of all these activities so that the right product reaches the right place at the right time at the lowest reasonable cost. The core problem is uncertainty. Nobody knows exactly how many shirts customers will buy next month, how long a shipment will take or whether a supplier will deliver on time. Companies protect themselves by holding extra stock, called safety stock, but stock costs money: it ties up cash, needs space and can become old or out of fashion. SCM tries to cut uncertainty with better information, so that less safety stock is needed.

The bullwhip effect: One of the most famous ideas in SCM is the bullwhip effect. It means that small changes in customer demand become larger and larger changes in orders as they travel upstream through the chain. A small flick of the wrist at the handle of a whip becomes a huge crack at the tip; in the same way, a small change at the shop becomes a huge swing at the factory and its suppliers.

A worked bullwhip example: Suppose a shop normally sells 100 bottles of a soft drink per week and orders 100 from the distributor. One hot week, sales rise to 120. The shop owner thinks demand is rising and wants a safety cushion, so he orders 150. The distributor sees orders jump from 100 to 150, a 50 percent rise, and also adds a cushion, ordering 220 from the factory. The factory sees 220 instead of 100, more than double, and plans a big production run, ordering lots of extra bottles and sugar from its suppliers. Then the weather cools and shop sales fall back to 100. The shop now has extra stock and orders only 50 next week; the distributor, sitting on extra stock too, orders nothing; the factory is stuck with a warehouse full of drinks. A real demand change of 20 percent became swings of more than 100 percent upstream.

Why the bullwhip happens: It comes from distorted information. Each link sees only the orders from the link below, not real customer demand, and each adds its own guess and cushion. Ordering in large batches, delays between ordering and receiving, price promotions that make buyers order extra, and rationing during shortages, where buyers order more than they need hoping to get enough, all make it worse. The main cure is sharing accurate demand information across the chain, for example letting suppliers see actual point-of-sale data and stock levels, and reducing delays and batch sizes. Information systems are at the heart of this cure.

Push and pull: There are two broad ways to drive a supply chain. In a push-based model, also called build-to-stock, production is based on forecasts of demand, and products are pushed to warehouses and shops hoping customers will buy them. This allows efficient large production runs but risks unsold stock or shortages if the forecast is wrong. In a pull-based model, also called build-to-order or demand-driven, actual customer orders trigger production and movement, so products are pulled through the chain by demand. This reduces unsold stock, but needs fast, flexible production and quick information. Most real supply chains mix the two: for example, fabric may be pushed based on forecasts while final sewing is pulled by confirmed buyer orders.

Just-in-time: Just-in-time, or JIT, is a strategy where materials arrive exactly when they are needed for production, not earlier, so the factory holds very little stock. It was made famous by Japanese car manufacturing. JIT lowers inventory costs and exposes waste, but it is fragile: if a supplier is late or a road is blocked, production stops because there is no buffer. JIT needs reliable suppliers, short distances or dependable transport, and tight information sharing. In places with frequent transport disruptions, firms usually keep somewhat more buffer stock than pure JIT suggests.

SCM software, planning: SCM systems are usually described in two groups. Supply chain planning systems help a firm model its supply chain, forecast demand, and plan what to produce, how much stock to keep where, and how to move it. Demand planning, the forecasting part, is one of the most important functions: it estimates how much of each product customers will need, which then drives purchasing and production plans. Planning tools can answer questions like: if we expect 20 percent more orders before Eid, how much more fabric should we buy and which lines should run overtime?

SCM software, execution: Supply chain execution systems manage the flow of products through warehouses and transport day to day. They handle order fulfilment, warehouse operations such as receiving, storing, picking and packing, transportation and shipment tracking, and returns. Technologies like barcodes and RFID tags help track items automatically as they move. Many firms also exchange documents with partners electronically, for example purchase orders and advance shipping notices, so a buyer knows what is on the truck before it arrives. Global supply chains increasingly use internet-based portals and extranets where suppliers and buyers see the same order and shipment data.

A small stock calculation: SCM systems often decide when to reorder using a simple rule called the reorder point. Reorder point equals average daily demand times lead time in days, plus safety stock. Suppose a factory uses 200 metres of a lining fabric per day, the supplier takes 10 days to deliver, and the manager wants 600 metres of safety stock for surprises. The reorder point is 200 x 10 + 600 = 2,600 metres. When stock falls to 2,600 metres, the system raises a purchase order automatically. If the supplier becomes more reliable and the lead time drops to 6 days, the reorder point falls to 1,800 metres, so less money sits in the store room. Notice how better information about demand and lead time directly cuts the stock a firm must hold.

Business value of SCM: Good SCM brings lower inventory and warehouse costs, fewer stock-outs and lost sales, faster delivery, better use of factory capacity, and better relationships with suppliers and customers. One useful measure is the order cycle time, from receiving an order to delivering it. Another is inventory turnover, how many times stock is sold and replaced in a period: higher turnover usually means less money sitting idle in stock. A third is on-time delivery rate. Managers watch these numbers on dashboards.

Real life example 1, lead time in RMG: For Bangladeshi garments exporters, lead time, the time from receiving a buyer's order to shipping it, is a major competitive factor. Foreign brands want fresh styles in stores quickly. A factory that must import fabric from abroad faces a longer lead time than one with nearby local fabric mills, which is one reason backward linkage, building local spinning, knitting and dyeing capacity, matters so much in the industry. An SCM system helps by tracking each order's materials: when fabric was booked, when it shipped, when it arrived, whether trims are ready, and which orders risk missing their ship date. Instead of discovering a delay a week before shipment, the merchandiser sees the risk weeks earlier and can expedite, change suppliers or talk to the buyer.

Real life example 2, a supershop and fresh food: A supershop chain selling vegetables, fish and milk deals with perishable goods. If it orders too much, food spoils; too little, shelves are empty. Sharing daily point-of-sale data with central purchasing helps planners order closer to real demand for each branch. Planners can see that one branch sells more fish on Fridays and another sells more milk in the morning, and adjust deliveries. This is the bullwhip cure in action: real demand data replaces guesses.

Risks in supply chains: Global supply chains are long and exposed. Port congestion, floods, political unrest, pandemics, fuel price jumps or a single supplier failing can stop a whole chain. Firms reduce risk by having more than one supplier for critical items, keeping strategic buffer stock, sourcing closer to home where possible, and having clear visibility of where every order is. Visibility itself is an information system achievement: you cannot manage a risk you cannot see.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think SCM is only about transport. It covers planning, sourcing, making, delivering and returns, plus the information and money flows. Another mistake is explaining the bullwhip effect without saying its cause; always mention distorted, delayed demand information and the cure of sharing real demand data. Exams often ask: define supply chain and SCM; explain upstream and downstream; explain the bullwhip effect with an example and how IS reduces it; compare push and pull models; describe JIT with its benefits and risks; and distinguish SCM planning and execution systems. A small numeric bullwhip example like the soft drink one earns marks.

Recap: A supply chain links suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customers, with flows of products, information and money. Upstream is toward suppliers, downstream toward customers. SCM coordinates it all to reduce cost and uncertainty. The bullwhip effect amplifies small demand changes into big order swings upstream, and sharing real demand information is the main cure. Push builds to forecast, pull builds to order, and most chains mix both. JIT keeps little stock but is fragile. SCM software splits into planning and execution. Next lesson we turn to the customer end of the chain with customer relationship management.
key_points: A supply chain is the network of firms and processes that source materials, make products and deliver them, with product, information and money flows.
Upstream means toward suppliers; downstream means toward distributors, retailers and customers.
SCM coordinates the chain to deliver the right product at the right place and time at low cost, mainly by reducing uncertainty.
The bullwhip effect: small changes in customer demand grow into large order swings upstream because of distorted, delayed information.
Sharing real demand data, cutting delays and smaller batches reduce the bullwhip effect.
Push (build-to-stock) produces to forecasts; pull (build-to-order) produces to actual orders; real chains often mix both.
Just-in-time keeps very little stock but is fragile when suppliers or transport fail.
SCM software has planning (demand forecasting, production and stock plans) and execution (warehouse, transport, tracking) parts.
lessons.tip: Draw every supply chain as boxes in a line with three arrows under it: products going right, money going left, information going both ways. Most SCM exam answers become easy once this picture is in your head.
