lessons.task: Choose one product in your home, such as a packet of biscuits or a bottle of oil. On paper, draw its likely supply chain from raw material to your kitchen, mark upstream and downstream from the factory's point of view, and write one way the bullwhip effect could hit this chain.

quiz.q: From a garments factory's point of view, which is upstream?
options: The fabric mill that supplies cloth
The shipping agent sending finished goods
quiz.explain: Upstream is toward the suppliers, so the fabric mill is upstream of the factory.

quiz.q: What is the bullwhip effect?
options: Small changes in customer demand becoming large swings in orders further up the chain
A pricing strategy for luxury goods
quiz.explain: Distorted demand information gets amplified at each link upstream, like the crack of a whip.

quiz.q: Which is the main cure for the bullwhip effect?
options: Adding more safety stock at each link
Sharing accurate real demand information across the chain
quiz.explain: When every link sees real customer demand instead of guessing from orders, amplification falls.

quiz.q: A factory starts sewing only after a buyer confirms an order. This is:
quiz.explain: Production triggered by actual orders is the pull, build-to-order model.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of just-in-time?
options: With little buffer stock, a late supplier or blocked road can stop production
It makes stock costs very high
quiz.explain: JIT keeps minimal stock, so any supply disruption quickly halts production.

lessons.title: Enterprise Systems III: Customer Relationship Management
lessons.content:
Every neighbourhood has a shopkeeper who knows everyone. When Mrs Rahman walks in, he already knows she buys a particular brand of tea, that her son is in class eight, and that she pays on the first of the month. He keeps her favourite biscuits aside, asks about her son and gives her a little credit when needed. She would not dream of shopping anywhere else. Now imagine a bank with five million customers, or a mobile operator with tens of millions. No person can remember them all. Customer relationship management is the attempt to give a huge organization the memory and personal touch of that neighbourhood shopkeeper, using information systems.

What CRM is: Customer relationship management, or CRM, is a business strategy and set of information systems that capture and integrate customer data from all over the organization, analyse it, and use the results to improve sales, marketing and customer service and to build long-term, profitable relationships with customers. The word strategy matters: CRM is not just software. It is a decision to organize the business around customers rather than around products or departments, supported by software.

The problem CRM solves: In many firms, customer information is scattered. Sales has a contact list in one system, the call centre has complaint records in another, billing has payment history in a third, and the marketing team buys a separate email tool. When a customer calls, the agent may not know that she complained twice last week or that she is one of the most valuable customers. Each department sees only a slice. CRM aims for a single, complete view of the customer, sometimes called a 360-degree view, across all touch points: branches, call centre, website, app, email and social media.

Why customers are worth managing: Keeping an existing customer is generally cheaper than winning a new one, because winning new customers needs advertising, discounts and sales effort. Loyal customers also tend to buy more over time and recommend the firm to others. And customers are not all equal: a small share of customers often brings a large share of profit. CRM helps a firm find out which customers are most valuable, which are at risk of leaving and what each one is likely to want next.

Customer lifetime value: A key CRM idea is customer lifetime value, or CLV, which estimates the total profit a firm can expect from a customer over the whole relationship. A simple version: CLV equals average profit per year times expected number of years as a customer. Suppose a mobile customer brings 1,200 taka profit a year and stays about 5 years: CLV is about 6,000 taka. If the firm spends 500 taka on a retention offer that makes her stay 2 more years, it gains about 2,400 taka of profit for 500 taka of cost. Real CLV models also discount future money and include the cost of serving the customer, but even this simple version helps managers decide how much to spend to win or keep each type of customer.

Churn: Churn means customers who stop doing business with a firm, like leaving a mobile operator or closing a bank account. The churn rate is the share of customers who leave in a period. If a firm starts the month with 10,000 customers and 300 leave, the monthly churn rate is 300 divided by 10,000, or 3 percent. High churn is like filling a bucket with a hole in it: marketing pours new customers in while existing ones leak out. Analytical CRM tries to predict which customers are likely to churn, for example those whose usage is falling or who complained recently, so the firm can act before they leave.

Operational CRM: CRM systems are often divided into operational and analytical parts. Operational CRM covers customer-facing applications used in day-to-day work: sales force automation, call centre and customer service support, and marketing automation. These are the tools employees use when talking to customers. They capture data with every interaction.

Sales force automation: Sales force automation, or SFA, helps salespeople work more productively. It stores contacts and accounts, tracks leads and opportunities through stages such as new lead, qualified, proposal, negotiation and won or lost, schedules follow-ups, prepares quotations and gives managers a view of the sales pipeline. With SFA, a sales manager can see that there are 40 open opportunities worth a total of 2 crore taka, of which about a quarter are at the proposal stage, and can forecast likely sales. When a salesperson leaves, the customer history stays with the company instead of walking out with that person.

A worked sales funnel: Sales pipelines are often drawn as a funnel because the number of prospects shrinks at each stage. Suppose a software company selling payroll systems to garments factories gets 200 leads in a quarter from a trade fair and its website. Sales qualifies 25 percent of them as real prospects with budget and need: 50. Of those, 40 percent ask for a proposal: 20. Of the proposals, half are won: 10 new customers. The SFA system records these conversion rates. Now the manager can reason backwards: to win 20 customers next quarter at the same rates, the team needs about 400 leads, or it must improve a weak stage, such as raising the proposal win rate with better demos. This is how CRM data turns sales from guesswork into something that can be planned and improved, and it is also why salespeople must actually enter their activities into the system.

Customer service: Customer service modules manage requests and complaints through cases or tickets. Each case gets an ID, a category, a priority, an owner and a status, and the system tracks how long it takes to resolve. Agents see the customer's history in one screen. Many systems include a knowledge base of answers to common questions, self-service options on the website or app, chat and automatic routing so that, for example, a card-blocking request reaches the right team quickly. Measures like first-call resolution and average resolution time help managers improve service.

Marketing automation: Marketing modules help plan and run campaigns: selecting target customers, sending messages through SMS, email, app notifications or social media, and measuring responses. Two important ideas are cross-selling, offering a related product to an existing customer, like a credit card to a savings customer, and up-selling, offering a higher-value version, like a bigger data pack. CRM data makes these offers more relevant, so customers are less likely to see them as spam.

Analytical CRM: Analytical CRM works on the data collected by operational CRM and other systems, often in a data warehouse, to understand customers. It segments customers into groups with similar behaviour, calculates lifetime value, predicts churn, finds which products are bought together and measures campaign results. It uses the business intelligence and analytics tools we met earlier. A useful way to remember the split: operational CRM is for doing things with customers; analytical CRM is for understanding customers.

Collaborative CRM: Some textbooks add a third type, collaborative CRM, which focuses on sharing customer information across departments and with partners, so that everyone dealing with the customer works from the same picture. For example, a dealer and the manufacturer may both see the same customer's service history for a motorcycle.

A small segmentation example: Suppose a supershop's loyalty card data shows three groups. Group A, 10 percent of members, visits weekly and spends a lot. Group B, 50 percent, visits monthly with medium spending. Group C, 40 percent, visited once or twice and has not returned for three months. The manager might give Group A special service and early access to offers, send Group B targeted discounts on items they often buy to increase visits, and send Group C a win-back offer. Without CRM data, the shop would send everyone the same message and waste money.

Real life example 1, a bank: A commercial bank in Bangladesh serves customers through branches, ATMs, a call centre, internet banking and an app. With CRM, when a customer calls about a card problem, the agent sees her accounts, recent transactions, previous complaints and the products she holds. The system may show a note that she is a high-value customer who has been with the bank for ten years, and prompt the agent to handle her case with priority. Analytics may show that customers who receive salary in their account are good candidates for a personal loan offer, while customers whose balances have dropped sharply may be about to move their money elsewhere. The relationship manager gets a list to call.

Real life example 2, a mobile operator: Mobile operators have huge numbers of customers and strong competition, so churn is a constant concern. Their CRM and analytics systems look at usage patterns, recharge habits and complaints to predict who might switch. A customer whose usage falls and who complained about network quality may receive an offer, a call or a check of network problems in her area. Operators also use CRM data to design packs for different segments, such as students who use more data at night, or businesses that need many connections. Customers may notice this when they receive offers in an app that fit their usage.

CRM challenges and privacy: CRM projects can fail when firms buy software without changing how staff work, when data is poor or duplicated, or when staff see data entry as extra work and skip it. Another serious issue is privacy. CRM collects detailed personal data, and customers may feel uncomfortable if offers reveal how much the firm knows, or if their data is shared without consent. Firms must protect customer data, use it for stated purposes and follow the law. We discuss these issues fully in the ethics and security lessons.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often define CRM as just a contact list or a call centre system. CRM is a strategy, supported by integrated operational and analytical systems. Another mistake is mixing up operational and analytical CRM; remember doing versus understanding. Exams often ask: define CRM and its objectives; explain the 360-degree customer view; distinguish operational, analytical and collaborative CRM; describe sales force automation; explain customer lifetime value and churn with simple calculations; and discuss benefits and challenges of CRM. A worked CLV or churn calculation makes your answer stand out.

Recap: CRM is a strategy plus systems that gather customer data from all touch points, analyse it and use it to sell, serve and keep customers profitably. Retaining customers is usually cheaper than winning new ones, and customers differ in value. Customer lifetime value estimates long-term profit per customer, and churn rate measures how many leave. Operational CRM includes sales force automation, customer service and marketing automation; analytical CRM segments, predicts and measures; collaborative CRM shares customer information. With ERP, SCM and CRM, we have now seen the three big enterprise systems. Next we step up to strategy: how information systems help a firm compete.
key_points: CRM is a business strategy plus integrated systems that capture, analyse and use customer data to sell, serve and retain customers profitably.
CRM aims for a single 360-degree view of each customer across branches, call centre, web, app and social media.
Keeping existing customers is usually cheaper than winning new ones, and customers differ greatly in value.
Customer lifetime value is roughly profit per year times expected years; it guides how much to spend to win or keep a customer.
Churn rate is the share of customers who leave in a period, for example 300 of 10,000 in a month is 3 percent.
Operational CRM: sales force automation, customer service and marketing automation; analytical CRM: segmentation, CLV, churn prediction, campaign analysis.
Cross-selling offers related products; up-selling offers higher-value versions.
CRM fails without process change and good data, and it raises serious privacy responsibilities.
lessons.tip: Remember the CRM split with two verbs: operational CRM does things with customers, analytical CRM understands customers. Then attach one example to each and you have a ready exam answer.
lessons.task: Think of one company you are a customer of (a bank, mobile operator or online shop). On paper, list every touch point you have with it, then write three pieces of data it probably has about you and one offer it could make using that data. Finally, write one thing about its use of your data that would make you uncomfortable.

quiz.q: What does a 360-degree customer view mean?
options: A camera view of the customer in the branch
Showing ads in every direction on a website
A single, complete picture of the customer combining data from all touch points
quiz.explain: CRM integrates data from all channels and departments into one complete view of each customer.

quiz.q: A firm starts the month with 8,000 customers and 400 leave. What is the monthly churn rate?
quiz.explain: 400 divided by 8,000 is 0.05, which is 5 percent.

quiz.q: Which is an example of analytical CRM?
options: Logging a customer's complaint as a ticket
A salesperson recording a meeting with a client
Sending an SMS to a customer about a payment
Predicting which customers are likely to leave next month
quiz.explain: Analysing data to segment, predict churn or measure campaigns is analytical CRM.

quiz.q: A bank offers a credit card to a customer who already has a savings account with it. This is:
quiz.explain: Offering a related, different product to an existing customer is cross-selling.

quiz.q: A customer brings about 1,000 taka profit per year and is expected to stay 6 years. Using the simple formula, the customer lifetime value is about:
quiz.explain: Profit per year times expected years: 1,000 x 6 = 6,000 taka.

lessons.title: Competitive Strategy I: Five Forces and Generic Strategies
lessons.content:
Walk down a street in Old Dhaka where ten shops sell the same plastic buckets. Prices are almost the same, customers bargain hard, and every shopkeeper complains that profit is thin. Now walk into a small shop that sells handmade leather bags with a brand name, a nice display and a Facebook page with thousands of happy reviews. The owner charges more and still has customers waiting. Same city, same customers, very different profit. Why do some businesses earn good profits while others struggle? This is the question of competitive strategy, and it is where information systems move from being a back-office tool to being a weapon.

Competitive advantage: A firm has a competitive advantage when it performs better than its rivals in a way that lets it earn higher profits or grow faster for some time. It might have lower costs, a product customers value more, better access to customers or suppliers, or knowledge others lack. In MIS, the central question is: how can information systems help a firm gain or protect competitive advantage? To answer it, we need a way to analyse the competitive environment. The most famous tool is Michael Porter's competitive forces model, usually called the five forces model.

The five forces model: Michael Porter, a professor at Harvard Business School, argued that the profitability of an industry is shaped not only by direct rivals but by five forces together. They are: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitute products or services, bargaining power of customers (buyers), and bargaining power of suppliers. When these forces are strong, profits in the industry tend to be low; when they are weak, profits can be high. A manager uses the model to understand where pressure comes from and where the firm could defend itself.

Force 1, rivalry among existing competitors: This is the most obvious force: other firms selling similar products to the same customers. Rivalry is intense when there are many similar-sized competitors, products are hard to tell apart, the industry is growing slowly or customers can switch easily. Intense rivalry leads to price wars, heavy advertising and thin margins. Our street of bucket shops is a perfect example.

Force 2, threat of new entrants: If it is easy for new firms to enter an industry, existing firms cannot keep prices high for long, because newcomers will rush in. Barriers to entry make entry harder. Examples include large capital needed, strong brands, government licences, economies of scale, access to distribution channels and network effects. A new bank needs a licence and large capital, so the threat of new banks is limited. A new Facebook clothing page needs almost nothing, so the threat of new entrants there is very high.

Force 3, threat of substitutes: A substitute is a different product or service that meets the same need. Bus travel is a substitute for train travel; video calls are a substitute for international phone calls; a mobile wallet transfer is a substitute for sending cash through a courier or a relative. The more good substitutes exist, the less a firm can raise its price before customers switch. Technology often creates new substitutes suddenly, which is why managers must watch outside their own industry.

Force 4, bargaining power of customers: Customers have strong power when they are few and buy in large quantities, when they can easily switch to rivals, or when they have full information about prices. Big foreign brands buying from garments factories have strong bargaining power: each brand places large orders and can move them to another factory or country. Internet price comparison also gives ordinary customers more power because they can see every seller's price instantly.

Force 5, bargaining power of suppliers: Suppliers are powerful when there are few of them, when their input is unique or critical, or when switching suppliers is costly. If only one company makes a special dye a factory needs, that supplier can raise prices. In the software world, a firm that depends on one cloud provider or one ERP vendor may find switching very hard, which gives the supplier power.

A worked five forces analysis, ride-sharing in Dhaka: Let us apply the model to app-based ride-sharing. Rivalry: several apps compete for the same riders and passengers, and both can easily install more than one app, so rivalry on price and promotions is strong. New entrants: building an app is not very hard, but getting enough riders and passengers on both sides at the same time is hard, so network effects form a moderate barrier. Substitutes: buses, CNG auto-rickshaws, rickshaws, private cars, walking and simply staying home with online delivery; plenty of substitutes limit fares. Customers: individual passengers are small, but they can switch apps in seconds and compare fares, so their power is fairly high. Suppliers: the most important supplier is actually the riders and drivers, who can also switch apps or work offline; fuel prices are another supplier-side pressure. Conclusion: an industry with strong forces on most sides, so profits are hard, and firms must find ways to build loyalty, lower costs or add services. Notice that the answer is a reasoned judgment, not one fixed number; that is how exam answers should be written too.

How the internet shifts the forces: The internet and mobile technology have changed many industries' forces, often in ways that hurt incumbents. Substitutes appear faster, because a new app can offer a digital version of an old service. Barriers to entry fall in many markets, because a website or a social media page is cheap to start. Customer power rises, because buyers can compare prices and read reviews in seconds. Rivalry often widens from local to national or even global, because a customer in Sylhet can buy from a seller in Dhaka as easily as from the shop next door. At the same time, the internet can help some firms build new barriers, such as large user networks or huge amounts of customer data. A manager should therefore ask, for each force, whether technology is making it stronger or weaker.

Limits of the model: The five forces model gives a snapshot of an industry's structure, but industries now change quickly and boundaries blur: is a ride-sharing app in transport, food delivery or payments? The model also focuses on competition and may underplay cooperation, such as firms sharing a payment network or suppliers working closely with buyers. Use it as a thinking tool, not as a formula.

Porter's generic strategies: Porter also argued that a firm can achieve competitive advantage in three generic ways. Cost leadership means becoming the lowest-cost producer in the industry, so the firm can charge similar or lower prices and still earn a good margin. Differentiation means offering something unique that customers value, such as quality, design, brand, service or features, so they are willing to pay more or stay loyal. Focus means concentrating on a narrow market segment, a niche, and serving it better than broad competitors, either with lower costs (cost focus) or with something special (differentiation focus). Porter warned that a firm that tries to do everything without a clear position risks being stuck in the middle, with neither the lowest cost nor real uniqueness.

Using IS for cost leadership: Information systems lower costs by automating transactions, cutting errors, reducing inventory and coordinating suppliers. A supershop that uses point-of-sale data and automatic reordering keeps less stock and loses less to spoilage. A garments factory that tracks line efficiency hour by hour can find and fix bottlenecks, lowering cost per piece. Big retailers around the world are famous examples of using sales data shared with suppliers to keep stock low and prices low.

Using IS for differentiation: Information systems can create new products and services or make existing ones better. An online bank app with instant transfers, clear statements and quick support differentiates a bank from rivals with slow branches. Personalized recommendations, real-time order tracking and easy returns differentiate an online shop. Sometimes the information system is the product itself, like a mobile wallet whose whole value is the digital service.

Using IS for focus: Data helps a firm find and understand a niche. A small online shop may focus only on modest fashion for young women, or on books for university admission tests. Using its customer data, it can stock exactly what this group wants and talk to them in their language, something a giant general store may not do as well.

Customer and supplier intimacy: Many MIS textbooks add a fourth way IS helps: strengthening ties with customers and suppliers. CRM systems learn customers' preferences and make it inconvenient to leave because the service fits them so well. SCM systems that link a factory with its key suppliers make coordination smooth for both sides. These ties raise switching costs, which we explore more in the next lesson.

Real life example 1, a garments exporter: Bangladesh's RMG industry faces strong buyer power, because large global brands place big orders and can move them elsewhere, and strong rivalry from factories at home and in other countries. A factory that chooses cost leadership uses IS to track efficiency, waste and overtime closely. Another factory may choose differentiation through compliance, sustainability and fast sampling, using systems that document safety, environmental standards and product data that buyers ask for. Both use information systems, but for different strategies.

Real life example 2, mobile financial services: Mobile financial services in Bangladesh are an example of an information system creating a new service that substitutes for older ways of sending money, like carrying cash or using informal channels. For the providers, the forces include rivalry among MFS providers and banks, substitutes such as bank apps and cash, and the power of agents, who are a key supplier of the cash-in and cash-out service. A provider's agent network and large user base, built through the system, can act as a barrier to new entrants.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often list the five forces without explaining how each affects profit; always say whether the force is strong or weak and why. Another mistake is confusing substitutes with rivals: a rival sells the same kind of product, a substitute meets the same need differently. Exams often ask: explain Porter's five forces with an example industry; explain the three generic strategies; show how information systems support each strategy; and analyse a given case. Build your answer as a small table: force, strong or weak, reason, and how IS can respond.

Recap: Competitive advantage means outperforming rivals in a way that brings higher profit or growth. Porter's five forces are rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power; strong forces mean lower industry profits. The generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus, with the danger of being stuck in the middle. Information systems support each: automation and data for low cost, new and better services for differentiation, customer data for focus, and CRM and SCM for customer and supplier intimacy. In the next lesson we look inside the firm with the value chain, and ask why advantages built on IT often do not last.
key_points: Competitive advantage means performing better than rivals in a way that brings higher profit or faster growth for some time.
Porter's five forces: rivalry among competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of customers and bargaining power of suppliers.
Strong forces push industry profits down; weak forces allow higher profits.
Barriers to entry include capital needs, licences, brands, economies of scale, distribution access and network effects.
A substitute meets the same need in a different way; a rival sells the same kind of product.
Generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation and focus; trying everything without a position risks being stuck in the middle.
IS supports cost leadership (automation, less stock), differentiation (new and better services), focus (customer data on a niche) and customer and supplier intimacy (CRM, SCM).
lessons.tip: When analysing any industry, make a five-row table: force, strong or weak, one reason, and one IS response. Examiners reward the reasoning in that table far more than a memorized list.
lessons.task: Pick one industry you see around you, such as coaching centres, food delivery, mobile phone shops or private universities. On paper, do a five forces table for it: rate each force strong, medium or weak with one reason. Then suggest which generic strategy a new firm should choose and one information system that would help.

quiz.q: Video calls replacing international phone calls is an example of which force?
quiz.explain: A substitute meets the same need, talking across countries, in a different way.

quiz.q: Large global brands that can move orders between garments factories mainly create:
quiz.explain: Few, large buyers who can easily switch suppliers have strong bargaining power.

quiz.q: A bank licence and large starting capital are examples of:
quiz.explain: They make it hard for new firms to enter, lowering the threat of new entrants.

quiz.q: A firm uses automation and tight stock control to become the lowest-cost producer. Which generic strategy is this?
quiz.explain: Aiming to be the lowest-cost producer is the cost leadership strategy.

quiz.q: What did Porter mean by being stuck in the middle?
options: Having a factory in the centre of the city
Having neither the lowest cost nor real uniqueness because of no clear strategy
Being in the middle of the supply chain
quiz.explain: A firm without a clear position fails to win on cost or on uniqueness.

lessons.title: Competitive Strategy II: Value Chain, Platforms and Lasting Advantage
lessons.content:
Think about how a cup of tea reaches you at a roadside stall. Someone grows tea leaves in Sylhet, someone packs and transports them, the stall owner buys milk and sugar, boils the water, pours the cup, smiles and takes your money. Each step adds a little value, and the price you pay has to cover all of them plus some profit. If the stall owner wants to beat the stall next door, he can look at every step and ask: where can I do this cheaper, or better, or both? That simple habit of looking at a business as a chain of steps is the core of this lesson.

Where we are: In the previous lesson we used Porter's five forces to look at an industry from the outside, and the generic strategies of cost leadership, differentiation and focus to choose a position. That told us where a firm should stand. This lesson looks inside the firm and asks how it creates value step by step, and then at the special economics of the digital world: network effects, platforms and switching costs. We finish with a hard truth: most advantages built on technology do not last, and the real skill is aligning IS with the business strategy again and again.

The value chain idea: Michael Porter also proposed the value chain model in the 1980s. It views a firm as a series of activities that each add value to a product or service. The value of the final product, what customers are willing to pay, minus the total cost of all those activities, is the margin. A firm gains competitive advantage when it does some activities at lower cost than rivals, or in a way that creates more value for customers, or both. The model is useful because it breaks a big vague question, how can IT help us, into small concrete ones, how can IT help this particular activity.

Primary activities: These are the activities directly involved in making and delivering the product. Inbound logistics means receiving and storing raw materials, such as fabric arriving at a garments factory. Operations means turning inputs into the product, such as cutting, sewing and finishing. Outbound logistics means storing and delivering finished goods, such as packing cartons and shipping containers from Chattogram port. Marketing and sales means getting customers to buy, such as merchandisers meeting foreign buyers and sending samples. Service means support after the sale, such as handling quality complaints or repairs.

Support activities: These make the primary activities possible. Firm infrastructure covers general management, accounting, finance, legal and planning. Human resource management covers hiring, training and paying people. Technology development covers research, product design and also the information systems that improve other activities. Procurement covers buying the inputs the firm needs, from fabric to office paper. Support activities run across the whole chain: a good HR system, for example, helps every primary activity because every activity needs trained people.

A worked value chain for a garments exporter: Let us map IS onto each activity for a factory in Gazipur. Inbound logistics: a warehouse system that records every fabric roll with a barcode, so stores know exactly what is in stock. Operations: a production tracking system where each sewing line reports hourly output against target. Outbound logistics: a shipment planning system that matches finished cartons to containers and export documents. Marketing and sales: a merchandising system that keeps buyer orders, approved samples and price history in one place. Service: a system that logs buyer quality claims and links them to the line and batch that caused them. Procurement: an e-procurement system to compare supplier quotes. HR: a payroll and attendance system with digital wage payment. Each of these is a place where IS can cut cost or add value.

Small numbers to see the margin: Suppose a shirt sells to the buyer for 6 dollars. The activities cost: materials 3.20, operations 1.50, logistics 0.40, sales and admin 0.40. Total cost 5.50, so margin is 0.50 dollars per shirt. If a better cutting plan software reduces fabric waste so that materials cost 3.05 instead of 3.20, margin rises to 0.65. That is a 30 percent increase in margin from one small improvement in one activity. On an order of 100,000 shirts, that is 15,000 dollars more profit. This is why managers love the value chain: small savings in big activities add up fast.

The value web and linkages: Activities are not isolated. A linkage is when the way one activity is done affects the cost or value of another. Better quality checks in operations reduce service costs later. Sharing sales forecasts with procurement reduces stockouts. Modern firms also link their value chain to the value chains of suppliers and customers, forming what textbooks call a value web. When a buyer's system shares its sales data with a factory, both can plan better. Enterprise systems such as ERP, SCM and CRM, which we studied earlier, are largely tools for strengthening these linkages.

Benchmarking and best practices: How does a firm know which activity to improve? One way is benchmarking: comparing its performance on each activity against industry standards or the best competitor. If rivals take 3 days to process a buyer order and you take 7, order processing is where IS should help first. Best practices are the most successful known ways of doing an activity, often built into packaged software. This connects to the ERP trade-off we saw earlier: adopting the software's best practices is cheaper, but if everyone uses the same practice it stops being an advantage.

Network effects: Now to the digital economics. A product has a network effect when it becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. One telephone is useless; two can call each other; a million phones make each one very valuable. A simple way to see it: with n users, the number of possible pairs that can connect is n times (n minus 1) divided by 2. With 10 users there are 45 pairs; with 100 users there are 4,950 pairs. Value grows much faster than the number of users. This is why messaging apps and payment wallets fight hard for early users.

Platforms and two-sided markets: A platform is a business that creates value by connecting different groups of users rather than by making a product itself. Daraz connects sellers and buyers. Pathao and Uber connect riders and drivers. bKash connects customers, agents and merchants. These are often called two-sided or multi-sided markets: more buyers attract more sellers, and more sellers attract more buyers. This is an indirect network effect. Platforms often subsidize one side, for example with discounts or cashback, to get the cycle started. That is the chicken and egg problem: no buyers come without sellers, and no sellers come without buyers.

Switching costs: A switching cost is anything that makes it costly or painful for a customer to move to a competitor. It can be money, such as a cancellation fee; time and effort, such as learning a new system; or lost data and history, such as a bank account with years of records linked to salary and loans. In IS, switching costs are very strong. A company that has put all its processes on one ERP finds it very expensive to change. A merchant who receives all payments through one wallet and has customers used to that QR code thinks twice before moving. High switching costs lock customers in and protect a firm's market share.

Winner-take-most markets: Network effects and switching costs together often push a market towards one or a few large players. Once a platform is far ahead, new users join it because everyone else is there, and existing users stay because leaving is costly. This is why we often see one dominant ride-sharing app, one dominant social network or one dominant mobile wallet in a country, with smaller rivals fighting for second place. For managers, it means timing matters: being early and growing fast can decide the market. For regulators, it raises questions about competition and fair treatment of users.

Why advantage does not last: Here is the uncomfortable part. Many IS-based advantages are temporary. Competitors can copy technology, because software and hardware are available to everyone who can pay. Talent moves between firms. Customer expectations rise, so yesterday's special feature, like online balance checking, becomes today's basic requirement. And new technology can make old advantages useless: a firm with the best network of physical branches may find customers moving to mobile apps. Researchers have argued that IT has become a commodity like electricity, so simply buying it gives no edge. The more balanced view is that the technology alone rarely gives lasting advantage; what lasts is how a firm combines it with its own processes, data, skills and relationships.

Sources of more durable advantage: What is harder to copy? Unique data built up over years, such as purchase histories. Network effects and switching costs once a large user base exists. Organizational capabilities, meaning the skills, culture and routines of using IS well, which take years to build. Complementary assets like brand, distribution networks and agent networks. And the ability to keep innovating, so that by the time rivals copy one thing, you have moved to the next.

Strategic alignment: The last idea is simple to say and hard to do. Strategic alignment means the IS plans and investments support the business strategy, and the business strategy takes advantage of what IS can do. A firm with a cost leadership strategy should spend on systems that cut cost, like automation and efficient supply chains. A firm with a differentiation strategy should spend on systems that make the customer experience special, like personalization and fast service. Misalignment, such as an IT department building fancy features nobody in the business asked for, wastes money. Alignment is usually achieved by having business and IT leaders plan together, and by measuring IS projects by their business results.

Real life example 1, a mobile wallet: Think of a mobile wallet in Bangladesh. Its value chain includes onboarding customers, running an agent network for cash in and cash out, processing transactions, partnering with merchants and billers, and customer service. Its information systems make each transaction fast and cheap. Its network effect is clear: the more people have the wallet, the more useful it is to send money to family or pay shops. Its switching costs include the habit of customers, saved billers and the agent nearby. Rivals can copy the app, but copying a huge user base and agent network takes years.

Real life example 2, an online marketplace: An e-commerce marketplace like Daraz is a platform with a two-sided network effect: buyers come for choice, sellers come for buyers. Its value chain includes seller onboarding, catalogue management, payment collection including cash on delivery, logistics and returns. Information systems power the search, recommendations, seller dashboards and delivery tracking. Its advantage depends less on the website itself, which many could copy, and more on its seller base, logistics network, brand and customer data. When a new rival appears, the question is whether it can attract both sides fast enough to break the cycle.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often list value chain activities without saying how IS helps each one; always attach a system example to each activity. Another mistake is to treat network effects and economies of scale as the same thing. Economies of scale mean cost per unit falls as you produce more; network effects mean value per user rises as more users join. Also do not claim that any technology gives permanent advantage. Typical exam questions: draw Porter's value chain and explain primary and support activities; explain how IS can add value at each activity for a given firm; define network effects and switching costs with examples; explain why IT-based competitive advantage is often not sustainable; and define strategic alignment.

Recap: The value chain breaks a firm into primary activities, inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service, and support activities, infrastructure, HR, technology development and procurement. IS can lower cost or add value in each, and linkages connect activities within and across firms into a value web. Digital markets add network effects, platforms with two or more sides, and switching costs, which often lead to winner-take-most outcomes. Technology alone is easy to copy, so lasting advantage comes from data, networks, capabilities and continuous innovation, all kept in strategic alignment with the business.
key_points: Porter's value chain splits a firm into primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities (infrastructure, HR, technology development, procurement).
Margin is the value customers pay minus the total cost of all activities; IS helps by cutting cost or adding value in specific activities.
Linkages connect activities inside a firm and across suppliers and customers, forming a value web.
Network effects make a product more valuable to each user as more people use it; possible connections grow as n(n-1)/2.
Platforms create value by connecting two or more groups of users, such as buyers and sellers, and often subsidize one side to start.
Switching costs (money, effort, lost data or habits) lock customers in and protect market share.
Technology alone is easy to copy, so IS-based advantage is often temporary; data, networks, capabilities and continuous innovation last longer.
Strategic alignment means IS investments support the business strategy and the strategy uses what IS can do.
lessons.tip: When you study the value chain, draw it once for a business you know, like a tea stall, a bakery or a phone shop, and write one possible system under each activity. One personal drawing beats memorizing the box names.
lessons.task: Pick one app you use every week, such as a ride-sharing, food delivery or payment app. On paper, write down: which groups of users it connects, one network effect it has, two switching costs that keep you using it, and one thing a new rival would find hard to copy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a support activity in Porter's value chain?
quiz.explain: Procurement, buying inputs, supports the whole chain. The other three are primary activities.

quiz.q: A shirt sells for 6 dollars and total activity cost falls from 5.50 to 5.35 dollars. What happens to the margin per shirt?
quiz.explain: Margin = 6 - 5.50 = 0.50 before and 6 - 5.35 = 0.65 after.

quiz.q: With 10 users, how many possible pairs can connect in a network?
Why is a competitive advantage based only on buying new technology usually short-lived?
options: Competitors can buy and copy the same technology
Laws ban using technology for advantage
quiz.explain: Hardware and software are available to anyone who pays, so rivals can copy them; lasting advantage needs harder-to-copy assets.

quiz.q: A merchant keeps using one payment wallet because customers know its QR code and all records are there. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: The effort, habits and lost history of moving to a rival are switching costs.

lessons.title: Ethics, Privacy and Intellectual Property
lessons.content:
Imagine you order a pressure cooker online one evening. The next morning, Facebook shows you ads for pressure cookers, rice cookers and gas stoves. A day later, an unknown number calls offering you a kitchen appliance loan. How did they know? Somewhere, your data travelled from one system to another without you really noticing. Nobody broke into your phone. You probably clicked agree on something. This is the world of information ethics: the technology works perfectly, but the question is whether what it does is right, fair and legal.

What ethics means here: Ethics is the set of principles of right and wrong that people use to make choices about their behaviour. It is different from law. Law is what the state forces you to follow; ethics is what you should do even when no law forces you. Many things are legal but unethical, such as designing an app that tricks people into sharing contacts. Information systems raise new ethical questions because they make it cheap and fast to collect, copy, combine and spread data, and the law usually catches up years later.

Why IS creates new ethical problems: A few technology trends make these issues sharper. Computing power keeps getting cheaper, so organizations can process data about everyone. Storage costs keep falling, so data is kept forever instead of being thrown away. Data analysis has improved, so firms can combine small pieces of data from many sources to build a detailed profile of a person; this is sometimes called profiling. Networks and mobile devices mean data moves instantly and everywhere. Each trend is useful for business, but each also makes it easier to hurt people.

Five moral dimensions: Many MIS textbooks group the ethical issues of the information age into five moral dimensions. Information rights and obligations: what rights do people have over information about themselves? Property rights: how is intellectual property protected when copying is free? Accountability and control: who is responsible when information systems harm people? System quality: what standards of data quality and system safety should we demand? Quality of life: what values should be protected in a society built on information, such as family time, jobs and fairness? We will touch each of these in this lesson.

Basic concepts, responsibility, accountability, liability: Responsibility means you accept the costs, duties and obligations of the decisions you make. Accountability means there are mechanisms to find out who took an action and who is responsible. Liability means there are laws that let injured people recover damages from those responsible. Due process means laws are known and understood, and people can appeal to higher authorities to make sure laws are applied correctly. A key idea: technology does not do things by itself. People and organizations choose how to use it, so they are responsible for its effects.

A five-step ethical analysis: When facing an ethical problem, a manager can follow simple steps. One, identify and describe the facts clearly: who did what, to whom, where, when and how. Two, define the conflict and identify the higher values involved, such as privacy, freedom or protection of property. Three, identify the stakeholders, everyone who has an interest in the outcome. Four, identify the reasonable options, knowing that some options may satisfy some stakeholders but not others. Five, identify the possible consequences of each option, in the short and long term.

Classic ethical principles: Several rules of thumb help with the choice. The Golden Rule: do unto others as you would have them do unto you. Kant's categorical imperative: if an action is not right for everyone to take, it is not right for anyone. The slippery slope rule (also called Descartes' rule of change): if an action cannot be taken repeatedly, it is not right to take it even once. The utilitarian principle: take the action that achieves the greater value overall. The risk aversion principle: take the action that produces the least harm or the least potential cost. The no free lunch rule: assume that almost everything belongs to someone else unless you are told otherwise, and if someone created something of value, they may want payment for it.

Privacy: Privacy is the claim of individuals to be left alone, free from surveillance or interference by other people, organizations or the state, and the claim to control information about themselves. In the digital world, privacy is threatened by collection, which is gathering data you did not expect; by combination, which is linking data from many sources; by secondary use, which is using data for a purpose different from the one you agreed to; and by sharing or selling data to third parties. A phone number you gave a shop for a delivery should not end up on a telemarketing list.

Fair information practices: Many privacy laws around the world are built on a set of principles called fair information practices. Notice or awareness: people should be told what data is collected and why. Choice or consent: people should be able to decide how their data is used, especially for secondary uses. Access or participation: people should be able to see their data and correct it. Security: data collectors must protect data from unauthorized use. Enforcement: there must be a way to make organizations follow these rules. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, the GDPR, which took effect in 2018, is a well-known strong law built on such ideas and it applies to organizations anywhere that process data of people in the EU.

Opt-in and opt-out: Consent can be designed in two ways. In an opt-out model, the firm collects or uses your data by default unless you take action to stop it, for example by unticking a box. In an opt-in model, the firm cannot use your data until you actively agree. Opt-in protects privacy better, which is why privacy advocates prefer it. A small worked contrast: if 1,000 users sign up and only 10 percent bother to change default settings, an opt-out marketing box gives the firm about 900 users to market to, while an opt-in box gives about 100. Defaults matter enormously.

Tracking technologies: Websites and apps use several tools to track you. Cookies are small text files a website stores in your browser to remember you, such as your login or cart; third-party cookies from advertisers can follow you across many sites. Web beacons or tracking pixels are tiny invisible images or scripts that report when you open a page or an email. Mobile apps may request permissions to your location, contacts, camera or SMS. Spyware is software installed without proper consent that secretly reports your activity. Not all tracking is bad; a cart cookie is useful. The ethical question is whether users know, agree and can control it.

Intellectual property: Intellectual property, or IP, is intangible property created by individuals or organizations, such as software, music, books, designs and inventions. It is protected in several ways. Copyright protects the expression of an idea, such as the actual code you wrote, a song or a book, for a long period, but not the idea itself. A patent gives the inventor exclusive rights to an invention for a limited time, typically 20 years, in return for publicly disclosing how it works; it must be new, useful and not obvious. A trademark protects names, logos and symbols that identify a brand. A trade secret is valuable business information kept confidential, such as a recipe or a formula, protected as long as it stays secret, often through contracts like non-disclosure agreements.

Challenges to IP in the digital world: Digital copies are perfect and nearly free. Software, movies, textbooks and music can be shared in seconds. Software piracy, using or distributing software without a licence, is a serious issue in many countries, including in Bangladesh, where pirated copies of popular operating systems and office software have long been common. Piracy hurts developers, including local software firms, and pirated software often carries malware. Free and open-source software offers a legal alternative: its licences allow use, study and sharing under certain conditions, so a small business can use tools like LibreOffice or Linux legally at no licence cost.

Accountability, liability and system quality: Who is responsible when software fails? If a bank's system wrongly deducts money, the bank is accountable to its customer, even if a software vendor made the bug. Software makers often limit their liability through licence terms, but organizations that deploy systems remain responsible to the people they serve. System quality is also an ethical issue: no software is perfectly bug-free, and data has errors. The question is what level of quality is acceptable. Common causes of problems are software bugs, hardware or facility failures, and, most often, poor input data quality.

Quality of life: Information systems also affect society in broad ways. They blur the boundary between work and home, as office messages arrive at midnight. They can make organizations dependent on systems that, if they fail, stop everything. They can replace jobs through automation, while creating new kinds of jobs. They enable computer crime and abuse such as spam and online harassment. And they raise health issues, such as eye strain and repetitive stress injuries from long hours at screens. The digital divide is another concern: unequal access to technology and digital skills between rich and poor, urban and rural, men and women. In Bangladesh, mobile phones have spread widely, but differences in smartphone ownership, internet cost and digital literacy still leave many people behind.

The Bangladesh legal picture: Bangladesh has laws covering cyber offences and digital information, starting with the Information and Communication Technology Act of 2006, and later cyber security laws that have been revised and replaced more than once in recent years. Copyright is protected by national copyright law. Work on a dedicated personal data protection law has also been going on. Because these laws change, a professional should always check the current version rather than rely on old notes. The bigger lesson for exams and work is the principle: collect only the data you need, tell people what you do with it, protect it, and respect other people's creations.

Real life example 1, a mobile wallet and customer data: A mobile financial service holds very sensitive data: national ID details, phone numbers, transaction history and location of agents used. Ethically, it should collect only what regulation and service require, protect it with strong security, use it for fraud detection and service, and not sell transaction histories to advertisers. If it wants to use data for marketing new products, it should be transparent and give customers a real choice. Staff access should be limited and logged, so that an employee cannot look up a celebrity's or an ex-friend's transactions out of curiosity.

Real life example 2, a software firm and IP: A small Dhaka software company builds an inventory app for a client. Questions immediately arise: who owns the code, the firm or the client? That must be written in the contract. Can a developer who leaves take the code to a new job? Not if it is the employer's property and protected as a trade secret or by copyright. Can the team copy a code snippet from the internet? Only if its licence allows it, and some open-source licences require you to share your changes too. Respecting IP here is both ethical and good business.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse copyright and patent: copyright protects the expression, like the code text, while a patent protects the invention or method itself. Another mistake is thinking privacy only means secrecy; it also means control over how your data is used. And do not say something is ethical just because it is legal. Typical exam questions: define ethics and explain why IS raises new ethical issues; list the five moral dimensions; explain the five-step ethical analysis and ethical principles; explain fair information practices and opt-in versus opt-out; compare copyright, patent, trademark and trade secret; and discuss the digital divide.

Recap: Ethics is about right and wrong choices, beyond what the law requires. Cheap computing, storage, analytics and networks make it easy to collect and combine data, raising issues in five moral dimensions: information rights, property rights, accountability, system quality and quality of life. Managers can use a five-step analysis and principles like the Golden Rule, Kant's imperative, the utilitarian and risk aversion rules. Privacy rests on fair information practices, and opt-in protects people better than opt-out. Intellectual property is protected by copyright, patents, trademarks and trade secrets, and piracy is a real challenge. Responsible organizations collect less, explain more, protect well and accept accountability.
key_points: Ethics is about right and wrong choices beyond what the law forces; IS makes collecting, combining and spreading data cheap, raising new ethical issues.
Five moral dimensions: information rights, property rights, accountability and control, system quality, and quality of life.
Responsibility, accountability, liability and due process decide who answers for harm caused by systems; people, not technology, make the choices.
A five-step ethical analysis and principles like the Golden Rule, Kant's imperative, utilitarian and risk aversion help managers decide.
Fair information practices: notice, choice or consent, access, security and enforcement; GDPR is a strong law built on such ideas.
Opt-in requires active consent and protects privacy better than opt-out, because most users keep defaults.
Copyright protects expression, patents protect inventions, trademarks protect brand marks, trade secrets protect confidential know-how.
The digital divide and piracy are real concerns in Bangladesh; always check the current version of local cyber and data laws.
lessons.tip: For each ethics question, write the stakeholders first: who gains, who could be hurt, who has no voice. Most ethics answers in MIS exams become easy once the stakeholders are clear.
lessons.task: Open the settings of one app on your phone and list every permission it has (location, contacts, camera, SMS and so on). For each, write whether the app truly needs it to work, and turn off one it does not need. Then note whether the app used opt-in or opt-out for marketing messages.

quiz.q: Which of these protects the actual code a programmer wrote, but not the underlying idea?
quiz.explain: Copyright protects the expression of an idea, such as the code text, not the idea itself.

quiz.q: An app uses your contacts for marketing unless you find and untick a box. This is:
quiz.explain: In opt-out, data is used by default until the user acts to stop it.

quiz.q: Which principle says that if an action is not right for everyone to take, it is not right for anyone?
quiz.explain: Kant's categorical imperative tests whether an action could be a rule for everyone.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the fair information practices?
quiz.explain: Fair information practices ask for notice, choice, access, security and enforcement; they push towards collecting only what is needed.

quiz.q: A bank's system wrongly deducts money because of a vendor's bug. Who is accountable to the customer?
options: Nobody, because software can have bugs
Only the programmer who wrote the line
The customer, for using the system
The bank, which deployed the system and serves the customer
quiz.explain: The organization that deploys a system remains responsible to the people it serves, even if a vendor caused the bug.

lessons.title: Security and Controls I: Threats to Information Systems
lessons.content:
Your phone buzzes with an SMS: Dear customer, your wallet account will be blocked today. To keep it active, tell us the code we just sent you. A minute later someone calls, sounding polite and official, asking for that same code. If you share it, your balance may be gone in seconds. Nobody had to break any encryption or hack any server. They only had to trick one person. This is the real face of information security: systems are attacked through machines, networks and, very often, people.

What security means: Security is the set of policies, procedures and technical measures used to prevent unauthorized access, alteration, theft or physical damage to information systems. Controls are the methods, policies and organizational procedures that ensure the safety of an organization's assets, the accuracy and reliability of its records, and that operations follow management's standards. Security is about stopping bad things; controls are about making sure things are done correctly. This lesson is about threats, what can go wrong. The next lesson covers the management framework, how organizations defend themselves.

The CIA triad: A simple way to think about what we protect is the CIA triad. Confidentiality means only authorized people can see the data; a customer's account balance should not be visible to strangers. Integrity means data is accurate and not changed without permission; nobody should be able to edit a transaction amount. Availability means systems and data are there when needed; a bank app that is down on salary day fails its users even if no data is stolen. Every threat in this lesson attacks one or more of these three.

Why systems are vulnerable: When data is stored electronically and connected to networks, it can be reached from many more places than paper in a locked cabinet. A typical system has many weak points. At the client side, users may install bad software or lose devices. On the communication lines, data can be tapped or altered, especially on open Wi-Fi. At the servers, hackers may exploit software bugs. In the databases, data can be copied or deleted. Hardware can fail, power can cut out, and disasters like fire or flood can destroy equipment. Software has bugs, and some bugs are security holes. And people make mistakes or act dishonestly.

Internet and wireless risks: The internet is open by design, so a server connected to it can be reached by anyone in the world. Systems that stay connected all the time with fixed addresses are easier targets. Wireless networks add more risk: signals travel through walls, so someone in the next room or outside a shop can try to join a poorly protected Wi-Fi network. A free cafe Wi-Fi without encryption lets an attacker nearby watch traffic that is not otherwise encrypted. This is why apps that move money must encrypt everything end to end.

Malware, the main families: Malicious software, or malware, is any software designed to harm. A virus attaches itself to other programs or files and spreads when they are run or shared, often by USB drives or email attachments. A worm is an independent program that copies itself from one computer to another over a network without needing a user to run anything, so it can spread very fast. A Trojan horse looks harmless or useful, like a free game or a cracked software, but carries hidden harmful code. Spyware secretly watches what you do; a keylogger, one kind of spyware, records every key you press to steal passwords and card numbers.

Ransomware and bots: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files or locks the system and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, to unlock them. Hospitals, companies and city offices around the world have been hit, and the damage is not just the ransom but days of stopped work. A botnet is a large group of infected computers, called bots or zombies, secretly controlled by an attacker. Owners usually do not know their computer is part of it. Botnets are used to send spam, steal data and launch attacks on other systems. Mobile malware is also growing, often hidden in fake apps outside official app stores.

Hackers and cybercrime: A hacker, in everyday use, is someone who gains unauthorized access to a computer system; some people use the word cracker for the criminal kind and keep hacker for skilled programmers in general. Hacking includes system intrusion, damaging websites (cybervandalism), and stealing data. Spoofing means pretending to be someone else, for example faking an email sender address or creating a fake website that looks exactly like a bank's site. Sniffing means using a program that monitors data travelling over a network, which can capture unencrypted passwords. Computer crime is any violation of law that involves computers, either as the target, such as breaking into a server, or as the tool, such as using email to cheat people.

Denial of service: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack floods a server or network with so many fake requests that real users cannot get through. Nothing is stolen; availability is the target. In a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, thousands of machines, often a botnet, send the requests at once, which makes it much harder to block. A small worked example: if a website can handle 2,000 requests per second and a botnet of 10,000 bots each sends 5 requests per second, that is 50,000 requests per second, 25 times its capacity. Real customers simply see a page that never loads. For an e-commerce site during a big sale, even an hour of downtime means lost sales and angry customers.

Identity theft and phishing: Identity theft is a crime in which someone obtains key pieces of personal information, such as national ID number, account number, card details or passwords, in order to pretend to be someone else, usually to get money or loans. Phishing is a common way to steal such information: the attacker sends emails or messages that look like they come from a real bank, wallet or company and asks the victim to click a link, enter details or share a code. Spear phishing targets specific people with personalised messages. Evil twins are fake Wi-Fi networks with legitimate-sounding names, set up to capture data from people who connect. Pharming redirects users to a fake website even when they type the correct address.

Social engineering: Social engineering means tricking people into revealing confidential information or doing something harmful, by exploiting trust, fear, urgency or helpfulness rather than technical tricks. Common patterns: pretending to be from the IT department and asking for a password to fix a problem; pretending to be a senior manager urgently asking an accountant to transfer money; or a caller saying a relative is in trouble and money is needed now. The common ingredient is pressure: act now, do not tell anyone, it is urgent. Training people to pause and verify through a separate channel is one of the strongest defences.

Insider threats: Not all threats come from outside. Employees know the systems and often have legitimate access. Some cause harm by mistake: entering wrong data, sending a file to the wrong person, using weak passwords, or plugging an infected USB drive into an office computer. A few act dishonestly: copying customer lists before leaving for a rival, changing records to hide theft, or helping outsiders. Studies of security incidents regularly find that a large share involve some human error or insider action. This is why organizations limit each employee's access to what their job needs and keep logs of who did what.

Software vulnerabilities: Software bugs are a constant source of risk. A vulnerability is a weakness that an attacker can exploit, often in widely used software like operating systems, browsers or databases. Vendors release patches, small updates that fix these holes, but organizations often delay installing them because updates might break other systems or because no one is responsible. Attackers know this and scan the internet for unpatched machines. A zero-day vulnerability is one that attackers find and use before the vendor knows about it or has a fix. Pirated software is especially risky because it cannot be updated properly and may already contain malware.

The business value of security: Why should managers spend on security when it does not directly earn money? First, the cost of a breach can be huge: stolen money, system downtime, investigation and recovery costs, legal penalties and, most painfully, lost customer trust. Second, laws and regulators, such as central banks for financial firms, require certain controls and can punish firms that fail. Third, good security and controls create evidence that can be used in investigations and in court, which is the field of computer forensics. Fourth, customers choose services they trust, especially for money. Security is part of the product, not an optional extra.

Real life example 1, mobile wallet fraud: In Bangladesh, fraudsters have widely used calls and SMS that pretend to be from a mobile wallet company, a bank or a prize lottery, and ask for the one-time password or PIN. Some claim money was sent by mistake and ask the user to send it back. Others pretend an account will be blocked. The wallet's own systems may be secure, but the attack goes around them through the customer. This is why providers repeatedly announce that they will never ask for your PIN or OTP, and why the right response is to hang up and call the official helpline yourself.

Real life example 2, the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist: In February 2016, attackers who had gained access to Bangladesh Bank's systems sent fraudulent payment orders through the SWIFT interbank messaging network to the bank's account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Most of the orders were blocked, but about 81 million dollars was transferred to accounts in the Philippines, and much of it was never recovered. The case is studied worldwide because it showed that strong international systems can be abused if the local computers and procedures that connect to them are weak. It pushed banks everywhere to tighten controls around payment systems.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up viruses and worms: a virus needs a host file and some user action to spread, while a worm spreads on its own over networks. Another confusion is between phishing (tricking users into giving information through fake messages or sites) and spoofing (pretending to be someone or something else, which phishing often uses). Do not forget insiders and plain human error in answers. Typical exam questions: explain why information systems are vulnerable; define and compare virus, worm, Trojan, spyware and ransomware; explain DoS and DDoS; define identity theft, phishing, evil twins and pharming; discuss social engineering and insider threats; and explain the business value of security and control.

Recap: Security protects systems from unauthorized access, change, theft and damage, while controls keep records accurate and operations correct. Threats attack confidentiality, integrity or availability. Systems are vulnerable at clients, networks, servers, databases and hardware, and the internet and Wi-Fi widen exposure. Malware includes viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, keyloggers and ransomware, often spread by botnets. Attackers use hacking, spoofing, sniffing, DoS and DDoS, phishing, pharming, evil twins and social engineering, and insiders and unpatched software add more risk. Spending on security protects money, trust and legal standing, so it is a core business investment.
key_points: Security protects systems from unauthorized access, change, theft and damage; controls keep records accurate and operations following standards.
The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability are what attackers target.
Systems are vulnerable at clients, communication lines, servers, databases and hardware; the internet and Wi-Fi widen exposure.
Malware: virus needs a host and user action, worm spreads alone over networks, Trojan hides inside harmless-looking software, spyware and keyloggers watch you, ransomware locks data for money.
DoS floods a system to stop real users; DDoS uses many machines, often a botnet.
Identity theft is often done through phishing, spear phishing, evil twins and pharming.
Social engineering and insider mistakes or dishonesty are among the biggest real risks; unpatched and pirated software add more.
Security has business value: it protects money, trust, legal compliance and evidence for forensics.
lessons.tip: Make a two-column list: threat name and which part of CIA it attacks. Doing this for every threat in the lesson fixes the definitions in your head and gives you a ready structure for long exam answers.
lessons.task: Look through your SMS and email from the last month and find any message that might be phishing or social engineering. For each one, note the trick it used (urgency, fear, prize, fake sender) and how you could verify it safely. If you find none, write a realistic fake one yourself and mark its warning signs.

quiz.q: Which malware spreads by itself across a network without a user running anything?
quiz.explain: A worm is an independent program that copies itself over networks; a virus needs a host file and user action.

quiz.q: A shopping site goes offline because 10,000 infected computers send it fake requests at once. This is:
quiz.explain: Many machines flooding a server to block real users is a distributed denial-of-service attack.

quiz.q: A DoS attack mainly targets which part of the CIA triad?
quiz.explain: DoS stops real users from reaching the system, so it attacks availability.

quiz.q: A caller pretends to be from a wallet company and asks for your OTP to stop your account being blocked. This is best described as:
quiz.explain: It tricks a person using fear and urgency instead of technical hacking: social engineering.

quiz.q: What is an evil twin?
options: A fake Wi-Fi network with a trustworthy name set up to capture data
quiz.explain: Evil twins are rogue wireless networks that look legitimate so victims connect and leak data.

lessons.title: Security and Controls II: Building the Defences
lessons.content:
Think about how a family protects its home in Dhaka. There is a gate with a lock, a guard downstairs who checks visitors, grills on the windows, a cupboard key kept by one person, gold kept in a bank locker, and photocopies of important documents kept with a relative in case of fire. Nobody relies on just one lock. Each layer stops a different danger, and the most valuable things get the strongest protection. Protecting an organization's information works exactly the same way. This lesson is about those layers and how managers decide where to put them.

From threats to a framework: In the previous lesson we listed the threats: malware, hacking, phishing, DoS, insiders, bugs and disasters. Buying an antivirus or a firewall is not enough. Organizations need a framework: a planned way to find their risks, decide what to protect first, set rules, apply technical tools, and check regularly that everything works. Security is mostly a management problem that uses technology, not a technology problem alone.

Information systems controls: Controls come in two broad types. General controls govern the design, security and use of computer programs and the security of data files across the whole organization. Application controls are specific to each individual application, such as payroll or order processing, and make sure only authorized data is completely and accurately processed. General controls are the foundation; application controls sit on top of them for each system.

General controls in detail: Software controls monitor the use of system software and prevent unauthorized access to programs. Hardware controls ensure equipment is physically secure and checked for faults, for example servers in a locked room with backup power. Computer operations controls cover the work of the IT department, such as how jobs are run and how backups are done. Data security controls protect data files on disk or tape from unauthorized access, change or destruction. Implementation controls audit the system development process to make sure it is properly managed. Administrative controls are formal standards, rules and procedures, including segregation of duties, which means splitting a job so that no single person can complete a risky transaction alone. For example, the person who creates a new supplier in the system should not be the same person who approves payments to suppliers.

Application controls in detail: Input controls check data for accuracy and completeness when it enters the system, for example rejecting a date of 31 February, or a check digit on an account number that catches typing mistakes. Processing controls make sure data is complete and accurate during updating, for example comparing the total of all transactions processed with a control total counted separately. Output controls ensure that the results are accurate, complete and properly distributed, for example making sure salary slips reach only the right employee. A tiny worked example: a clerk enters 100 vouchers with a batch total of 2,45,000 taka. After processing, the system reports a total of 2,40,000. The 5,000 difference immediately shows that a voucher was missed or mistyped.

Risk assessment: An organization cannot protect everything equally, so it starts with risk assessment: identifying assets, the threats to them, how likely each threat is, and the potential loss if it happens. A common simple formula is expected annual loss = probability of occurrence in a year times loss per occurrence. Worked example for a small e-commerce firm: power failure has a 30 percent chance per year and would cost 1,00,000 taka, expected loss 30,000. A ransomware attack has a 5 percent chance but would cost 20,00,000 taka, expected loss 1,00,000. Staff data entry errors happen almost surely, say 100 percent, costing 20,000 taka a year, expected loss 20,000. Even though ransomware is the least likely, it has the highest expected loss, so it deserves the most attention, such as good backups. Risk assessment turns vague fear into a priority list.

Security policy: A security policy is a set of statements ranking information risks, identifying acceptable security goals and identifying how to achieve them. It answers: what are our most important information assets, who creates and controls them, what policies protect them, and what level of risk will management accept? An acceptable use policy (AUP) defines what employees may and may not do with the firm's computers and networks: for example, no installing personal software, no sharing passwords, no using office email for private business.
